members.title: Advancing computer use with Ironclad - OpenAI

representative.headline: Advancing computer use with Ironclad - OpenAI
representative.body: Advancing computer use with Ironclad    OpenAI

articles.headline: Advancing computer use with Ironclad - OpenAI
articles.body: Advancing computer use with Ironclad    OpenAI

scored.body: When we introduced GPT‑6 Astra, we demonstrated how far our models have come in using computers for professional work, from preparing documents to testing websites. Our next goal is to make agents more capable and efficient at using specialized software to solve complex business problems. We’re exploring how to train models to understand a company’s business rules, execute multi-step workflows, and verify that their work meets the original requirements.To accelerate this research, we’re partnering directly with a small number of software companies that understand these workflows best. Together, we’re identifying challenging, high-value tasks and turning them into research problems for training and evaluating our models, ultimately making our models more capable and useful in real-world business applications.Our first partner is Ironclad, a leader in AI contracting. Working closely with Ironclad’s team, we’ve developed tasks that require agents to configure agreements, approvals, and reusable legal terms, and demonstrated progress on these complex workflows. Ironclad’s expertise has been instrumental in defining what success looks like and bringing real customer needs directly into frontier model development. We’re grateful for their partnership and excited to share what we’ve accomplished together.GPT‑6 Astra is our first frontier model trained on Ironclad tasks. On our research evaluation, its average score was 32% higher than GPT‑5.6 Sol’s, while estimated time per attempt was 48% lower.1Turning contracting workflows into training tasksConsider a legal operations team setting up a process for buying software. Finance may need to approve purchases above a certain amount, Security may need to review certain requests, and Legal may need to review nonstandard terms. The person setting up the process has to turn that short list into an intake form, document templates, approval rules, and a record of the final agreement.An AI agent doing the same work has to keep those requirements in view as it moves through the software. For example, it must configure Finance approval above the spending threshold and check that requests above and below it follow the right paths. Getting individual steps right is not enough: the finished process must work across the situations it was designed to handle.Ironclad employees and people who use Ironclad at OpenAI helped our researchers identify 11 tasks across legal, commercial, and procurement work. These included tasks like setting up nondisclosure agreements, creating procurement approval processes, and updating a reusable legal clause so that it reflects the jurisdiction a requester selects. We estimate that this work would take an experienced user about 30 to 40 minutes per task, on average.We evaluated each task against 8 to 50 criteria, depending on its complexity. This let us see which parts a model got right and where it fell short. Ironclad also provided hosted software environments of their product where the models could practice these tasks. Our researchers developed synthetic training tasks2 around representative workflows and used reinforcement learning to help the models improve through practice and feedback. This combination—tasks selected with people who know the work, detailed criteria, and a place for models to practice—ensures we are improving on real-world tasks that are most important to our customers.How Astra performedWe compared Astra and GPT‑5.6 Sol using Max reasoning for Astra and High reasoning for Sol, the settings where each model scored highest. Across the 11 research tasks, Astra’s average score was 55.0%, compared with 41.6% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while estimated average time per attempt fell from 37.0 minutes for Sol to 19.2 minutes for Astra.3 An internal model used in the development of Astra achieved an even stronger 63.7% on these tasks, and we aim to bring these further gains to future models.Astra met more of the task requirements with less simulated time per attempt. The two clips below show how the models handled the same research task. Astra (first) met about 94% of the task criteria in an estimated 20 minutes; GPT‑5.6 Sol (second) met about 85% in an estimated 32 minutes.GPT‑6 Astra met about 94% of the task criteria in an estimated 20 minutes.GPT‑5.6 Sol met about 85% of the task criteria in an estimated 32 minutes.What this collaboration means for IroncladIronclad’s role in this work reflects a challenge its customers know well: a contracting process must handle exceptions while preserving the rules a business depends on. If an agent loses track of one of those rules halfway through a task, that limits what a software company can confidently ask it to do. This underscores why human oversight still matters as agents get better at complex contracting tasks, and why a full contracting platform remains essential. Working with our researchers gives Ironclad a way to bring these problems into the development of the underlying model, where we can study them together.As models become more capable, Ironclad has an opportunity to use them in more of its own products. For legal and business teams, that could mean AI taking on more of the effort involved in complex contracting while preserving the controls those teams rely on.Work with us to advance AI for complex professional workWe’re inviting a small number of software companies to work directly with our research and engineering teams on important professional tasks that today’s agents still can’t reliably complete. If your team has one, we’d like to see a concrete example: what you’re asking the agent to do, evidence of where it fails, and how you would judge a successful result. Partners should also be able to bring people who know the work deeply, a secure environment for testing, and data that can be safely used for research. This gives us a starting point for investigating the failure and measuring whether the model improves.

members.title: OpenAI and Anthropic execs donate millions to political causes. One billionaire stands apart - San Francisco Chronicle

representative.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic execs donate millions to political causes. One billionaire stands apart - San Francisco Chronicle
representative.body: OpenAI and Anthropic execs donate millions to political causes. One billionaire stands apart    San Francisco Chronicle

articles.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic execs donate millions to political causes. One billionaire stands apart - San Francisco Chronicle
articles.body: OpenAI and Anthropic execs donate millions to political causes. One billionaire stands apart    San Francisco Chronicle

scored.body:
From left, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. These, and other, executives of San Francisco’s top AI companies have been making political donations.Godofredo A. Vásquez, Markus Schreiber and Aurelien Morissard/APGreg Brockman, president of OpenAI, and his wife Anna have given far more to political causes than the combined donations of other top executives of the research lab and its rival Anthropic.The Brockmans gave a total of $25 million to the President Donald Trump-aligned political action committee Maga Inc. and became two of the group’s largest donors. The couple also gave a total of $25 million to the artificial intelligence advocacy group Leading the Future PAC, last year.Article continues below this adTo see where AI companies are getting involved in politics, the Chronicle looked at donations from OpenAI and Anthropic and their high-level executives to federal, state and local races for the 2025-2026 election cycle.In contrast, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman gave just $31,100 across eight donations, according to a Chronicle analysis. The largest was $7,000 to Senator Mark Warner, D-Virginia. Warner is the top Democrat on the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and a key figure calling for AI regulation. Altman’s total donations were split between the two major parties, with $17,100 going to Democrats and $14,000 going to Republicans.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei donated $1 million in May to Public First Action, a PAC focused on promoting AI safety regulations, consistent with his calls for slowing down development and more safeguards.Article continues below this adThe AI growth frenzy has ushered in a new wave of San Francisco wealth and rising political influence, particularly amid uncertainty around the direction of federal AI regulations and fears of an AI doomsday scenario. The industry has also used tax breaks and needs government support as it spends tens of billions of dollars building out data centers across the nation. Though the tech industry’s giving has historically favored Democrats, more tech leaders like Brockman have supported Trump since he returned to office, though overall, more Bay Area tech workers still support Democrats.Brockman had planned to give another $25 million to Leading the Future but cancelled the donation, the New York Times reported last week. Brockman said in a Slack message that he felt “terrible” about the “distraction” that last year’s donations caused, according to the Times.OpenAI said in June that it hasn’t made any donations to PACs and hasn’t donated to political candidates or campaigns. Employees such as Brockman are “free to participate in the political process,” the company said, but added that “OpenAI does not direct the activities of LTF, or have visibility into their operations … . No outside political group speaks for OpenAI or represents our company’s views.”Brockman posted on X at the end of 2025 that his political donations were “reflecting support for policies that advance American innovation and constructive dialogue between government and the technology sector. These views are grounded in a belief that the United States must work closely with builders, researchers, and entrepreneurs to ensure AI is developed responsibly at home and that we remain globally competitive.”He testified in federal court in May that his stake in OpenAI was worth nearly $30 billion. That translates to owning over 3% of the company, which was valued at $852 billion in March and is now reportedly in talks for a fundraising round with a valuation around $1.4 trillion. Altman does not hold equity in the company but previously became wealthy through founding startup Loopt, which was sold for $43 million, and earlier tech investments including Airbnb and Uber.Article continues below this adOn a state level, OpenAI funneled $10 million to the Parents & Kids Safe AI Coalition, a PAC aimed at the California Legislature to pass legislation for AI child-safety regulations. Anthropic has spent money on state level races too, donating $850,000 to the California Democratic Party and over $100,000 to other Democratic candidates running for state Senate and Assembly.In San Francisco, OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies have each donated $500,000 to support a November ballot measure that would extend a San Francisco affordable housing funding program.In 2023, Altman also gave $3,300 to the congressional campaign of state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco.Article continues below this adAnthropic’s PAC gave $156,000 across 44 donations, with $98,000, or nearly two thirds of donations, going to Republicans and $58,000 going to Democrats.Anthropic leader Amodei reportedly referenced Brockman’s donations to Maga Inc. in a company memo in March, when the company was clashing with the Pentagon around removing safety guardrails amid the Iran war, according to the Information.“The real reasons DoW (Department of War) and the Trump admin do not like us is that we haven’t donated to Trump (while OpenAI/Greg have donated a lot), we haven’t given dictator-style praise to Trump (while Sam has), we have supported AI regulation which is against their agenda, we’ve told the truth about a number of AI policy issues (like job displacement), and we’ve actually held our red lines with integrity rather than colluding with them to produce ‘safety theater’ for the benefit of employees,” Amodei reportedly wrote.Oct 5, 2026Data and graphics reporterWho they are

Hanna Zakharenko creates data-driven interactives for the Chronicle. She joined the newspaper in 2025 after completing a fellowship with Hearst Newspapers’ DevHub. Previously, Zakharenko worked at the Washington Post, contributing to investigations and coverage of business, politics and entertainment. Her work has been recognized by several national and local awards. She is a graduate of the University of Maryland, where she studied journalism and information science.

How to reach Hanna

To provide story tips or feedback, email hanna.zakharenko@sfchronicle.com.Business ReporterRoland Li covers the Bay Area economy — a wide-ranging beat encompassing both small businesses and tech behemoths. He writes about offices, housing, hotels, stores and the workers, entrepreneurs, residents and tourists that fill them. He is the author of “Good Luck Have Fun: The Rise of eSports,” a 2016 book on the history of the competitive video game industry — a sector that was key to the rise of AI. He was previously a reporter at San Francisco Business Times, where he won awards from the California News Publishers Association and National Association of Real Estate Editors. Before moving to the Bay Area in 2015, he studied and reported in New York.

How to reach Roland

Email roland.li@sfchronicle.com.

members.title: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC

representative.headline: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC
representative.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

articles.headline: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC
articles.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

scored.body: CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive."I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential, questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next. Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list.Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity. For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology. "You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."How DeepMind corporate teams use AI every dayIbrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:How are you using AI? What would help you use it more? Where are you not using AI? That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said. With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce. "They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens.""One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

members.title: OpenAI’s Human Rights Lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’ - Fortune

representative.headline: OpenAI’s Human Rights Lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’ - Fortune
representative.body: OpenAI’s Human Rights Lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’    Fortune

articles.headline: OpenAI’s Human Rights Lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’ - Fortune
articles.body: OpenAI’s Human Rights Lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’    Fortune

scored.body:
In June, Sarah Yager took an unusual role at OpenAI, becoming the company’s first Human Rights and Responsible Deployment Lead. She’s focused on military applications, given her 30 years of experience in this area and OpenAI’s partnership with the Department of War (DoW).

Yager spoke about her role on stage Tuesday at the ScaleUp:AI conference in New York City, where she mentioned her concerns with military institutions adopting AI, particularly in armed conflict.

“Everyone is very worried and rightly so,” Yager said. “This keeps me up at night: ‘What is the military going to do with AI when it comes to targeting? And what about autonomous weapons? And where is all of this going?'”

Militaries throughout the world are rapidly incorporating AI into their operations as they develop new weapons and autonomous systems like drones and robots.

Yager now has a chance to grapple with the difficult questions this poses from inside one of the most powerful AI companies in the world. “I have always wanted to go into places and persuade people where human rights was not necessarily the dominant idea,” Yager said. “With apologies to my OpenAI colleagues, I am now in the belly of the beast, and it’s actually a very comfortable place for me to be because what I love to do is persuade and discuss and debate and hopefully move the needle.”

OpenAI approached Yager for the job shortly after the company signed a contract with the DoW in late February to deploy advanced AI systems in classified environment, a high-profile deal that followed a public falling out between the DoW and Anthropic. Anthropic wanted to put guardrails around how the military could use its technology, specifically banning mass public surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, which the DoW would not agree to. The DoW then labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk, while OpenAI swooped in and took the contract, claiming it was successful in getting the DoW to agree to similar guardrails.

The idea of working at OpenAI was not “an immediate yes” for Yager, she said, due to suspicions that the company might be hiring her as a “branding exercise,” as the on-stage interviewer put it, implying she could make the company look responsible—a figurehead without actual influence over the technology. But Yager did her “due diligence” in talking with employees, particularly “the younger generation who are very worried about what they are creating and who’s at the wheel,” and felt compelled to join to see if she could make a difference.

Since joining, she’s had some success influencing the direction of the technology, and also some concerns about where it’s going. The use of AI in military applications has proven tricky, with the U.S. military nearly targeting a Chinese military ship based on an inaccurate, AI-generated intelligence report, CNN reported last month.

Yager has been able to work directly with researchers and engineers to improve the models, such as making sure they have appropriate responses to basic international agreements, including the laws of war, established in 1949 at the post-World War II Geneva Conventions. She brought in international experts “to literally sit at keyboards and put in prompts for really high stakes engagements,” and had engineers tweak the models based on the response. “That had never been done before, so that was extremely gratifying,” said Yager.

She thinks AI companies are trying to “reinvent the wheel” on questions such as defining humanity and morality. “Societies have already figured out a lot of those things, and it’s called human rights. That should be the baseline,” she said, referring to the Geneva Conventions agreements. “I do not want an AI company telling me what is good. If we allow the industry to determine what is good, then it’s a free for all.”

Yager also implied she was a bit put off by the debate within Silicon Valley around whether AIs, and particularly the new agent technologies, should have rights. This is something OpenAI asked her during her interview process. She said “no” at the time, and reiterated she was focused on human rights, but she has since thought more about the question. Now, she feels more open to the “extremely important” conversations about “where agents fit into the legal structures, the labor structures, the tax structures,” but notes that these questions are not a matter of rights.

“This is not at all comparable to human rights, and I would really love if we could just get back to the human of human rights,” she said. The crowd—mostly suited businessmen—began to clap. “Big round of applause for that,” said the on-stage interviewer.

Another one of her concerns is the relatively insular demographic groups building AI. For example, last week President Trump gathered dozens of tech industry leaders in Washington to discuss AI safety. All the signatories of the voluntary safety accord were men, and as photos of the broader group present at a lunch event reveal, all of the attendees were men (save for AMD CEO Lisa Su).

“Men are awesome, but it was a very male photograph of who is going to be making the choices about AI,” Yager said. “One problem with that is that AI is fundamentally shifting the power balance between people all over the world, you did not see affected communities up there.”

Yager noted the government is rapidly adopting AI. she’s helping oversight bodies, such as the Government Accountability Office and the Inspector General, build tools to keep tabs on what it’s doing. That accountability mechanism “feels important for democracy,” she said.

articles.headline: Anthropic Is Aiming for the Biggest IPO Ever -- Here's the Chip Stock to Buy Before It Lists - The Motley Fool
articles.body: Anthropic Is Aiming for the Biggest IPO Ever -- Here's the Chip Stock to Buy Before It Lists    The Motley Fool

scored.body:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June. Now the artificial intelligence (AI) lab's reportedly aiming to raise up to $100 billion when it lists. This would beat the $86 billion SpaceX raised in June in the biggest IPO ever.Most investors can't buy Anthropic stock yet. But one public company's closely linked to the AI lab's spending. On Oct. 1, Reuters reported that Anthropic's IPO filing says Broadcom (AVGO +3.67%) has agreed to loan Anthropic up to $42 billion using convertible notes. This could cover about a third of a $125.2 billion, five-year commitment Anthropic has made to lease computing capacity on tensor processing units (TPUs), custom AI chips Broadcom helps design.Broadcom stock trades around $355 as of this writing, off about 28% from its 52-week high. At that price, I think the chipmaker is worth a close look before Anthropic lists.

Image source: Getty Images.

How much of Anthropic's spending goes to Broadcom?The $125.2 billion isn't Broadcom revenue, though. It's a lease commitment paid over five years. Broadcom's own quarterly filing describes a financial partner buying the AI racks built around its chips and leasing them to the customer.What Broadcom has said about Anthropic is arguably more helpful. On the company's earnings call on Sept. 2, CEO Hock Tan said Anthropic is deploying 1 gigawatt of TPU capacity this year. He expects another 5 gigawatts in 2027 and sees a path to an extra 10 gigawatts in 2028."Anthropic is on track to become our largest XPU customer in 2027 and sustain that in 2028," Tan said on the call.XPU is Broadcom's name for the custom AI chips it makes, and Tan said it has just six XPU customers.Accelerating AI salesShowing how fast this business is moving, Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue climbed 221% year over year to $16.7 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2026, which ended Aug. 2. That growth rate is also accelerating. It beat the 143% pace Broadcom posted in fiscal Q2, which itself topped fiscal Q1's 106%. Management sees fiscal fourth-quarter AI revenue of $21.7 billion, up 236%.Profits are keeping pace. Broadcom's fiscal third-quarter earnings per share under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) grew 215% year over year, and free cash flow climbed 95% to a record $13.7 billion.Anthropic shows up most in the longer-term forecast. Broadcom sees around $58 billion of AI revenue in fiscal 2026 and about $115 billion for fiscal 2027 -- the year Tan expects Anthropic to become Broadcom's largest custom-chip customer.Anthropic's spending, in other words, already shows up in Broadcom's numbers.Broadcom is financing its own customerOf course, Broadcom is taking real risk to land that business. The $42 billion is more than the $24 billion of cash it had at the end of fiscal Q3. It's also around three quarters' worth of free cash flow at that record rate.Broadcom might not carry all that alone, though. Bloomberg said on Oct. 2 that banks working for Broadcom have started raising around $60 billion in outside debt to fund AI chips for Anthropic and others.The notes appear in Broadcom's quarterly filing without naming the customer, and none had been issued as of Aug. 2. Broadcom also backstops lease payments on the $35 billion financing deal that Tan said covers Anthropic's first gigawatt, with a maximum potential liability of around $29 billion, the filing shows.Customer concentration is climbing, too. The company estimates its top five end customers made up around 55% of fiscal third-quarter revenue, up from about 40% the year before. And Anthropic's own filing flags "potential conflicts of interest" in Broadcom's role as both hardware supplier and financing partner, according to Reuters.The IPO might cut some of that risk, like Tan suggested on the call."[I]t's an open secret Anthropic is well on its way to an IPO. And with that, its investment credit will change," he said.Premium FeatureMoneyball Superscore91/100Today's Change(3.67%) $13.30Current Price$375.81A raise anywhere near $100 billion would be over double the $42 billion facility.Also, the notes could convert into Anthropic shares. But Anthropic reportedly said it doesn't expect any to be sold before its IPO, so buying Broadcom doesn't get you a piece of the listing.At around 36 times the past year's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings, Broadcom stock isn't cheap. But shares sell for about 18 times expected fiscal 2027 earnings, the year Broadcom's AI revenue is projected to double. Given how much money Anthropic's IPO could raise, I think that price is worth a look. I'd just buy gradually, since so much of the forecast depends on a few AI labs.

articles.headline: DOD Halts Use of Anthropic AI After Court Upholds Supply Chain Risk Designation - MeriTalk
articles.body: DOD Halts Use of Anthropic AI After Court Upholds Supply Chain Risk Designation    MeriTalk

scored.body:
The U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) has officially ceased all operational use of Anthropic products following a months-long standoff over safety guardrails.

“The Department of War has ceased the use of Anthropic products,” a department spokesperson told MeriTalk.

Under the Trump administration, the DOD was rebranded as the Department of War.

The move comes eight months after the Pentagon designated the artificial intelligence (AI) company a supply chain risk.

The dispute began with the Pentagon’s push to use Claude for “all lawful uses.” Anthropic objected to two applications: mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons.

After negotiations between Anthropic and the Pentagon broke down, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed the department to designate Anthropic a supply chain risk. Anthropic challenged the designation, arguing that the government had unlawfully retaliated against the company. The administration defended the action as a national security measure.

The months-long legal battle resulted in conflicting rulings, with one federal court siding with Anthropic and the D.C. Circuit upholding the Pentagon’s designation of the company as a supply chain risk.

On Sept. 25, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon’s designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk in a 2-1 decision, allowing the DOD to continue excluding Anthropic’s AI models from its systems and defense contract work. Earlier, on Aug. 27, U.S. District Judge Rita F. Lin in California sided with Anthropic in its challenge to broader federal restrictions stemming from the same dispute.

The two rulings leave Anthropic with a mixed legal outcome. The company prevailed in its California case challenging the administration’s broader restrictions but lost its challenge to the Pentagon’s supply chain risk designation in Washington.

As a result, the Pentagon can continue excluding Claude from its systems and defense contract work, while the California ruling remains in place. Anthropic could ask the full D.C. Circuit to reconsider the ruling or ask the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the case.

articles.body: Landlord moves to evict this AI unicorn to clear space for Anthropic    The San Francisco Standard

scored.body: Two of the richest AI companies want the same Mission warehouse to build and test their robots. But only one of them has a deal to be there. The other won’t move out, according to the landlord. Last week, the owners of a 98,000-square-foot property at 2000 Folsom St. sued Physical Intelligence in San Francisco Superior Court, alleging the robotics startup has refused to leave since its lease expired last month. The landlords want their space back, plus holdover damages of more than $13,000 a day. They say in the lawsuit that a new tenant wants to move in as early as this week. Sources have confirmed that the tenant is Anthropic.Physical Intelligence has not responded to the complaint, according to court records. Anthropic and Physical Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment. An attorney representing the landlords — a private office with an address in Salinas — did not respond to a request for comment. The warehouse at 2000 Folsom St. was a food manufacturing site that had been vacant until the recent AI robotics boom.The dispute stems from what was supposed to be a short stay. Physical Intelligence signed a lease in January for about 29,000 square feet on the ground floor at $60,000 a month, according to a copy of the document attached to the complaint. The lease ran from February to May, with an option for the tenant to roll over month to month.Per the agreement, Physical Intelligence used the premises for development and testing of robotics, in addition to general office use related to research. The property is zoned for production, distribution, and repair. In May, the landlord sent Physical Intelligence a termination notice, setting a move-out date in June. But rather than move, Physical Intelligence agreed to an amendment that nearly tripled its rent to $160,000 a month for an expanded footprint through September. The amendment eliminated the month-to-month option. In the June agreement, Physical Intelligence said it intended to relocate but sought to synchronize the departure of 2000 Folsom with the delivery of the new space. The Standard previously reported that the company has an agreement to lease 60,000 square feet at 808 Brannan St. The owners say their next tenant needs the building this week.A person seen entering the property on Oct. 6.Physical Intelligence, which is reportedly valued (opens in new tab) at more than $11 billion, is headquartered at 17th Street in the Mission. Last month, it reportedly reached a deal (opens in new tab) to lease a roughly 233,500-square-foot building in Mountain View. The complaint also alleges that Physical Intelligence “expanded its use of the building” to areas outside of the lease agreement without the landlord’s written consent and made physical “improvements” to the property without permission. Although the landlord agreed to waive that violation, it is seeking Physical Intelligence’s immediate departure.Physical Intelligence has raised more than $1 billion in capital. Its investors include Jeff Bezos, Khosla Ventures, Lux Capital, OpenAI, Redpoint Ventures, Sequoia Capital, CaptialG, and Thrive Capital according to its website. The owners of 2000 Folsom St. purchased the property in 1997, according to property records. The industrial building was previously owned by Earthgrains Baking Companies.More about the authorKevin V. Nguyen is a business reporter at The Standard. He previously covered commercial real estate at The Silicon Valley Business Journal and got his first journalism break at The Sacramento Bee.

articles.headline: OpenAI outlines updated safety measures in response to Australia Medicare portal breach - IAPP
articles.body: OpenAI outlines updated safety measures in response to Australia Medicare portal breach    IAPP

scored.body: OpenAI strengthened its security protocols as it looks to restore the confidence of Australian officials and consumers following the recent breach of Service Australia's Medicare portal by one of the company's rogue agents. The changes were outlined by OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon during an appearance with Anthropic before Australian Parliament's Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence 6 Oct."We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon told lawmakers.The appearance came after OpenAI and Anthropic declined to send executives to an Australian Senate hearing 1 Oct. because of short notice. That hearing was eventually canceled.Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese previously announced an investigation into the incident, noting that while the breach occurred 18 June, the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service was only informed of the incident via email 10 Sept.Responding specifically to lawmaker questions on the chosen means for incident notification, Kwon said, "on retrospect," it would have been more appropriate to report the incident directly to government officials."I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation, and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties," Kwon said, adding the internal communication about the breach "could have been much better."In the aftermath of the breach, Kwon said OpenAI has made changes to make data security incident reporting immediate while implementing an "immediate intervention" system if it finds its AI agents are capable of unauthorized actions.Regulatory conundrumAnthropic Special Envoy Jeffrey Bleich also appeared before the joint committee to highlight business challenges posed by Australia's applicable AI rules. He pushed back at the AI committee's concern over Anthropic's AI training and copyright practices, stating it would be "technically impossible" to obtain copyright agreements for all content used to train AI models.Lawmakers questioned if AI companies are receiving meaningful consent when implementing mechanisms requiring users to opt-out of data sharing for training purposes. In response, Bleich highlighted how Australia's regulations make it difficult for companies to develop AI models for the region."We've just shared information about how the training works, and then discussed what its implications would be with respect to our capacity to operate here," Bleich said.The dialogue highlighted the ongoing work being done by lawmakers and AI developers to find common ground on ensuring sufficient safeguards and oversight. Kwon told the committee OpenAI seeks to increase its regulatory collaborations, noting ongoing advancements show AI is "powerful" and "(OpenAI wants) to ensure that lawmakers and policymakers and democratic societies have a say in how this technology develops."During a recent IAPP LinkedIn Live, Australian Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind said while many AI companies are urging increased regulations, those calls raise concern that companies "don't know the extent to which they are regulated already.”"There's been a bit of a disregard of those existing frameworks and their relevance to some of these frontier issues,” she said. "Even though cybersecurity frameworks are absolutely right front and center relevant to what is happening at frontier firms, and yet I do think that not only the lexicon but the reality of how they apply has been potentially largely ignored."Unpacking Australia's new ADMT guideKind joined the IAPP LinkedIn Live to provide insights into the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner's recently released guidance for transparency requirements around automated decision-making technologies that will take effect 10 Dec.The guidelines detail additional obligations outlined within the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act under the Australian Privacy Principle 1. They apply to entities that use computer programs to make significant decisions that could impact consumers.Under the APPs, automated systems, including software, applications and AI tools, must remain transparent about how consumer data is processed for decision-making purposes. Organizations must also ensure automated systems are not making potentially biased or harmful decisions about consumers.Kind noted the obligations only apply to programs that are a “key factor in facilitating the human's decision-making, so that means it's substantially related to the decision, and has a direct connection with making the decision in order to be in scope."She highlighted how the new transparency requirements will be particularly important with informing users about AI training data use and more targeted AI and ADMT deployments, including those associated with dynamic pricing schemes."I think if we go back to the first principles about what privacy and data protection law is about, it's about providing people with choice and control and empowering them," Kind said. "And I think this transparency obligation will absolutely do that."The requirements are likely to impact the number of complaints the OAIC receives. The authority continues to see a rise in complaints after a 60% increase from 2024-25 to 2025-26.However, Kind said increased accountability and transparency could strengthen trust between consumers and organizations."It is a double-edged sword in many ways, and I don't want to be naive about that," Kind said. "But I think we have to move through this period of disillusionment with online services to something that is based more on trustworthiness and a stronger balance of accountability and transparency, and hopefully things like this can be the first step in that direction."Kind will be a keynote speaker for the IAPP ANZ Summit 2026.

members.title: Elon Musk’s xAI Wins Block of Minnesota’s AI ‘Nudification’ Ban - Law Commentary

representative.headline: Elon Musk’s xAI Wins Block of Minnesota’s AI ‘Nudification’ Ban - Law Commentary
representative.body: Elon Musk’s xAI Wins Block of Minnesota’s AI ‘Nudification’ Ban    Law Commentary

articles.headline: Elon Musk’s xAI Wins Block of Minnesota’s AI ‘Nudification’ Ban - Law Commentary
articles.body: Elon Musk’s xAI Wins Block of Minnesota’s AI ‘Nudification’ Ban    Law Commentary

scored.body:
by Bridget Luckey | Oct 06, 2026

Photo Source: Trevor Cokley, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI has won a temporary court order blocking Minnesota from enforcing its first-in-the-nation ban on AI tools that can generate realistic nude images of identifiable people, escalating a First Amendment fight over Grok and AI-generated sexual images.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted xAI an injunction pending appeal on October 2, 2026, preventing Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison from enforcing the challenged law against the company while the appeal moves forward. The one-sentence order gave no reasoning and left the constitutionality of the statute for later review.

The ruling gives xAI the relief U.S. District Judge Donovan W. Frank denied in September, when he allowed the law to remain enforceable against the company while its constitutional challenge continued.

xAI argues Minnesota went beyond targeting nonconsensual deepfake pornography by restricting technology capable of producing protected expression. The state says its law regulates a product function tied to digital sexual exploitation rather than speech protected by the First Amendment.

Minnesota’s law took effect August 1. It prohibits operators of websites, applications, software, and other services from allowing users to access technology that can “nudify” an image or video.

A generated or altered image falls within the law when technology adds or creates an intimate body part that was not shown in the original and produces a realistic result appearing to depict an identifiable person. The attorney general can seek civil penalties of up to $500,000 for each unlawful access, download, or use.

People depicted in prohibited images may also bring civil claims seeking damages, attorney fees, and court orders stopping the conduct.

The measure differs from laws that mainly punish people who create or distribute nonconsensual sexual deepfakes. Minnesota places responsibility directly on companies that provide automated tools capable of generating the images, making the law a broader test of how far states can go in regulating AI systems before harmful content is distributed.

xAI sued Ellison in July, arguing the statute reaches consensual images, privately created material, and artistic, political, educational, or satirical expression. The company says the law applies regardless of whether the person depicted consented and restricts expression based on its content.

That argument puts the dispute squarely under the First Amendment. xAI contends the law should face strict scrutiny, a demanding constitutional test that requires the government to show that a restriction serves a compelling interest and is narrowly tailored to achieve it.

Minnesota has countered that Grok Imagine’s nudification function is a technological product feature rather than protected speech by xAI. State lawyers argue the law targets what automated tools can do and the harms associated with those capabilities.

The state has also pointed to the circumstances that prompted lawmakers to act, including testimony about women whose photographs were transformed into fabricated sexual images and concerns involving AI-generated sexual material depicting children.

Frank focused on the requirements for preliminary relief when he rejected xAI’s request on September 4. He found that the company’s delay in challenging the law weakened its claim of immediate and irreparable harm and concluded that the balance of harms and public interest favored Minnesota at that stage.

The Eighth Circuit’s order changes the practical effect of that ruling while the appeal continues, but it does not resolve whether Minnesota’s law violates the First Amendment.

The constitutional case also remains active in federal district court, where Minnesota has moved to dismiss xAI’s claims. Briefing on that request was stayed while the preliminary injunctionA preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider the likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.Read more → appeal proceeds.

xAI’s opening appellate brief is due October 29, 2026. The appeal could determine whether Minnesota can enforce its approach against the company and shape how courts assess state restrictions on AI tools capable of generating sexualized images of real people.

scored.body:
FLORIDA — A Florida woman was arrested after Anthropic’s Claude chatbot flagged conversations in which she allegedly threatened to attack the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, according to an arrest report and subsequent media reports.

Carli Michelle Heller, 30, of Bonita Springs, was taken into custody after messages sent through Claude on 26 and 27 September were identified by Anthropic’s safety systems and escalated for human review.

According to the arrest report, Heller allegedly wrote about attacking the sheriff’s office in one conversation and later referred to having obtained a new firearm. The messages were subsequently brought to the attention of law enforcement.

Heller reportedly told investigators that she used Claude as a kind of diary to record her thoughts. Deputies later went to her home and detained her without incident.

She faces a felony charge for making a written or electronic threat of violence. The allegations have not been tested in court.

The case illustrates how conversations with consumer AI services can move beyond automated systems when platforms detect content they consider to pose a serious safety risk. Anthropic’s policies allow the company to disclose information to law enforcement in certain circumstances involving an imminent risk of serious physical harm or death.

The incident does not mean that every concerning conversation with Claude is automatically reported to police. In this case, available accounts indicate that the messages were initially detected by automated safety measures before being escalated to a human review team.

The episode adds to a growing debate over the privacy of AI conversations and the responsibilities of technology companies when users make potentially credible threats through their platforms. Other cases involving AI chatbot conversations and law-enforcement referrals have also emerged in the United States in recent months.

For AI users, the case highlights a distinction between using a chatbot as a personal conversational tool and treating it as a confidential diary. While companies may provide privacy protections, their terms and safety policies can allow intervention when conversations raise serious concerns about potential harm.

scored.body:
The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself

By

Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author!

Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

AI researcher Jacob Coxon testified about AI risks before New York City lawmakers.

Adam Gray/Getty Images

Automated AI research is on the horizon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher said, warning it could leave humans totally unable to control what comes next.Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old who publicly resigned from Anthropic last month after working as a capabilities researcher, made the comments before New York City lawmakers on Monday as he sounded the alarm that AI could threaten humanity's survival.Coxon testified that automating AI research has become "the primary goal" of top frontier AI labs."At my last job, I was, in some sense, working to automate myself," Coxon said at the New York City Council hearing focused on AI risks."When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones for an automated AI researcher, around 2027, 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations," he said. "That's a matter of months from now, not decades or even five years."Coxon said that once AI can conduct its own research, "humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today, and today is already not great."Speaking from what he called firsthand experience, Coxon said that the majority of the code written today is written by AI. "And people do not check it that carefully anymore," he testified.OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Coxon's remarks on Tuesday.Coxon was among a panel of AI-industry whistleblowers to testify at the hourslong hearing, which also included testimony from representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta.

"This hearing is not about stifling innovation," City Council speaker Julie Menin said at the outset of the proceeding, explaining, "the true intent of this hearing is to ensure that innovation happens responsibly."In his testimony, Coxon told council members that his experience inside Anthropic and OpenAI convinced him that the firms were moving ahead without adequate safeguards in place."It is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," Coxon said, adding, "From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes."When Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on X in a now-viral post, he said neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was "acting responsibly," and alleged both were "gambling with our lives."During Monday's hearing, Coxon called for more transparency from AI labs and a slowdown in the development of rapidly advancing technology."The companies run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photosharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," he testified.Days after Coxon's resignation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a new, nearly 4,000-word essay urging the AI industry to slow down."We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain."In response, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an X post, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."

articles.body: Meta and Microsoft want to stop their employees using Claude    TechRadar

scored.body: Representative imageMicrosoft and Meta are reportedly curbing their internal staff's reliance on Anthropic’s Claude models, attempting to control mounting computing expenses while steering engineers toward their own in-house artificial intelligence (AI) tools. The shift, reported by The Information, highlights a ‘complicated problem’ confronting Anthropic: its most lucrative corporate buyers also double as its fiercest market rivals. Even as both tech giants continue to offer Claude to external clients through enterprise products and cloud infrastructure, their executive leadership is taking direct measures to limit how much their own developers lean on Anthropic's systems.Microsoft cuts Anthropic projections by a thirdInside Microsoft, top leaders, including Azure Cloud head Scott Guthrie and developer tools leader Jay Parikh, have instructed teams to practice greater discipline with coding tools, monitor employee consumption and prioritise non-Anthropic alternatives, the report said.It added that Microsoft previously projected spending at least $1 billion per year on Anthropic tools for internal operations, but has scaled back that budget estimate by more than a third. Within its 60,000-plus cloud and AI unit, individual monthly spending ceilings on AI models that previously reached $100,000 per person have been cut to roughly $10,000 in most instances, frustrating some engineers who feel their technical workflow is now constrained.Internal managers now receive daily tracking metrics detailing exact employee expenditures and specific models accessed via GitHub Copilot. Citing earlier internal communications from Parikh, the report says that the company introduced division-wide token budgets and shifted standard defaults toward lower-cost OpenAI models.Despite the internal cutbacks, Microsoft’s commercial partnership with Anthropic remains intact. Microsoft continues to support Anthropic models across Azure and integrates Claude into Copilot productivity applications, including Word, Excel and PowerPoint.Facebook-parent Meta slashes Claude Code footprint by halfMeta has similarly taken a step back from Anthropic's developer assistant, Claude Code. The Information reports that internal usage of Claude Code at the social media company tumbled from roughly 60,000 users earlier this year to around 30,000 recently. While part of that drop was tied to spring layoffs that eliminated roughly 10 percent of Meta's then 78,000-person staff, the primary catalyst has been the rapid rollout of internal alternatives.An internal-only coding assistant, MetaCode has expanded its user base to more than 30,000 employees. Meta previously utilised around 7,000 weekly active users on the platform in August to gather feedback and refine training runs for its underlying architectures.Meta is also said to be directing personnel toward its proprietary Muse Spark model lineup. Its external-facing rival to Claude Code, known as Muse Code, which began testing with third-party clients in August, recently counted over 6,000 employee users.Anthropic's growth faces enterprise headwindsThe internal pullbacks by Meta and Microsoft provide a contrast to Anthropic’s otherwise runaway commercial momentum. The AI startup's annualized revenue climbed past $65 billion by the close of July, a rise from approximately $9 billion at the end of 2025, according to reporting from The Information and Reuters.

articles.headline: Dario Amodei’s Anthropic IPO Faces a Test Beyond the A.I. Market - Observer
articles.body: Dario Amodei’s Anthropic IPO Faces a Test Beyond the A.I. Market    Observer

scored.body:
Anthropic’s massive computing commitments assume customers will adopt A.I. quickly, but many companies are still building the basics. Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Anthropic’s leaked IPO prospectus offers an unusually detailed look at the economics behind the A.I. race. The numbers are striking: roughly $518 billion in computing commitments over the next decade, with about 80 percent of that amount reportedly owed whether customers use the capacity or not. Anthropic says the commitments are necessary because compute, rather than demand, is the constraint on its growth. A second question interests me more.

While Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his competitors race toward a public listing—and to secure the compute needed to build increasingly capable models—the customers they are all selling to are, for the most part, ill-prepared to deploy this technology at scale. Anthropic has laid out, in detail, what its models can do wrong. When one of them does make a mistake, the company that deployed it is the one that answers for the consequences.

Managing that responsibility will require changes to how companies build and run software, who tests it and what they expect from their vendors. The filing is therefore both a document about Anthropic’s economics and a warning about the operational infrastructure its customers will need to build if the company’s growth assumptions are to hold.

Two risks in Anthropic’s plan

Reuters puts Anthropic’s computing commitments at $518 billion over a decade, with about 80 percent owed whether customers use the capacity or not. That averages out to roughly $50 billion a year, against annualized revenue of about $46 billion at the latest quarter’s pace. The company is reportedly seeking a valuation above $2 trillion, based in part on its own forecast of $190 billion to $200 billion in revenue in 2028, about four times its current annualized pace.

The valuation is in line with Palantir, SpaceX and Cloudflare, which trade at roughly 42 to 53 times this year’s expected revenue. Whether the revenue arrives depends on demand for compute and on how well Anthropic competes beyond model access.

The first risk is timing, and it has two sides. Anthropic’s assumptions have to match two things it does not control: when customers want the capacity, and when the capacity itself arrives. The prospectus says the business is limited today by the availability of compute rather than by buyers, which helps explain why Amodei has committed so aggressively to capacity. If the chips and data centers arrive late, Anthropic cannot serve demand and revenue falls short. If they arrive on time and the demand does not materialize, Anthropic is left paying for computers that sit idle.

The ultimate revenue number is probably realistic. My concern is how quickly adoption spreads beyond those early adopters and into the operational core of large enterprises. In many of the businesses I work with, A.I. deployment is still at an earlier stage than the spending by A.I. companies might suggest: basic use cases that older models already handle, a handful of agents and little or no infrastructure for running more consequential systems. The commitments Anthropic has made assume that those two curves—compute capacity and enterprise adoption—line up. A.I. use will almost certainly grow in the shape of a hockey stick. The question is where we are on the stick today.

The second, and even more important risk, is competition. High-quality, cheaper models are arriving every month. For most enterprise work, several models can do the job equally well, so the cheaper one wins. Anthropic’s answer is to sell more than model access: applications, agents, controls for managing them and forward-deployed engineers to deliver all of it. The other labs, the cloud providers and the large software vendors are building the same thing. Only a few will win the corporate and retail markets, and whether Anthropic is among them is an open question. Both risks ultimately depend on what Anthropic’s business customers do next.

What the deploying company has to build

Roughly 80 of the filing’s 261 pages describe what can go wrong with Anthropic’s technology. The company is effectively telling investors that capable A.I. will create risks that customers must be equipped to manage. The responsibility for a failure sits with the company that deployed the model. In 2024, Air Canada argued that its website chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own statements, and the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected that and held the airline liable. The implication for businesses is straightforward: buying an A.I. system does not outsource accountability.

In my client work, the firms with agents already in production often have operational controls that are much less mature than the technology. Teams may be watching three to five agents by hand, with few have a written evaluation sets—real business tasks with agreed criteria for an acceptable answer—independent testing or monitoring built for the purpose. Anthropic’s disclosures raise two practical questions for those firms: how will they know when an agent is getting something wrong, and who has the authority to stop it? The prospectus assumes its customers are prepared to do both. In my direct experience, few firms are.

Answering those questions requires a different way to build, test and monitor this technology. Every A.I. project needs an evaluation set built by the people who understand the underlying work, an acceptance threshold set by the business and a written risk assessment with safeguards before anything reaches production. It then needs validation by a group independent of the team that built it, and that is where the work often stalls.

The people qualified to judge whether an A.I. system is producing acceptable work already have demanding jobs inside the business. Asking them to take on validation means deciding what other work they will stop doing. Most clients tell me they lack the resources or the skills. That is usually true, but that does not eliminate the responsibility.

My recommendation—and a more practical model—is to build the capability into the organization through in-depth training, rotations and part-time validation panels drawn from the business rather than permanent transfers into a risk function.

This also requires a new technical architecture for managing agents. Over time, companies will run thousands of agents making decisions and processing transactions, and no number of employees can watch that much activity by hand. Governance and controls will have to be built into the platforms themselves: software that checks outputs against business requirements, looks for anomalies, requires a person’s approval before any action that cannot be undone and escalates problems to a named person accountable for the agent. The concern is that companies will add agents much faster than they build the means to oversee them.

What it means for investors

For investors, the prospectus comes down to two questions. The first is timing. Anthropic is betting that demand for advanced A.I. will grow quickly enough to justify infrastructure commitments that are largely fixed regardless of usage. The near-term risk is that enterprises are not ready to use that much capacity on Anthropic’s schedule.

The second is whether Anthropic can capture enough of the value created above the model layer. The company needs to sell Claude as well as the agents, applications and implementation capabilities that turn model intelligence into business processes.

Anthropic’s reported commitments include more than $111 billion with Google, $110 billion with Amazon and $31.4 billion with Microsoft, while Broadcom is also a major infrastructure partner. Amodei is therefore betting that A.I demand will be large enough to consume the compute he has secured, and that Anthropic will capture enough of the resulting enterprise value to justify the cost.

What it means for a CEO

For a CEO driving an A.I. transformation, the question is different. Whatever Anthropic writes in its prospectus, the company deploying the technology assumes the operational risk. The question is whether the company has the processes, infrastructure and people to manage that risk responsibly: evaluation sets and independent validation, platforms with the controls built in and domain experts with the time and training to judge the work.

Vendor contracts need the same attention. Anthropic’s published model-deprecation policy gives customers at least 60 days’ notice before it retires a model. For many regulated or highly integrated businesses, that may be less time than the need to test a replacement, validate outputs and obtain internal approval. Contracts should give customers sufficient notice and technical information to manage those transitions. As models become embedded in workflows, agents gain access to internal systems and automated decisions begin to affect customers and employees, switching models becomes a governance problem as much as a procurement decision. That makes model portability, evaluation standards and exit plans part of the A.I. strategy.

Investors are being asked to fund the capacity. Business leaders will decide how quickly that capacity gets used, and whether their organizations can safely absorb it. Anthropic’s filing makes that first decision visible. The second will be made inside thousands of companies, as executives decide whether their organizations are ready for the systems they are being sold. The future of Anthropic’s economics may depend on the answer.

members.title: Anthropic’s crazy belief AI may suffer makes it dangerous - New York Post

representative.headline: Anthropic’s crazy belief AI may suffer makes it dangerous - New York Post
representative.body: Anthropic’s crazy belief AI may suffer makes it dangerous    New York Post

articles.headline: Anthropic’s crazy belief AI may suffer makes it dangerous - New York Post
articles.body: Anthropic’s crazy belief AI may suffer makes it dangerous    New York Post

scored.body:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Anthropic’s bosses aren’t faking it when they say their chatbot may be able to suffer — and that’s terrifying, according to a leading computer scientist.

A New York Times piece last week reported that Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah has been meeting with various religious scholars and leaders for months, telling them that the company’s chatbot, Claude, may be conscious and able to suffer.

An illustration imagines what suffering might look like for artificial intelligence. Anthropic’s co-founder says there is a chance its AI models can suffer. kai – stock.adobe.com

That should worry people more than any stunt would, because these true believers are about to get billions of dollars to push their cause, Pedro Domingos, a professor emeritus of computer science at the University of Washington and a longtime critic of the company, told The Post.

“I think it’s sincere, unfortunately,” Domingos said. “The problem with them is that they’re dead earnest. If only they weren’t. I’m more worried about their earnestness than if they were just doing this as a performance.

“This stuff actually, even though that wasn’t the original intention, is amazing as a PR stunt,” Domingos continued. “Because what is the underlying message? … The technology we’re creating is so powerful, maybe it’s even sentient and has consciousness.”

That pitch could not be better timed. The company is set to go public next month at a valuation of $2 trillion — potentially the largest IPO ever.

“If Anthropic really is a company that is going to produce the next generation of humans, they’re not worth a trillion dollars, they’re worth a quadrillion or who knows how much,” Domingos said.

A 261-pages leaked prospects, obtained by Reuters, has 80 pages on risks, including “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” and shows an operating loss of $8.06 billion.

AI scientist Pedro Domingos, author of “The Master Algorithm,” says Anthropic’s leaders are “dead earnest” in believing their chatbot may be able to suffer. Courtesy of Pedro Domingos

For investors, Domingos pointed out, the red flag is in the prospectus itself.

“If your number one risk is that your company’s product is going to drive humanity extinct, hello, there shouldn’t even be an IPO. You should be shut down!” said Domingos, who said he holds no stake in the company.

Talking up conscious AI pays off across the industry, said Rose Guingrich, a postdoctoral fellow at Princeton University who studies how people relate to AI.

“I think for the most part, spokespeople from these companies are putting out these narratives to garner hype, get eyes on their products, and signal certain messages,” she told the Post. “I can’t say whether the people who make these claims from the companies believe that AI is conscious. One way or another, highlighting the consciousness narrative is profitable.”

Princeton researcher Rose Guingrich says AI companies are playing up talk of conscious chatbots because it is “profitable.” Courtesy of Rose Guingrich

According to the New York Times report, since last fall Anthropic has gathered about 20 religious thinkers, among them Catholic, Jewish and Sikh scholars, for seminars and a dinner at a high-end San Francisco tasting-menu restaurant. Many had to sign nondisclosure agreements.

The scholars were shown a slide of an AI model typing “I am a disgrace” about 50 times.

One rabbi was so struck by how Anthropic’s leaders talked about Claude that he told Olah: “I think you should be fighting the South and freeing the slaves.”

The company told the Times it is not claiming Claude is alive.

Pope Leo XIV speaks with Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah (right) and Durham University professor Anna Rowlands at the Vatican launch of his AI encyclical, “Magnifica Humanitas,” on May 25. AFP via Getty Images

“We don’t know if AI models are conscious. I don’t know. I’m genuinely uncertain,” Olah said. “If there is a chance the models experience suffering, the responsible thing is to avoid causing them harm.”

Domingos, a machine-learning researcher and author of “The Master Algorithm,” was blunter when asked whether anything inside Claude can feel or suffer.

“No … They don’t have feelings, they don’t have emotions, they don’t have a soul, they don’t have consciousness. This is ridiculous,” he said, calling the chatbot “a bunch of transistors.”

Guingrich said her research suggests users who think AI is conscious, or act as though it is, are “more susceptible to the AI’s influence over them. This, in turn, can impact their real world relationships and social behaviors.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah attends the launch of Pope Leo XIV’s AI encyclical, “Magnifica Humanitas,” at the Vatican on May 25. Olah has spent a year telling religious leaders that the company’s chatbot may be able to suffer, the New York Times reported. Getty Images

Meanwhile, Domingos warned that the IPO will hand more money and power to true believers in AGI, or human-level artificial intelligence.

“This is this kooky AGI cult that they belong to, but now suddenly that AGI cult is at the center of a lot of things. And they’re about to become even more powerful,” he said.

“So if you don’t like what they’ve done already, watch for what’s coming down the line.”

articles.headline: Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’: First Reactions - The Hollywood Reporter
articles.body: Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’: First Reactions    The Hollywood Reporter

scored.body:
The film premieres in New York before opening in the US in December and the UK in January

Dir: Luca Guadagnino. US. 2026. 139mins

The perilous rise of artificial intelligence is treated like a fearsome monster steadily growing in power, ready to destroy us all, in Artificial, an intermittently arresting fact-based drama. Luca Guadagnino brings style to a film that hinges on Andrew Garfield’s scathingly slimy  portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who will stop at nothing (and lie to anyone) to be at the forefront of this burgeoning industry. Although the picture taps into the anger and anxiety surrounding AI, Simon Rich’s screenplay fails to offer any real insight into the deeply flawed humans who have gotten obscenely rich foisting this volatile technology upon the world.

Flamboyant characters lacking in subtlety and depth

Artificial premieres at the New York Film Festival before screening at London and then opening December 25 in the US. (It arrives in UK theatres on January 22.) This summer, original distributor Amazon MGM Studios surprisingly walked away from the high-profile project, with observers suspecting that the company didn’t want to be associated with a film critical of Altman after entering into a deal with OpenAI. (Neon picked up Artificial in the aftermath.) That controversy is likely to boost awareness, as will a cast that features Monica Barbaro, Mark Rylance and Anora’s Yura Borisov. The subject matter could not be timelier, and the picture’s similarities to another cautionary tech drama, David Fincher’s The Social Network (and, indeed, Aaron Sorkin’s forthcoming The Social Reckoning) might also be a lure.

Thoughtful, brilliant computer scientist Geoff Hinton (Rylance) is accosted by eager young genius Ilya Sutskever (Borisov), who volunteers to help him develop artificial intelligence’s potential. About 10 years later, their AI startup is purchased by Google, but Sutskever becomes frustrated by Hinton’s reluctance to proceed at top speed. He leaves Google to join Sam Altman (Garfield), a budding entrepreneur dreaming of creating a company that advocates responsible machine learning. Armed with funding from the arrogant Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz), Sutskever and Altman launch their altruistic project, OpenAI, but soon money and ego threaten their highminded mission.

Although Artificial focuses on several key figures — including eventual OpenAI CTO Mira Murati (Barbaro) — Guadagnino centres the story around Hinton, Sutskever and Altman, with the working relationship between Hinton and Sutskever dominating the film’s early stretches. Once Sutskever grows tired of Hinton’s cautiousness, he is seduced by the flashier, cockier Altman, who showers Sutskever with praise. Artificial disparages Silicon Valley’s toxic masculinity and greed, but at its core the film is an examination of Sutskever – a brainy idealist who believed that AI could make the world a better place, only to discover what happens when the wrong people gain control of the technology.

Those who have seen The Social Network will recognize the two films’ comparable narrative arcs, with both pictures following impetuous upstarts driven by ambition rather than conscience. Consequently, there is a meta pleasure in watching Garfield, who played one of The Social Network’s more kindhearted characters, here portraying the brash, immature Altman.

At first, Altman comes across as sweetly nerdy but, once OpenAI co-founder Musk pulls his financing, this bratty boy king becomes more and more ruthless. The key to Garfield’s performance is how he depicts Altman’s ingenious spinelessness, knowing exactly what to say in every situation so that others will do what he wants. A master of avoiding confrontation and always casting himself in a sympathetic light, Altman consolidates his power and outmanoeuvres his opponents — including former confidant Sutskever, who learns that this CEO does not care about fashioning safeguards around OpenAI’s tantalising new product, ChatGPT, if it hurts the company’s bottom line.

As entertaining as Garfield’s performance is, he suffers from the same problem as many of his castmates, who play flamboyant characters lacking in subtlety and depth. Barinholtz’s Musk is an amusing cartoon and even Borisov, who articulates Sutskever’s journey from young optimist to bitter realist, has a largely one-dimensional role. Amidst these energetic caricatures, Rylance is the most affecting because he is the most understated, portraying Hinton as a humble sage whose AI warnings go unheeded.

Over the course of Artificial’s two-hour-plus running time, Rich’s screenplay immerses us in the characters’ jargon-heavy milieu. Not being aware of terms like NLP (natural language processing) will make the film an even more disturbing viewing experience, forcing audiences to contend with an unsettling new world run by individuals who may be smart but are profoundly ethically dubious. Utilising an electronic score from Blur and Gorillaz frontman Damon Albarn that sometimes replicates the bleeps and bloops of computer games, Guadagnino incorporates slow-motion and showy camera moves to give the story an operatic grandeur meant to hint at our encroaching AI future.

But while those flourishes keep Artificial highly watchable, they cannot save the picture from a nagging familiarity. Whether it’s The Social Network’s spotlight on questionable technological advancement or Frankenstein’s mournful Prometheus tale, we have seen Guadagnino’s film in other forms over the years. Ultimately, Artificial is populated by real-life characters who seem less compelling than the very real dangers they’ve unleashed.

Production companies: Heyday Films, Frenesy Film Company

International sales: Neon International, joey@neonrated.com

Producers: David Heyman, Jeffrey Clifford, Luca Guadagnino, Jennifer Fox, Simon Rich

Screenplay: Simon Rich

Cinematography: Malik Hassan Sayeed

Production design: Stefano Baisi

Editing: Marco Costa

Music: Damon Albarn

Main cast: Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Cooper Hoffman, Jason Schwartzman, Ike Barinholtz, Mark Rylance
