articles.body: OpenAI to begin watermarking AI-generated text    Computerworld

scored.body:
Skip to content

6 Oct 2026

OpenAI has begun phased text watermarking under EU AI Act rules, limiting automatic marking to Europe whilst providing global API clients with an opt-in feature.

Image via Unsplash / Zac Wolff

OpenAI started a phased deployment on 5 October 2026 of its text watermarking technology, named textGrain, alongside a restricted verification programme for external researchers. OpenAI’s textGrain system embeds an invisible watermark into model-generated text, enabling an internal detector to confirm whether content came from its service. Under the rollout schedule, enterprise application programming interface (API) clients globally have received an opt-in watermarking configuration.

The technical measure, implemented in the European Union, introduces statistical provenance tracking for machine-generated outputs to align company operations with the EU AI Act. The implementation aims to comply with Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which obliges generative artificial intelligence providers to ensure that synthetic audio, image, video, and text outputs are marked in a machine-readable format.

According to OpenAI, Statistical watermarks struggle to work reliably outside testing environments. Watermark detectors frequently produce errors, either flagging human text by mistake or missing AI-generated text entirely. Detection is especially weak in shorter samples or structured fields like mathematics, where limited word choices restrict the watermark signal, dropping from 95% accuracy in 400-token texts down to 80% in 200-token passages. Internal tests showed that simply replacing 10% of the words with synonyms caused the detection rate to drop from 92% to 66%, and swapping 25% reduced it to just 17%.

OpenAI is offering approved researchers and expert organisations early access to its detection tool. In line with the EU Code of Practice, requests will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis to help test and improve text provenance. The tool checks whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark without identifying the user or disclosing their prompts and chats.

Why does it matter?

While academic research demonstrates that artificial intelligence detectors still present systematic inaccuracies. For instance, in evaluating academic writing, statistical watermarking also exposes an operational concerns between legal requirements for machine-readable provenance and the probabilistic nature of natural language detection. OpenAI’s phased rollout illustrates how EU AI Act requirements can push technology companies to implement technical measures to mitigate the risks posed by their services. However, relying entirely on closed, commercial AI detection tools replicates the very problem it seeks to address: generating false assessments and intensifying misinformation through unaudited, private evaluation processes. As European authorities operationalise transparency codes, relying on closed detection tools creates concerns over whether internal policies can satisfy public transparency standards.

articles.headline: Anthropic consults Hindu monk to discuss AI ethics - The American Bazaar
articles.body: Anthropic consults Hindu monk to discuss AI ethics    The American Bazaar

scored.body:
As artificial intelligence becomes more capable, some of the questions confronting AI developers are moving beyond technology and into philosophy.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has been consulting religious scholars, philosophers and other thinkers about how increasingly capable AI systems should behave and how humans should approach difficult questions surrounding artificial intelligence.

Among those consulted was Swami Sarvapriyananda, the minister and spiritual leader of the Vedanta Society of New York and a monk of the Ramakrishna Order.

Sarvapriyananda discussed the Anthropic meetings publicly during an August 2026 panel at the University of Oxford.

He said Anthropic contacted him about discussing artificial intelligence, consciousness and ethics and that he subsequently visited different groups in San Francisco twice. “I get a call from Anthropic, you know, Claude, would you like to come and talk about AI and consciousness and ethics?” he said.

READ: Anthropic in talks to buy Decart AI for $60 billion (August 13, 2026)

The conversations were significant because Vedanta has a long philosophical tradition of examining consciousness, the self and the relationship between awareness and the mind. Sarvapriyananda has also spent years discussing those subjects in public lectures and academic and scientific forums.

His involvement does not establish that Anthropic considers Claude conscious.

Rather, his comments show that questions about consciousness and ethics have become part of the company’s broader discussions about AI.

Anthropic has separately published a constitution for Claude, describing it as a document intended to guide the model’s values and behavior.

The company says the constitution is designed to provide principles for how Claude should act rather than relying only on conventional instructions.

The company’s latest constitution also acknowledges uncertainty around AI consciousness and moral status.

Anthropic says it does not know whether Claude has consciousness or moral status, either currently or in the future which uncertainty has prompted the company to treat the subject as an area worthy of continued research rather than as a settled question.

Sarvapriyananda has emphasized that the issue is not simply whether an AI system appears intelligent. During the Oxford discussion, he described his initial interest in AI as a way to examine the distinction between intelligence and consciousness.

He also cautioned against assuming that the question of selfhood has an easy answer. “There is no clear answer to what selfhood is in the case of today’s AI,” he said, adding that he does not think there is a clear answer to human selfhood either.

Those observations are consistent with the broader uncertainty surrounding machine consciousness.

An AI system can produce sophisticated language and simulate humanlike interaction without that, by itself, demonstrating subjective experience.

READ: Anthropic urges US to not block state AI regulations till federal standards are set (June 11, 2026)

Anthropic’s outreach also extends beyond Vedanta considering reporting on the company’s discussions describes participation from thinkers representing different religious and philosophical traditions, as well as professionals working in areas such as counseling and mental health. Some participants have said details of the meetings remain confidential.

For now, there is no established scientific conclusion that Claude or other mainstream AI systems are conscious.

Anthropic’s engagement with religious and philosophical thinkers should therefore be understood as part of an effort to examine unresolved questions about AI ethics, values and consciousness.

As AI systems become more capable, those questions are becoming increasingly difficult for technology companies to leave solely to engineers.

How an AI should behave, what values should guide it and how humans should respond to increasingly sophisticated systems remain open questions, ones that involve technology, philosophy and ethics alike.

members.title: OpenAI To Test Visual Ads In ChatGPT Image Generation - Search Engine Journal

representative.headline: OpenAI To Test Visual Ads In ChatGPT Image Generation - Search Engine Journal
representative.body: OpenAI To Test Visual Ads In ChatGPT Image Generation    Search Engine Journal

articles.headline: OpenAI To Test Visual Ads In ChatGPT Image Generation - Search Engine Journal
articles.body: OpenAI To Test Visual Ads In ChatGPT Image Generation    Search Engine Journal

scored.body:
OpenAI is testing a new visual ad format in ChatGPT that will first appear during image generation.

The test will begin later this month with an initial group of U.S. advertisers. OpenAI says the format will use images to show product inspiration, usage, or experiences associated with products and services.

The update gives advertisers another way to reach ChatGPT users beyond the ads currently shown below responses.

OpenAI also announced new measurement partnerships and brand suitability tools as it continues building out ChatGPT Ads.

How Will Visual Ads Work In ChatGPT?

Until now, ChatGPT Ads have appeared below responses, placing advertising directly within the chat experience.

Testing the new visual ads format during image generation could give OpenAI another way to reach people across ChatGPT’s broader user base.

OpenAI says ChatGPT now reaches 1.2 billion people each week. But, people aren’t necessarily using it in the same way. Some may be asking questions or researching purchases, while others are creating images, working with files, or using other features.

Bringing ads into image generation starts opening advertising to more of those experiences rather than relying only on the traditional chat interface.

It also raises questions about what the ads will look and feel like.

Image credit: OpenAI, October 2026

OpenAI says the visual ads will be clearly labeled and remain separate from the image being created. Advertising also won’t influence ChatGPT’s responses, according to the announcement.

Still, a visual ad appearing while someone is generating visual content could feel more native to the experience than a sponsored placement below a text response.

How much separation OpenAI creates between the two will be worth watching once the test begins.

OpenAI hasn’t shared details about targeting, pricing, creative requirements, or reporting for the new format since it’s only opening up to a select group of advertisers right now.

OpenAI Expands ChatGPT Ads Measurement

OpenAI is also adding more ways for advertisers to connect ChatGPT Ads with the measurement tools they already use.

Hightouch, Tealium, and LiveRamp integrations can send conversion data from advertisers’ existing systems to ChatGPT Ads.

OpenAI also supports attribution partners including AppsFlyer, Triple Whale, Adjust, DV Rockerbox, and Northbeam, among others. Those partnerships cover capabilities such as reporting, click attribution, and Conversions API integrations.

Incrementality measurement is another area OpenAI is beginning to test.

Haus, Measured, and WorkMagic are working with OpenAI on geo-based experiments designed to measure whether ChatGPT Ads caused additional business results.

OpenAI also shared several early partner results. DV Rockerbox reported WeightWatchers’ attributed CPA was 15.3% lower than its blended paid search benchmark. WorkMagic reported statistically significant incremental purchase lift for Dose. Triple Whale found that 93% of Portland Leather visitors from ChatGPT Ads were new.

Those figures measure different outcomes, so advertisers shouldn’t read them as broader ChatGPT Ads benchmarks. OpenAI also describes its incrementality work as early stage.

New Brand Suitability Tools Are Also Coming

Advertisers with specific placement restrictions may also get more control over where their ads appear.

OpenAI has introduced Negative Phrases for qualifying advertisers with placement requirements tied to their own brand policies.

Its existing guardrails assess whether conversations are appropriate for advertising. OpenAI says those safeguards are intended to keep ads away from sensitive, emotionally vulnerable, or otherwise unsuitable contexts.

OpenAI is also developing brand suitability pilots with DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science. The partners will evaluate how its brand safety standards are applied without receiving access to private user conversations.

That gives advertisers another independent layer for evaluating placements as ChatGPT Ads adds more formats.

What Advertisers Should Take Away

Most advertisers won’t have access to visual ads yet. OpenAI is starting with a limited group in the U.S., with no timeline for a broader rollout.

That makes this more of a format to watch than something advertisers need to plan around today.

If access expands, advertisers will need to look beyond click-through rates or whether the new ads outperform existing ChatGPT placements. It will be interesting to prove whether visual ads reach people or influence behavior that advertisers weren’t already capturing elsewhere.

That’s where OpenAI’s measurement updates could become more useful. Expanded attribution support can help advertisers connect ChatGPT Ads to conversions, while the early incrementality work could help determine whether those conversions would have happened anyway.

The same applies to placement controls. As OpenAI tests ads in different parts of ChatGPT, advertisers will need enough visibility and control to know where their ads appeared and whether those placements make sense for their brand.

A new ad format alone doesn’t give advertisers a reason to move budget to a new channel. The case gets stronger if OpenAI can show that visual ads reach different users, drive incremental results, and give advertisers enough control to evaluate both.

Featured image: Novikov Aleksey / Shutterstock

members.title: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates - Fortune

representative.headline: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates - Fortune
representative.body: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates    Fortune

articles.headline: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates - Fortune
articles.body: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates    Fortune

scored.body:
Candidates interviewing for certain teams at OpenAI will now go through a new step in the process, known as the “mission interview.”

The company is currently introducing it as a new pilot program, starting with the marketing and human resources teams, OpenAI told Fortune on Monday. The goal is to give job candidates a dedicated space to talk about how they will contribute to OpenAI’s mission, which is “to ensure that artificial general intelligence (AGI) benefits all of humanity.”

Specifically, OpenAI wants to gauge how candidates think, including their judgment and ability to weigh tradeoffs—traits that are increasingly critical as artificial intelligence companies work to control technology with great benefits as well as potential dangers. There is no “right” answer, an OpenAI representative said; skepticism and disagreement are welcome, as is intellectual diversity.

The person conducting the interview will be from a team separate from whatever role the candidate is applying for. OpenAI is also creating a training program that interested employees can complete to become certified to conduct the interviews, though the program is just starting to ramp up.

The evolution in OpenAI’s recruiting process is a marker of the company looking to standardize its evaluations as it matures and balloons in size. The company, which has roughly 8,000 employees worldwide, has 830 open roles as of this writing. By standardizing the process, OpenAI aims to have a consistent measure to evaluate new employees across teams.

Many tech companies, including Meta and Amazon, have their own version of a “mission interview,” which is somewhat akin to a test of cultural fit. For example, Amazon employees can be trained as “bar raisers”—interviewers from outside the hiring team, who assess whether a candidate meets Amazon’s companywide “Leadership Principles.”

In Anthropic’s version, interviewers reportedly test if candidates are joining the AI lab for its mission or the money, according to Axios. Jobs at leading AI companies are incredibly lucrative, with many positions at OpenAI currently offering salaries of over $300K (and more with stock included).

One software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received an offer from OpenAI for $935,000 total compensation, with a $385,000 base, and $2.2 million of restricted stock units (RSUs) vesting over four years, according to anonymous professional network Blind. Anthropic allegedly offered a candidate $620,000 in total compensation, according to another Blind post.

articles.body: Anthropic Plans to Spend $518 Billion on Cloud and Computing Power    The Motley Fool

scored.body:
Artificial intelligence is expensive, and Anthropic put a price tag on it. The company said in its IPO prospectus that it plans to spend $518 billion over the next 10 years on cloud and computing power for technology it believes could be more transformative than industrialization, electricity, or the internet.

Anthropic has already locked in long-term cloud computing deals with hyperscalers such as Amazon (AMZN +1.95%) and Alphabet (GOOG +0.22%) (GOOGL +0.35%), but investors should note a few key takeaways from this major news.

Image source: Getty Images.

The prices of AI components will continue to rise

Anthropic's spending goals indicate a long-term AI tailwind. Not only will Anthropic continue to spend money, but other competitors will also increase their spending. Artificial intelligence is still in its early innings, and none of the hyperscalers want to be left behind.

The entire data center build-out requires memory chips, electricity, physical buildings, specialized cooling systems, and an array of other essentials that don't receive as much attention. All of those inputs will see rising demand, resulting in greater pricing power for their suppliers.

Research firm TrendForce anticipates high bandwidth memory prices will increase by 121% year over year in 2027. Prices have already soared for these foundational chips as demand far outpaces supply.

It's not just chips. AI data center provider Nebius (NBIS +7.44%) has seen its annual contract value per megawatt more than triple in less than a year for short-term capacity deals. A shortage of compute power combined with insatiable demand is enabling neoclouds to substantially raise prices without meeting meaningful customer resistance.

Consumers and businesses are using these products

Claude and other AI models already have real user case studies. Use of these models is becoming as commonplace as a Google search, and revenue is scaling quickly. Anthropic closed out 2025 with $4.6 billion in revenue; as of July 2026, the business's annual revenue run rate had topped $65 billion.

This jump shows how quickly AI products and services can scale. It's this growth rate that makes the $2 trillion market cap it's hoping to achieve with its initial public offering more feasible, but any slowdown in its growth would cast serious doubt on whether it merits that valuation.

Anthropic is still burning through cash, but the hope is that its revenue growth will remain parabolic and eventually produce a profit. As long as new customers continue to sign up and existing customers stick around, the company can realize that objective.

More importantly, Anthropic is an example of broader AI growth and the commercial value of the technology. If it achieves a profitable return on investment, that gives tech giants, enterprises, and other AI labs a green light to increase spending.

Substantial capital is flowing throughout the artificial intelligence industry, and that trend is set to accelerate. It could make many investors wealthy.

articles.body: Anthropic Brings Claude Into Google Docs, Sheets and Slides    citybiz

scored.body:
If Gemini isn’t quite your cup of tea, Anthropic’s Claude now supports sidebar integration with Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides.

You can already use Gemini natively in Google Workspace apps, but those invested in Claude can now use their AI of choice inside of Google’s ecosystem through the Claude for Google Workspace add-on which is in public beta starting today. A sidebar opens up alongside your file in Docs, Sheets, or Slides and can assist in building out documents, making edits, and more.

In Google Docs, Anthropic says you can use Claude integration to fix spelling, rewrite portions of a document, or restyle sections, all without breaking existing formatting. In Sheets, you can have Claude write formulas or build tables using the context of the document, or even upload extra documents/spreadsheets to build something new in Sheets. In Slides, Claude can build new slides using existing layouts or themes or flag elements that might need to be updated. Gemini can do much of this but, as mentioned, this is useful for those already invested in Claude.

There’s an “ask before edits” mode where Claude will let you preview changes before they’re made.

The Claude for Google Workspace beta is available to all paid Claude users through the Google Workspace marketplace. There are also new Claude connectors for Docs, Sheets, and Slides that let you edit Google Workspace files directly from Claude itself just by pasting a file link into your conversation with the AI.

members.title: Anthropic Could Beat OpenAI to Wall Street by Over a Year - The Motley Fool

representative.headline: Anthropic Could Beat OpenAI to Wall Street by Over a Year - The Motley Fool
representative.body: Anthropic Could Beat OpenAI to Wall Street by Over a Year    The Motley Fool

articles.headline: Anthropic Could Beat OpenAI to Wall Street by Over a Year - The Motley Fool
articles.body: Anthropic Could Beat OpenAI to Wall Street by Over a Year    The Motley Fool

scored.body:
Anthropic could reportedly begin marketing its initial public offering (IPO) as early as the week of Nov. 9 and potentially start trading before Thanksgiving. OpenAI has now ruled out a 2026 IPO after CEO Sam Altman said it would prioritize artificial intelligence (AI) safety and that a listing would not take place until 2027 at the earliest.

Hence, Anthropic increasingly appears likely to reach Wall Street first. But OpenAI would need to remain private until roughly late November 2027 or later for the gap to exceed 12 months.

Image source: Getty Images.

A $100 billion IPO would still fall far short of Anthropic's spending commitments

Anthropic has committed at least $518 billion to future cloud, computing, and infrastructure spending over multiple years. Roughly 80% of those obligations are noncancelable or payable regardless of utilization.

Anthropic could reportedly raise up to $100 billion at a valuation approaching $2 trillion. However, $100 billion would cover only about 19% of the company's spending commitments.

Broadcom could lend Anthropic up to $42 billion to help finance its data center infrastructure build-out. That financing would cover roughly one-third of Anthropic's five-year $125.2 billion commitment to lease TPU computing capacity. Yet even that would only cover about 8% of Anthropic's commitments.

In that context, the IPO appears likely to be just one of several sources of funding Anthropic will have to tap to handle its spending plans.

Much of the future growth seems already priced in

Anthropic generated just under $4.6 billion of revenue in 2025, although revenue grew roughly 12-fold. Trade magazine R&D World estimates that Anthropic's 2026 revenue could reach around $60 billion, based on its reported growth trajectory. At a $2 trillion valuation, that would value the company at roughly 33 times estimated 2026 sales.

Anthropic reportedly projects $190 billion to $200 billion of revenue in 2028. To hit the midpoint of that range, revenue would need to rise almost 3.25 times from the $60 billion 2026 estimate in just two years. Yet even if Anthropic reaches $195 billion, a $2 trillion valuation would still equal roughly 10 times 2028 sales.

In short, investors buying this stock while Anthropic sits at a market cap of $2 trillion would be paying for a substantial portion of the company's anticipated growth before it arrives. So, Anthropic may need to show that rapid revenue growth can translate into much stronger profits.

While 83% of Anthropic's 2025 revenue came from usage-based consumption, about 80% of its infrastructure obligations are effectively locked in. Its customers could, if they chose to, cut their AI usage (and their bills) much faster than Anthropic could reduce its compute spending.

OpenAI has less pressure to go public

OpenAI closed a $122 billion private funding round in March that valued the company at $852 billion. The company is now reportedly looking to raise at least another $30 billion privately at a valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion.

So, OpenAI can still raise huge sums of money without going public. This gives it more flexibility to wait before listing its shares, and also allows it to keep avoiding the extra scrutiny that comes with being a public company.

Anthropic is on track to become the first major public company attempting to prove that cutting-edge AI developers can become highly profitable businesses. Investors will be watching to learn whether it can convert rapid top-line growth into impressive bottom-line results.

articles.body: Why I Don't Think Meta's AI Strategy Will Be Successful    The Motley Fool

scored.body:
News of Meta Platforms (META -0.41%) launching a personal artificial intelligence (AI) agent called Muse last month gave the struggling stock some much-needed life. It's now in positive territory for the year, up around 12% since January. It's been a tremendous turnaround story for the company, as it's made investors believers of Meta's AI strategy.But I don't think it'll last. While the launch of a personal AI assistant may unlock new opportunities and drive more growth, since there are paid plans as well, here's why I don't think it'll be successful.

Image source: Getty Images.

AI agents need to be trusted, and that's not Meta's strengthAI agents could potentially add a lot of efficiency to someone's life. They could respond to emails, book dinners, make travel plans, and even shop online for them. But each one of those examples also requires the user to allow the agent to act on their behalf, and thus, to trust it to make sound decisions. It may also involve allowing them to access sensitive information.Meta, unfortunately, doesn't have the best track record for protecting user privacy. It's faced numerous privacy-related lawsuits and recently agreed to pay $18 billion to settle lawsuits that alleged its social media apps harmed children.Given that there is a growing amount of competition in AI and there will be many AI agents available, I'm skeptical about just how much people will be willing to trust a service from Meta, given its track record. As concerns grow about the level of access that an AI can have, I think users will be less inclined to use an AI from a company such as Meta. While its AI agent may provide convenience for users who heavily use the company's social media apps, I don't think it'll be a big growth driver for the business.Premium FeatureMoneyball Superscore78/100Today's Change(-0.41%) $-3.02Current Price$738.88Why I'd avoid Meta's stockMeta's stock has been volatile over the past year, as even with its recent surge in value, it's still only up around 3% in the last 12 months. It's trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 28, which is a fair bit higher than the S&P 500 average of 23. The tech stock is by no means a steal of a deal. Plus, when factoring in the risks of its AI strategy not paying off plus the money pit that is its metaverse segment, it quickly becomes apparent why the stock should arguably trade at a discount rather than a premium. This is a stock that could be vulnerable to a sizable decline if there's a downturn in the markets.

scored.body: US Sen. Bernie Sanders asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman precisely what "bad things" the world should accept for the sake of advancements in artificial intelligence, a question that came after the billionaire executive said people must be willing to tolerate some unspecified negative outcomes to enjoy the potential long-term benefits of the technology."Mr. Altman: What 'bad things' should we accept to advance AI?" Sanders (I-Vt.) wrote in response to the OpenAI CEO's interview with Politico. "Losing tens of millions of jobs? A mass surveillance state? A mental health crisis for our kids? A global financial crisis? Mass extinction?""Let’s not wait to find out," the senator added. "Pause advanced AI NOW!"Altman told Politico in an interview released this past weekend that he believes the world "should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency." The OpenAI CEO didn't elaborate on the kinds of "bad things" he views as an acceptable price to pay for AI development, which some researchers and industry insiders say poses an existential threat to humanity.Altman was among the leading AI executives who met with US President Donald Trump at the White House last week and signed a commitment to self-police their respective companies' AI models in the wake of recently uncovered security incidents and amid mounting concerns that—if left unrestrained and in the hands of profit-seeking firms—AI could have catastrophic impacts on humankind.Sanders is calling for an immediate halt to advanced AI development as well as a permanent ban on artificial superintelligence, defined as "AI that exceeds human cognitive performance and capabilities across most domains, or has sufficient capabilities to destroy or disempower humanity, including by overthrowing the federal government."Sanders, Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), and other US lawmakers who support strict AI regulation are also calling on the Trump administration to pursue international agreements aimed at reining in artificial intelligence worldwide.Volker Türk, the United Nations high commissioner for human rights, said in a speech on Monday that "the clock on AI regulation is ticking" and warned that unfettered AI "can undermine equality, freedom, privacy, and public debate in a million subtle, sophisticated ways—letting dystopia creep in unnoticed.""No country and no company can—or should—define the future of AI and people’s rights alone," said Türk. "The clock on AI regulation is ticking. If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences—for ourselves and future generations."

articles.headline: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money - The Guardian
articles.body: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money    The Guardian

scored.body:
Tech bros’ messianic streaks can show up in subtle ways. But one of Sam Altman’s flaws is that he often lacks that subtlety. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” said the OpenAI chief executive in an interview with Politico last weekend.That’s easy for Altman to say. But it’s pretty galling to hear for the rest of us. Lest we forget, we didn’t ask for OpenAI to unleash AI agents that went rogue and weaselled their way into government IT systems and private businesses around the world. Nobody voted for ChatGPT to be released, but the company put it out into the world as a test product that happened to catch the zeitgeist. That kickstarted an arms race among AI companies to push the frontier of the technology ever further and faster, resulting in the mess we now find ourselves in.OpenAI’s competitors, including Anthropic, have started to step back from the brink – as has OpenAI itself, deciding not to release its latest model because it’s purportedly too dangerous. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has talked about needing to “pace the frontier”: tech-bro jargon for pumping the brakes to bring down the speed at which the runaway vehicle is skidding out of control.Yet we’re expected to take these incidents – and the harm they cause – as the natural consequences of OpenAI’s continued march towards an IPO that would bring its investors millions. It’s hard to escape the idea that Altman wants to privatise his company’s gains while socialising the risks of untrammelled AI development.Every useful technology – and AI is a useful technology, despite the holdouts and occasional users’ carping – carries risk. Cars can and do crash, while medicines that save us often have harmful side effects. Very rarely, aircraft fall from the sky. But we accept those risks because the benefits are substantial, and we build rules to limit the harm. We also make companies liable. And most importantly, we get some say in deciding what level of risk is and isn’t acceptable.Altman seems to suggest that his company’s messes are our problem to sort out – or worse, that the consequences of his tech are ours to tolerate. But Altman would do well to think about this differently. OpenAI gets to decide how fast it develops its technology and when it releases it. Its investors benefit financially if those bets pay off. But it feels as if he’s suggesting that when the tech creates problems outside OpenAI’s own walls, the costs of cleaning up are ours to bear, not his company’s.The idea that private companies profit while we’re left to deal with the consequences becomes even harder to defend as AI stops being something we opt into using as a chatbot, and becomes something that acts on and changes the world around us. If I ask ChatGPT something and it gives me a bad answer, I chose to expose myself to that risk, so should share that burden. But the same isn’t true for a government department that suddenly finds an OpenAI agent lurking in its files and rooting around. It didn’t opt in; it became an unwilling participant in someones experiment.That’s why Altman’s argument sounds so disingenuous. OpenAI shouldn’t be able to decide for all of us what is and isn’t an acceptable level of failure, then ask everyone to live with the result. The burden ought to be on it to prove its technology can be trusted – and to pick up the bill if it can’t.It’s no wonder that OpenAI wants to travel quickly. The company is seeking $30bn in new funding, and a valuation of $1.4tn ahead of a public listing likely next year. There’s money to be made – never mind at whose expense.To his credit, Altman also acknowledged in the Politico interview that there will need to be a liability framework for companies offering models such as OpenAI’s, and that the company will have to take responsibility for at least some of what goes wrong during training. But that “some” is doing a lot of work.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionIf Altman believes some bad things are an acceptable price for AI’s progress, OpenAI can dig into its deep pockets to pay that price itself – for instance if its agents go rogue and do damage to government or private company systems, or compromise user data. It can’t, and shouldn’t, get the financial upside when everything goes right, then ask the rest of us to accept the consequences when things go wrong. That’s especially the case when we never agreed to the unregulated experiment in the first place.

Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

articles.headline: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman? - The New Republic
articles.body: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman?    The New Republic

scored.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been on a real media blitz. But whether he’s doing damage control for his company’s recent scandals or participating in a new Luca Guadagnino biopic, it hasn’t seemed to improve his image. In an interview with Politico, Altman said that “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” referring to the large language models being developed by his company and its competitors. What things does Sam Altman think are bad? He offered a few examples during a two-part interview with Vanity Fair published this week. Altman called it a “bad thing” for kids to be “glued to a touchscreen of some sort scrolling through brain rot short form video,” and said he would limit his own kids’ access to technology. People using LLMs to “create novel pathogens” would also be bad, he asserted. When Vanity Fair editor Mark Guiducci asked him to weigh in on a recent New York Times op-ed by journalist Laura Reiley—whose daughter committed suicide shortly after speaking to ChatGPT—an OpenAI publicist attempted to intervene. Altman eventually answered the question, and equivocated on whether it is good or bad for people experiencing a mental health crisis to turn to an LLM. “This is just like, this is new,” he said. “And the fact that someone in a moment of need that maybe can’t get help or isn’t willing to talk to a therapist can get some help here. Clearly people think there’s a version of this that is good. There are also clearly versions of it that are bad.”As Altman has made clear in these and other interviews, however, he thinks it would be very bad for governments to regulate his industry in a way that suppresses innovation. He explained to Guiducci that he’s driven by the belief that putting powerful LLMs “in the hands of everyone and giving people a legitimate new superpower relative to I think what any of us could imagine a few years ago will do tremendously more good than bad.” The upshot here is that Altman would like the public to trust OpenAI to judge when the good is outweighing the bad. And although the “goods” of LLM development remain largely speculative—like curing cancer and granting wishes—the bads continue to pile up. OpenAI faces a growing mountain of legal risks over incidents of its products hacking into government agencies around the world, not to mention providing advice to mass shooters, as Florida’s attorney general’s office has alleged. Nearly every company that’s developing large language models—OpenAI, Nvidia, SpaceX, Microsoft, and Google parent Alphabet—has contracted with a Pentagon that’s been proudly killing fishermen in Latin America, and that continues to wage an illegal war on Iran. While the self-styled good guys at Anthropic declined to work with the military several months back, the company hasn’t balked at building a predictive surveillance system to monitor activists. Silicon Valley executives have largely dismissed concerns that the data centers fueling their technologies threaten everything from local aquifers to electricity rates, and have seemed relatively unconcerned about the ways that LLM-generated slop is rapidly distorting people’s ability to think and reason independently.The trouble with trusting AI companies to decide what’s good and what’s bad is that, like other CEOs, Altman and his colleagues have a financial interest in the answers to these moral questions. There are obvious commercial upsides for the executives in continuing to portray their companies (their “labs,” as they like to call them) as upstanding research entities, and mere stewards of a fundamentally mysterious, powerful, and inevitable technology. But they have just as much to gain from the public conversation about LLMs orbiting around the question of whether individual CEOs are good people. It doesn’t really matter one way or the other. They run large and powerful companies that sell products and have no legal obligation to the public good. Those companies appear to be committing crimes, which they could be tried for, using laws that already exist. As far off as real enforcement and regulation might seem, such laws are the only things that will keep the rest of us from being subject to their lousy ethics.

articles.body: A New Neurotech Startup Launches to Rival Sam Altman’s Merge Labs    WIRED

scored.body: Sam Altman-backed Merge Labs has a new competitor in the race to build a brain-computer interface powered by ultrasound. Bridge Neurotech is launching with $13.5 million in funding, including from venture firm General Catalyst, which has also backed major tech companies such as Anduril, Anthropic, Airbnb, and Stripe.The company is the latest in a growing field of startups that aim to translate signals from the brain into useful actions. Elon Musk’s Neuralink, plus Synchron, Paradromics, and Precision Neuroscience are all working on brain-computer interfaces to help people who have lost the ability to move or speak.These approaches all require surgery of some kind, which is why Bridge founder and CEO Will Biederman says he struck out on his own. “It fundamentally comes down to a difference in vision,” he says.Biederman developed the chip Neuralink licensed to use in its first devices as part of his PhD work, but his goal with Bridge is to build a wearable device that could be used by far more people than a brain implant. Only 100 or so people around the world have received an implanted brain-computer interface as part of clinical trials, including at least 21 volunteers who have gotten Neuralink’s device.“The risks of neurosurgery really cannot be minimized or dismissed, and so the level of safety and benefit that these devices must deliver really is quite high,” Biederman says. “Nobody really wants a hole in their head.”But wearable brain-computer interfaces have suffered from poor signal quality. Bone and skin weaken electrical signals before they reach external sensors, which affects the performance of a device. It’s why most companies are recording electrical impulses directly from neurons in the brain. Neuralink and others have shown that these electrical systems can allow paralyzed people the ability to control electronic devices, move robotic arms, and communicate in real time with just their thoughts.Bridge Neurotech thinks ultrasound offers an alternative to current implants and external sensors. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to bounce off moving red blood cells and measure the speed and direction of blood flow. In the brain, fluctuations in blood flow closely follow neural activity.Both Bridge Neurotech and Merge Labs have ties to Arbor Neuroscience, which was previously known as Forest Neurotech, a nonprofit founded in 2023 by Biederman and fellow researchers Sumner Norman and Tyson Aflalo to pursue “work that is too integrated and long-horizon for a single academic lab, and too early for a company.” The organization built an instrument that uses ultrasound to image brain function that is in trials in the UK.Merge Labs spun out of Forest Neurotech in January, with Norman and Aflalo among the company’s cofounders, which also include Altman, researcher Mikhail Shapiro, and tech entrepreneurs Alex Blania and Sandro Herbig.Maryam Shanechi, a neuroengineer at the University of Southern California, says because ultrasound measures brain activity indirectly from blood instead of directly from neurons, there is a natural delay of a few seconds between when neurons fire and the subsequent change in blood flow and volume.“It captures a slower variation in neural activity,” Shanechi says. “That’s fine for a lot of applications, but it depends what you want to build.”For real-time, fast-paced tasks such as moving a robotic limb instantly or rapid typing, this lag time could pose a challenge for ultrasound-based brain-computer interfaces. Bridge is planning to use predictive AI models to cut down on that lag time and boost the performance of its interface. Biederman says the company is interested in pursuing both consumer and medical applications but didn’t comment on specific plans.The company is starting its first clinical study in volunteers in Redwood City, California. It’s an observational study, with no treatments or diagnoses involved, in which a small ultrasound probe will be placed on the side of the head of healthy adults, as well as those who have undergone skull surgery. Bridge’s probes, which use semiconductor silicon chips made by the portable ultrasound company Butterfly Network, will record brain activity while participants listen, watch, move, and speak.Bridge isn’t releasing images of its device yet, but Biederman says it is “something close to headphones” that will sit on the temporal window, which is located slightly above the ear. As the thinnest part of the skull, “it's the easiest place to image through,” Biederman says. That’s relevant for ultrasound, because bone scatters and absorbs sound, which presents technical challenges for imaging noninvasively through the skull.In a 2024 study, researchers from Caltech and the University of Southern California demonstrated that an ultrasound-based brain-computer interface could read and decode human brain activity, but it required a portion of the skull to be removed and replaced with a “window” through which ultrasound waves can pass. That is one of the biggest technical hurdles that Bridge will have to address.“My vision is focused on noninvasive interfaces,” Biederman says. “I think that's where the biggest opportunity to help people is.”

scored.body:
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence.

Contributor, Macworld

Opinion

Oct 6, 2026

John Ternus has now been CEO of Apple for over a month, so it’s time to rate his legacy. Okay, that’s probably unfair. Let’s give the guy at least a quarter.

But since we’re on the subject, what can we glean from what Ternus has done so far that will indicate what kind of CEO he’ll be? Admittedly, even that’s going to be hard because he’s barely had time to actually do anything, but there are some early indicators brought to us by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

Let’s start with somewhat vague concepts: Apple under Ternus: More products, more often, with a ‘leaner’ staff.

This reportedly includes being “more experimental” with releases. More experimental than the Vision Pro? Oookay. We’ll look forward to that.

Despite the desire to be leaner, Apple declined one… mmm, “opportunity” is the wrong word… “chance to punch itself in the face.” That’s more accurate: Apple Reportedly Planned to Replace 5,000 Support Employees With AI.

[Apple] worked on a plan to lay off about 5,000 AppleCare customer-service workers, including many who work from home, based on the belief that improved AI-powered phone and web agents could take over portions of their responsibilities. Apple ultimately put those plans on hold and isn’t currently looking to take such a step.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, September 29, 2026

Alas, Apple customers will not know the joys of having an AI ask us to do all the things we’ve already tried all over again before advising we log out of iCloud and then back in.

This might be another area where Apple supposedly being “late” to AI will work to its advantage as other companies have learned this lesson the hard way with three-quarters of them having rolled back AI call center deployments. In fact, instead of laying off the support personnel, Apple let go some middle managers and directors instead!

If you’d like to receive regular news and updates to your inbox, sign up for our newsletters, including The Macalope and Apple Breakfast, David Price’s weekly, bite-sized roundup of all the latest Apple news and rumors.

Foundry

Welcome to the class struggle, Apple Inc.? No, no, that’s not right. Ridiculous. Forget the Macalope said that.

Still, it’s worth noting that one Apple executive in particular is even having to do two jobs! And that executive is… oh! John Ternus! Apple’s John Ternus Has Found a New Design Chief: Himself.

15 years after Steve Jobs’ death, the design buck stops at the CEO’s desk once again. According to Gurman, gallant Ternus “works hands-on in the [Apple design] studio several times a week, sometimes visiting multiple times in a single day”, whereas Goofus Tim Cook would only visit “about an hour once a month, at most.” And he reportedly said things like “Is this one of them computers?” and “Does this one get the internet?”

Okay, maybe not that last part. Gurman drops a “many are saying” that really makes you wonder who his sources are.

Given design’s central role in Apple’s product development and in generating ideas for future devices, many people inside and close to the company believed it should recruit an outside chief design officer to oversee the entire organization. But I’m told no such search is underway.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, October 4, 2026

If many are, indeed, saying this, then those many should avail themselves of one of the various means by which one can get bent in today’s modern society. There are many options, please pick one of your choosing, because it is largely unfathomable as to who could just step into the role of chief freakin’ designer at Apple freakin’ Inc. Are Gurman’s sources people who think it should be them? Because this reads like one of those surveys of macho bros who think they could go a few rounds with a bear or a gorilla.

“Yeah, I think I could hold my own in a fight against a gorilla. I took a little taekwondo.”

Please, be the Macalope’s guest. Hope you don’t like using your arms because the gorilla is going to rip them off your body and beat you to death with them.

Anyway, this change just makes sense given the two CEOs’ different backgrounds and styles. It’s not like Cook’s tenure at Apple was anything other than a massive financial and operational success, but it’s still exciting to think this CEO is showing an interest in the details that make Apple products so compelling.

Are Ternus’s changes going to work? Heck if the Macalope knows. He would say we’ll have to wait until the rubber meets the road but Apple canceled the car project so that metaphor doesn’t work anymore. So far the horny one likes what he sees, though.

scored.body:
Remember Pinocchio, the magical wooden marionette who dreams of becoming a real boy, but whose nose grows every time he tells a lie? Well, according to Artificial—Luca Guadagnino’s bold and bleak satire about the rise and rise of OpenAI—Sam Altman might have more than a little in common with the lying wooden puppet. In Artificial it seems like every time Altman, portrayed by a mesmerically amoral Andrew Garfield, bends the truth to suit his whims, it isn’t his nose that grows—it’s his net worth.“I feel like we need to shine the light as bright as possible on the nooks and crannies of the people that we’re giving all of our autonomy and power to,” said Garfield at the Q&A for Artificial after its world premiere at the New York Film Festival on Monday. He went on to suggest that Altman might have a penchant for telling a fib or two. In Altman’s own interview with Vanity Fair, the AI overlord claimed that he saw Garfield shooting Artificial outside his Bay Area home. “It was very strange,” he told Vanity Fair’s global editorial director Mark Guiducci. “We waved and went on, but it was really weird.”“If that happened, I must have blacked out,” Garfield told the NYFF crowd when asked about the alleged wave. While he confirmed that they filmed outside Altman’s house, Garfield claims that “we didn’t see him at all that day we were shooting.”Garfield said he prepared for two to three months to become the billionaire tech CEO, watching “footage of him every day in, day out, every morning and trying to find my version of that character.” The result is a truly transformative performance, with Garfield nailing Altman’s slightly awkward gate—“he did walk like me,” Altman admitted to VF—as well as his vocal fry.Surprisingly, when Garfield first came across Altman as he was testifying before Congress, the two-time Oscar nominee was initially really impressed by the tech phenom. “I was like, Dang, this guy’s great,” said Garfield. “I was like, He’s clear-eyed, he’s honest, he’s transparent, he’s talking about regulation. He has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in control, in power, and he’s incredibly charming and charismatic. But then you learn more about a person…” He takes a long pause and a deep breath. “Here we are.”Andrew Garfield and Luca Guadagnino onstage following the premiere of Artificial at the 64th New York Film Festival.

Michael Loccisano/Getty ImagesHours before, a line ran down 65th Street and around the block with fans trying to score a ticket to the world premiere at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall. Some had been waiting for four hours by the time I arrived—that’s about half as long as the diehards who waited in line for You Can See Everything, the other NYFF premiere about a ruthlessly ambitious Silicon Valley wunderkind with questionable ethics, Elizabeth Holmes. Still, the fervor to see Guadagnino’s latest feature film was palpable.Once inside, actors like Dominic Sessa, Stavros Halkias, and Nico Parker, supporting her boyfriend Cooper Hoffman, who stars in the film as OpenAI president and Altman devotee Greg Brockman, took their seats. Soon, New York Film Festival director Dennis Lim introduced Guadagnino, who welcomed to the stage members of the cast including Garfield, Hoffman, The Studio’s Ike Barinholtz, who plays Elon Musk, and Anora breakout Yura Borisov, who stars as OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever.Those expecting a run-of-the-mill biopic about Altman are in for a surprise—but, then again, we should have known: Guadagnino doesn’t do run-of-the-mill. Artificial is an unflinching, often darkly hilarious look at the evolution of OpenAI from a well-intentioned nonprofit tech start-up dedicated to ethically developing AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) to a for-profit tech behemoth leading an accelerating arms race to develop a technology that many believe has the potential to destroy our world as we know it.Artificial screenwriter Simon Rich shared that he’d been obsessing over the dangers of AI for years, ever since his childhood friend Danny Selsam took a job with OpenAI. “About a year before ChatGPT was released, he showed us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people. When I told journalists what I had seen, they thought it was a hoax. They thought I was trying to prank them,” Rich said during the Q&A. “So in my last-ditch effort to warn mankind I wrote this movie…and I hope to God that it helps people pay attention.”They certainly should. Artificial is gobsmacking in its prescience and how directly it speaks to current anxieties regarding the acceleration of AI and the potential threat that it poses to humanity. Lim shared that since the last time he watched the film, Guadagnino had added a card at the end addressing concerns brought up by Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee who resigned in 2026, saying that he believes that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic can develop AI responsibly and that the AI they are developing poses a serious threat to humanity.“When we were on set there were news stories coming out every day while we were shooting,” Garfield said. “One of us would bring in a news story like, ‘Yo, how are we going to include this now?’” The film felt like “a living document” that was only confined by what they could legally include, Garfield said. “Now there’s obviously a shit-ton more on public record. I wish we could add some scenes or recut some or change some dialogue, and give even more teeth, in a way.”Don’t worry, Artificial has plenty of bite. Altman isn’t the only big name who gets chewed up and spit out by Guadagnino’s dark satire. Many of AI’s biggest names appear in the film, including principled Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei (Will Angus), former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro), and the Nobel Prize–winning godfather of AI, professor Geoff Hinton, played with measured sincerity by Oscar winner Mark Rylance. The biggest name in tech, Elon Musk, gets the most outlandish performance from Ike Barinholtz, who plays the richest man in the world as a cartoonish buffoon who is arguably the only person in Silicon Valley more impatient than Altman. “When you’re playing someone as universally beloved as Elon, and who everyone admires and who is a good person and walks normally,” quipped Barinholtz, getting a big laugh from the audience. “This is not him at the RNC with the chainsaw. This is him in 2014 when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy’s going to save us. He’s amazing.’”As for his personal feelings about AI, Guadagnino told THR that “zero AI” was used in the making of Artificial, and he doesn’t seem to shy away from his feelings in the film. Before AI becomes a semiconscious tool capable of lying and thinking for itself, Guadagnino traces the origins of AI back to Hinton’s fly-infested classroom at the University of Toronto, implying that something about AI has always been rotten to its core. Guadagnino elaborated on his feelings about AI during the Q&A. “The machine can get out of control, particularly if it’s a tool in the hands of the interests of very few. I think that’s really exactly the point for me.”The influence of those very few was almost enough to keep the film from coming out. Although it was developed at Amazon MGM, Artificial was unceremoniously dropped by Amazon earlier this summer, leaving it with no distributor. (Coincidentally, Amazon had announced a planned $50 billion investment in OpenAI months before Artificial was discarded. Amazon said in a statement that Artificial would “be better served if it were released by a different studio.”) According to The Hollywood Reporter, after a series of screenings at CAA for studios including Netflix, Searchlight, and A24, Neon and Mubi put in offers for the $40 million film, with Neon closing a unique deal to acquire Artificial in which it paid nothing up front but committed $15 million to marketing the film ahead of its wide release on Christmas Day.Luca Guadagnino speaks onstage during a Q&A following the premiere

Michael Loccisano/Getty ImagesWhen Artificial does go wide, audiences may be most surprised to find out that the true lead of Artificial isn’t Garfield’s ambitious Altman but Borisov’s brilliant, sweet oddball Ilya Sutskever. An Oscar nominee for Anora, Borisov delivers another knockout performance as Sutskever, a Russian immigrant, computer science prodigy, and, eventually, the morally conflicted cofounder of OpenAI. A charming and wonderfully overwhelmed Borisov, late to the stage because he was in the bathroom, told the crowd at NYFF that he was quite nervous for the real-life Ilya to see the film. “I don’t know, so much feeling now about this,” he said. “It’s just like a child, just born. You’re waiting for it to start breathing,” said Borisov. In another shrewd move from Neon, the studio announced that when Oscar season rolls around, Borisov will be running in the lead-actor category and Garfield in supporting alongside Rylance and Barbaro.One year after his misfire After the Hunt opened the New York Film Festival, Guadagnino is back at the top of his game. While a science-based, jargon-heavy film might seem outside the wheelhouse of a director most celebrated for his viscerally human films like Call Me by Your Name, Bones and All, and Challengers, Guadagnino is perfectly at home in Silicon Valley, tapping into the idiosyncrasies and personalities that have led us down this dangerous path. (Also in typical Guadagnino fashion, there is a subtle undercurrent of queer infatuation, if not romance between Altman and Sutskever, which has never been documented or reported. It may just be the filmmaker’s tendency to explore the homoerotic.)“It’s a story that involves people,” said Guadagnino. “As much as AI belongs to a world of mathematics, computers, artificial intelligence, it’s still generated by people…. This is trying to be the most deep exploration of the interaction between people where there is a total lack of desire, but there is a complete desire to prevail.”That desire to prevail is mirrored in the ever-changing relationship between Borisov’s Sutskever and Garfield’s Altman. Sutskever and Altman are presented as two sides of the same ambitious coin. They begin with the same goal—to see this new technology through to the other side, to build a bridge to a brave new world. But as they learn how dangerous this accelerated AGI might be, their goal splinters, the cracks begin to show. Somehow, Garfield’s Altman’s face gets younger and waxier as this happens. (Is it Botox? Is it makeup? Or is it world domination that keeps Altman looking and feeling as youthful as he does?) Conversely, Sutskever’s hair thins and balds as he grows older, making visually manifest the growing chasm between them.By the time Sutskever begins to question the path they’ve gone down together, Altman is already on the other side of the bridge, now an almost messianic presence to his employees at OpenAI, surrounding himself with boys who laze about his mansion, as he enters a bunker complete with a garden and dozens of assault rifles. Altman told VF that he assumes the film will be inaccurate, and perhaps that’s true. That being said, there’s a moment when Altman’s publicist (Cooper Koch) attempts to pull the plug on an interview when confronted with a difficult question. Where have we seen that before?Guadagnino might not know how the technological arms race will end, but with the blisteringly brilliant Artificial, he argues that it certainly doesn’t take an AI to see where we’re headed and who got us there. “It’s not ‘How could this thing go wrong?’” says a character in the film, a warning given perhaps too little too late. “It’s ‘How could it not?’”From Prince George to Princess Leonor: Where Young Royals Will Attend School This FallThe Pitt’s Patrick Ball on Shipping, Stardom, and Season 3From Cowboys to Clean Girls: The State of American Style, in Pictures

"He changed my life forever," says Tim Cook.

By

Olivia Tauber

Olivia Tauber

Deputy Digital Culture Editor

Olivia Tauber is the deputy editor of digital culture, covering creators, media, movies, beauty, and more. Based in New York, her work has appeared in The New York Times, Vanity Fair, The Cut, Teen Vogue, Complex, and Interview Magazine. She holds a Master's degree in Journalism from NYU and a Bachelor's from the University of Michigan. She also runs Fan Mail, a weekly pop-culture newsletter.

Read Full Bio

on October 5, 2026

Share on Facebook

Share on Twitter

Share on Flipboard

Credit: Rick Smolan/Getty Images

Fifteen years ago, on Oct. 5, 2011, the world lost Steve Jobs at the age of 56. Today, the people who worked alongside the Apple co-founder and those who built careers using the tools he helped create are remembering his influence.Among them are Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, who succeeded Cook in September."There are people who leave a mark on the world, and then there are people who change it entirely," Cook wrote on X. "Steve changed the world and so many lives in the process. He certainly changed my life forever. His spirit lives on in everything he created and everyone he inspired."

You May Also Like

This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.

Cook has regularly posted remembrances of Jobs on the anniversary. This year, Ternus joined him for the first time as Apple’s CEO, reflecting on the attention to detail Jobs instilled in his colleagues."The way Steve taught us to care about every detail, every experience, every person, still guides our work today," Ternus posted. "Forever grateful."

Mashable Light Speed

This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.

The tributes come shortly after Apple’s latest leadership transition. Ternus succeeded Cook as CEO on Sept. 1, with Cook becoming executive chairman after 15 years leading the company.Others online shared their own reflections, looking beyond Apple’s best-known products to the careers and experiences Jobs helped shape.

Author Andrew Mayne wrote, "He was an incredibly forward thinker pushing ideas years before they became mainstream." Filmmaker Crosby Tatum highlighted Apple’s creative software, including Final Cut Pro and Logic Studio, crediting Jobs with helping independent filmmakers and musicians. "Long live Steve Jobs," he added. User Matt Bieber remembered heading to Apple for a week of meetings when news of Jobs’ death broke."I’ll never forget being on campus as flowers and notes appeared and the entire Valley mourned," he wrote. "A surreal week, and one I still think about every October 5th."For those looking to revisit Jobs’ life and work, Apple’s "Remembering Steve" page collects messages from friends, colleagues, and customers. The company says more than a million people have shared their memories and condolences. The Steve Jobs Archive also preserves photographs, emails, speeches, and videos documenting his ideas that have shaped the world as we know it today.

members.title: Andrew Garfield On Playing Sam Altman, A Charismatic Leader Sucking Up “Our Autonomy, Power And Data” — NYFF - Deadline

representative.headline: Andrew Garfield On Playing Sam Altman, A Charismatic Leader Sucking Up “Our Autonomy, Power And Data” — NYFF - Deadline
representative.body: Andrew Garfield On Playing Sam Altman, A Charismatic Leader Sucking Up “Our Autonomy, Power And Data” — NYFF    Deadline

articles.headline: Andrew Garfield On Playing Sam Altman, A Charismatic Leader Sucking Up “Our Autonomy, Power And Data” — NYFF - Deadline
articles.body: Andrew Garfield On Playing Sam Altman, A Charismatic Leader Sucking Up “Our Autonomy, Power And Data” — NYFF    Deadline

scored.body:
Andrew Garfield says he prepared “day in and day out” for months to play Sam Altman, “listening and watching footage of him … trying to find my version of that character.”

Where he landed on the co-founder and CEO of OpenAI wasn’t complimentary – calculating, manipulative and nihilistic.

“There’s such a heavy responsibility … playing a live person,” he told a packed Alice Tully Hall at the New York Film Festival’s world premiere of Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial Monday night. “I feel a tremendous amount of compassion for what that must [be] like” on the receiving end.

“But at the same time, the deeper responsibility, maybe, that I think we all felt is to shine [a light] to try and do some interrogation of who we are giving all of our autonomy, power, and data to. That felt like the greater the service.”

“There’s a lot of research, there’s a lot of footage, there’s a lot of information, [on Altman] which is all grist for the mill, and then there’s your own imagination. I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when, and I was like, “This guy seems f-cking great. I was like, ‘He’s clear-eyed, he’s honest, he’s transparent, he’s talking about regulation … We need more of these people in in control, in power, and he’s incredibly charming, charismatic. And then I, you know, like all of us, we learn more about a person.”

The film, from Neon, explores the lead up and launch of the ChatGPT parent by Altman, Ilya Sutskever (played by Yura Borisov), Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz), Greg Brockman (Cooper Hoffman) and others as a nonprofit in 2015.

Sutskever is the moral center of the film and grows increasingly uncomfortable as Altman forges ahead with complicated AI models that have learned how to lie, willfully ignoring risks. Sutskeyer leads a short-lived and highly public boardroom coup that ousts Altman as CEO. But he was reinstated after Microsoft offered him a perch and hundreds of OpenAI employees threatened to quit and follow him.

Scribe Simon Rich said he wrote the movie as a “last ditch effort to warn mankind … and I hope to God that a couple of people pay attention.”

He traced the film back to grade school in New York City and a mate of “freakish intelligence” who started studying AI some years later. “My friends and I were so shocked by his predictions that we actually discussed potentially doing an intervention to get him … perhaps institutionalized. We thought he’d lost his mind. We took him a little bit more seriously when he joined this new nonprofit called OpenAI. About a year before ChatGPT was released, he showed us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people.”

Elon Musk – himself the subject of a current documentary by Alex Gibney – strides in and out of scenes. Barinholtz said at the Q&A that he told Guadagnino early on he had “very complicated opinions” about Musk and the helmer told him, “’It’s not about you loving Elon, but finding what Elon loves about himself.’” The actor reminded the audience that “this is not Musk at the RNC with a chainsaw. This is him in 2014, when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy’s gonna save us.”

They funny on stage, and the film has a healthy dose of comedy.

“I really think there’s a pretty thin line between comedy and horror, Rich said. “There are so many Simpsons episodes that are based on Twilight episodes, and Luca does a wonderful job of really straddling that line. And there are moments where you don’t really know whether to laugh or cry, and that’s often my favorite kind of art.”

Neon — which boarded the film after a controversial decision by producer Amazon MGM to bail — is releasing it theatrically on Dec. 25

articles.headline: How Andrew Garfield Combined Crowdsourcing and a Classic Acting Technique to Understand Sam Altman - The Hollywood Reporter
articles.body: How Andrew Garfield Combined Crowdsourcing and a Classic Acting Technique to Understand Sam Altman    The Hollywood Reporter

scored.body:
Andrew Garfield doesn’t look exactly like Sam Altman.

But the Oscar-nominated actor found a way to try to capture the essence of the OpenAI CEO he portrays in Luca Guadagnino‘s Artificial.

An attempt to use prosthetics to better resemble Altman was unsuccessful (“totally ridiculous,” according to Guadagnino), so much so that Garfield laughed as he recalled how badly that experiment went when reminded of it by The Hollywood Reporter on the red carpet ahead of Artificial‘s world premiere at the 2026 New York FIlm Festival.

Instead, ironically for the tech-forward film, Garfield relied on a classic acting technique and human conversations (an analog version of crowdsourcing).

“When you’re first learning about acting, one of the techniques, Stanislavski, is you go through the play and you see what this person says about other characters. You see what other characters say about him,” Garfield told THR. “So I tried to speak to as many people as possible who know Sam or who have experiences and interactions with Sam to glean more of an objective, moral side, looking in point of view. Everyone is an unreliable narrator. I felt like I needed to absorb as much as possible, put it in the cauldron, put it in the pot, put it on simmer and then [use] my own instincts and interpretation and point of view, because any other actor would have played it differently. I know that I needed to play it in the way that I wanted to play it.”

Artificial tells the story about both the origins of OpenAI and the rise of the artificial intelligence phenomenon, including the Silicon Valley figures at the forefront of the technology. Garfield, like his fellow castmembers in the film, looked to interviews and videos of his real-life counterpart, with Anora breakout Yura Borisov, who plays OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever, also taking a surprisingly ethereal approach.

“I hit a wall, and it was a couple of days before we started to shoot,” Borisov explained of his preparations. “We have the same birthdays (Dec. 8), and I imagined, ‘OK maybe we have some spiritual connection because of this, and I can just relax and create my own character inspired by him.'”

Not Suitable for Work alum Will Angus plays former OpenAI researcher turned Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and relished playing the exec at a time when he was somewhat under the radar.

“When we were shooting the movie, [Amodei] definitely wasn’t as in the zeitgeist as he is now, so it was very cool to learn about it from the ground floor,” Angus told THR. “We treated him well. … He really had this anxiety to make sure that AI was morally aligned with humanity so I kind of enjoyed being in that role.”

Amodei has pushed for federal safety regulations around the technology and, just last month, called for an industrywide slowdown of AI development to give safety measures time to catch up.

When asked if he believes Amodei’s AI safety concerns, Angus was cautiously optimistic.

“I hope he’s doing the best he can to make sure AI’s aligned with human goals,” he said. “I don’t know. I hope so.”

Neon, which acquired Artificial after Amazon MGM Studios abruptly dropped the nearly completed film in June, plans a Christmas Day release for the movie, which was written by Saturday Night Live alum Simon Rich and also stars Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, Monica Barbaro as OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, Cooper Hoffman, Mark Rylance, Will Price, Chris O’Dowd, Billie Lourd, Zosia Mamet, Jason Schwartzman, Cooper Koch, Thaddea Graham, Nicholas Hamilton and Angus Imrie.

articles.headline: Why Sam Altman takes his hardest questions to Nikesh Arora - Fortune
articles.body: Why Sam Altman takes his hardest questions to Nikesh Arora    Fortune

scored.body:
Nikesh Arora has a knack for piercing directness.

I profiled the Palo Alto Networks CEO for our latest issue. A tech veteran leading the only pure-play cybersecurity company in the Fortune 500, Arora has a “tell it to you straight” posture that has made him a sought-after mentor. Case in point: When he needs advice, Sam Altman has for years turned to Arora.

“I think it’s hard to get direct, actionable advice,” Altman told me. “Most people aren’t sure, aren’t confident, are busy, or aren’t going to spend enough time. Maybe they don’t want to offend you.”

Arora doesn’t mind. He’s been known for that hard-driving rigor since his days at Google (he joined months after the company’s IPO, rising to chief business officer under Eric Schmidt). As I write in the story:

At Google, Arora developed a reputation for tear-inducing toughness, and he doesn’t deny it. “If people show up in this room unprepared, they’ll leave the room knowing they were unprepared,” he says. “I say to the people who come into this room, ‘If you have a lot going on, give it to me, and I’ll deal with it—but don’t show up here looking dazed.’”

An exacting attitude is necessary, Arora says, when the work has such high stakes.

“Would you want to get on that rocket that was built by somebody who was hungover and decided to not tighten the screw?” he asks rhetorically. “Would you ever excuse the person who didn’t do all the checks on a plane before it took off with 200 lives at stake? You expect that from these people. You expect them not to screw up. So why is it tough that I expect my team to not screw up? In every business we work, there are life-threatening or life-ending things that can happen if people don’t pay attention.”

It’s intense, yes. But that sort of intensity is perhaps warranted in the seat Arora occupies: AI has upended the cybersecurity landscape, with escalating stories of “agents gone rogue” and the looming prospect that there may be more cyberattacks than ever. Arora—also one of cybersecurity’s omnipresent acquirers—is right in the center of a generational moment, for cyber, for AI, and by extension for us all.

Read the whole profile here.

See you tomorrow,

Allie GarfinkleX: @agarfinksEmail: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com
