articles.headline: Glenn Thompson to Sam Altman: AI Must First 'Do No Harm' - Yahoo
articles.body: Glenn Thompson to Sam Altman: AI Must First 'Do No Harm'    Yahoo

scored.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman delivers a keynote speech at an annual event for developers in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026. (Kyodo via AP Images) ==KyodoHouse Agriculture Committee Chair G.T. Thompson, R-Pa., rejected OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's argument that society should tolerate some negative consequences from artificial intelligence in exchange for the technology's broader benefits."As someone who practiced healthcare for 28 years, I'm never willing to accept bad results. I think we just need to do our best," Thompson told reporters as concerns over AI increasingly spilled into the 2026 midterm elections.Asked directly whether he agreed with Altman's premise, Thompson replied, "No, I think we have to work harder to prevent any bad things from happening."Thompson was responding to Altman's comments to Politico earlier in the week, in which the OpenAI chief argued that some risks are an unavoidable consequence of allowing people broad access to increasingly capable AI systems."I think there's a lot of daylight," Altman said when asked how his approach differs from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's."We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said.Altman argued against concentrating control of powerful AI systems in the hands of a handful of companies, even if doing so might reduce some risks."I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits," Altman said, calling that approach "a completely unacceptable trade-off.""I wouldn't take a trade of saying, We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen," Altman added."Because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude more, good stuff than bad stuff."Altman drew a distinction, however, around existential dangers, saying he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks," including the possibility of "a serious loss of control to AI."Thompson acknowledged AI's potential upside, saying the technology could bring "tremendous solutions," including helping researchers pursue treatments for cancer and Alzheimer's disease. But he argued development should be governed by clear principles."The first principle is, 'Do no harm.' So we need to protect consumers, and that means, I think, building some guardrails, some guidelines, to do that," Thompson said, adding that a second principle should be to "foster innovation.""I think AI has a lot to do with that," Thompson said. "I don't think AI works without RI: real intelligence."The debate is no longer confined to theoretical concerns about rogue AI, deepfakes, fraud, or job displacement. The physical infrastructure required to power the AI boom has become an increasingly potent economic and environmental issue heading into November's midterm elections.Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, while many facilities also consume significant amounts of water for cooling.The Energy Information Administration says data centers are helping drive a sharp increase in U.S. electricity demand after years of relatively stagnant consumption.The agency expects U.S. electricity sales to rise nearly 2% this year to a record 4.135 trillion kilowatt-hours, with data-center development and manufacturing among the principal drivers.Those demands have fueled concern that households could ultimately shoulder the cost of new generation and transmission infrastructure required to serve data centers.They have also generated local opposition over water consumption, land use, noise and pollution, turning what was once largely a technology-policy debate into a pocketbook and quality-of-life issue.Congress has taken notice as the midterms approach.Energy prices are now playing prominently in competitive House and Senate races, including contests in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan and Colorado.The politics are scrambling traditional partisan divisions as Republicans who view AI leadership as critical to competing with China are confronting constituents worried about electricity bills and local development.Democrats, meanwhile, are seeking tougher environmental and consumer protections and are also weighing the jobs and investment promised by the AI boom.© 2026 Newsmax. scored.body: Sam Altman at the G7 summit on June 17, 2026, in Evian-les-Bains, France. In a new Vanity Fair interview, the OpenAI CEO also talks about Amazon dropping the movie, Elon Musk, his kids, his survivalist streak and why he still thinks AI’s future will be “all going to be great.”Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/Julia Demaree NikhinsonSam Altman has finally had his first real encounter with Andrew Garfield’s version of him.It happened outside Altman’s San Francisco home, where the actor was filming Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial,” the upcoming movie about Altman and the turmoil surrounding his artificial intelligence research and deployment company, OpenAI.One morning, Altman said, he walked down the street to get coffee and came upon a film set — and a man who looked eerily familiar.Article continues below this ad“There were all these cameras and there (was) a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something,” Altman told Vanity Fair in a new cover story interview published Monday, Oct. 5.“I waved at him that one time and that was it.”Garfield, Altman added, had apparently mastered one especially recognizable detail.Article continues below this ad“He did walk like me,” Altman said. “Actually, I’ll tell you something: They filmed outside of our house.”It’s a small, surreal detail from an unusually revealing interview with the OpenAI CEO, who spent two conversations with Vanity Fair discussing everything from the movie and his Hollywood doppelgänger to Elon Musk, parenthood, AI safety and the future of humanity.“Artificial,” directed by Guadagnino and starring Garfield as Altman, is scheduled to open in select theaters on Christmas Day.Here are the biggest revelations and lighter moments from the interview:Garfield’s Altman gets one thing very right — the walkPedestrians walk on Lombard Street past a driveway at the home of Sam Altman on April 10, 2026, in San Francisco.Lea Suzuki/S.F. ChronicleAltman has seen the trailer for “Artificial,” and he is not particularly worried about the filmmakers getting every detail of his life right.Article continues below this ad“I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” he said. “Except for the walk.”That, he added, was “good,” giving Garfield credit for capturing his distinctive style.But the experience of seeing somebody portray him outside his own house was more than a little weird.“I mean, it’s like a strange thing to see someone that has nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms or whatever,” he said.There is no Sam Altman bunker with guns on the wallThe trailer includes a particularly ominous image: Garfield’s Altman walking into a James Bond-style bunker with firearms displayed on the wall.Article continues below this adAltman says that part is fiction.“There’s no bunker with firearms on the wall,” he said.But the joke contains a kernel of truth. Altman revealed he does have what he calls a “survivalist mindset.”“At our ranch, we can survive off-grid, which I guess to many people would be considered a bugout plan,” he said.He then offered a line that seems destined for social media: “We don’t have a submarine.”Article continues below this adWhen asked whether he has a helicopter, he added: “No helicopter, no submarine.”Altman said he nevertheless became more convinced of the value of basic preparedness during the COVID-19 pandemic.“When COVID came, I had a big stack of masks ready to go, and I had enough canned food in the house that if the world had shut down, we could have had enough food for a while and we had water purification tablets.”Sam Altman speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on September 2, 2026 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. In a new Vanity Fair interview, the OpenAI CEO also talks about Amazon dropping the movie, Elon Musk, his kids, his survivalist streak and why he still thinks AI’s future will be “all going to be great.”Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesHe says Amazon had no role in the movie’s fateThe movie’s path to theaters became especially awkward after Amazon MGM Studios, which originally planned to distribute “Artificial,” abandoned the project.That decision came after Amazon announced a $50 billion investment in OpenAI. The companies’ strategic partnership also includes a major cloud-computing relationship.Altman said he had nothing to do with Amazon’s decision and no one on his behalf spoke to the tech giant about it.“No. I did not, and I don’t know of anyone else who did,” he said.Asked specifically about Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos, Altman was equally direct: “I never spoke to Jeff Bezos about it.”Amazon MGM ultimately said the movie would be “better served if it were released by a different studio,” he explained, and Neon picked it up.Altman isn’t exactly worried about being portrayed as the villain“Artificial” appears to take a darker view of the people and events behind the rise of OpenAI than Altman himself does, and that does not seem to bother him much.“I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie and maybe it will be good.”His qualification: “Good as a movie. It will not be good as an accurate depiction.”He calls Elon Musk a bully — but says he’ll work with himSam Altman (L) and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (R) attend a state dinner hosted by President Donald Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty ImagesThe interview also produced some unusually blunt words about Altman’s longtime rival.“Elon’s a bully,” Altman said. “And so I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose. And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while. But I will work with Elon, of course.”Altman was more forgiving when discussing another tech titan.He said he once had “a very evil caricature” of Mark Zuckerberg, co-founder of Facebook and Meta CEO, in his head before getting to know him personally.“I was projecting whatever people project onto someone with what they perceive as too much power and influence over the world,” he admitted.He wants more kids, but not for Silicon Valley’s pronatalist causeAltman, who already has two young children, said he plans to have more. But he rejected the idea that his interest in a larger family is connected to the Silicon Valley pronatalism movement, which advocates having more children partly in response to declining birth rates.“I love our kids so much and I know I’ll have more kids, but there’s no part of it which is like we got to fight against population decline,” he said. “I love a big family. It’s really great.”He also said his children have changed the way he thinks about AI, though perhaps not in the expected way.“I was very intent on not destroying the world before having kids,” Altman said. “I didn’t need kids to be like, ‘OK, I really shouldn’t gamble with the future’ or ‘We shouldn’t really gamble with the future of civilization.’”Despite running the company behind ChatGPT, Altman is cautious about putting the technology in front of young children.“I’m a big fan of limiting technology across the board for kids,” he said. “I think it’s good for kids to be running around outside and playing in nature and doing whatever kids have done for a long time.”As for his own children using ChatGPT?“I don’t have an age in mind where I would let my kids talk to ChatGPT yet, but it is certainly not now,” he said.He still says AI is close to AGISam Altman speaks at Dreamforce in San Francisco, Sept. 15, 2026. In a new Vanity Fair interview, the OpenAI CEO also talks about Amazon dropping the movie, Elon Musk, his kids, his survivalist streak and why he still thinks AI’s future will be “all going to be great.”Noah Berger/For the S.F. ChronicleOn one of the interview’s biggest questions, Altman stopped just short of declaring that artificial general intelligence, a theoretical form of AI that matches human cognitive abilities, has arrived.Asked whether it is here, he answered: “It’s subjective.”Asked how close it is: “It’s close.”Altman said OpenAI had been talking about this possibility for a decade and that the major change is that the rest of society is finally taking the prediction seriously.“10 years ago, very few people believed us,” he said. “Now most people believe us.”OpenAI has paused training because of safetyOne of the interview’s more significant revelations had little to do with Hollywood.Altman said OpenAI has already halted a model training run because its capabilities were advancing faster than the company expected.“We recently stopped a model training run, paused one because we thought we needed to make more progress on alignment and monitorability given how quickly the capabilities were advancing,” he said.When asked whether that means OpenAI needs to slow down now, Altman said the company has done so before.“There have been many times already, you just haven’t paid attention,” he said.He said OpenAI is talking with other AI companies and governments about shared safety standards and suggested cooperation between the United States and China could eventually be necessary.He says OpenAI would choose humanity over its stock priceWith OpenAI moving toward a potential IPO, Altman was asked what happens if investors demand faster growth at the expense of safety.His answer was blunt: “If we have to do something that is in the interest of the world, but not our particular shareholders, it’s going to be very easy about what we’re going to decide to do there.”And if investors punish the company?“Then it falls,” he said. “Maybe it falls a lot.”Altman said the company would accept volatility if necessary.“If there is ever a question about our share price going up or doing the right thing for the future of humanity, we are not going to pay attention to the share price in that moment,” he said.Privately, he’s more optimistic than he soundsDatebook PicksPerhaps the most revealing answer in the interview, Vanity Fair asked Altman to name something he privately believes about AI that he rarely says publicly because people might misunderstand it.His answer: “That it’s all going to be great.”Altman acknowledged that there are “very scary things” to deal with, and that OpenAI has to get those things right, “But I’m incredibly optimistic for the future.”

articles.headline: Did Sam Altman Lie About Waving to Andrew Garfield? - The Cut
articles.body: Did Sam Altman Lie About Waving to Andrew Garfield?    The Cut

scored.body:
By

Olivia Craighead,

a news writer for The Cut who covers pop culture and celebrity.

Previously, she wrote about pop culture and entertainment at Gawker.

Photo-Illustration: by The Cut; Photos: Getty Images

Sam Altman has always had what one might call a tenuous relationship with the truth. A New Yorker report from April revealed that OpenAI’s chief scientist once sent a secret memo to the board alleging that Altman had a “consistent pattern” of lying. So it makes sense that Altman may have embellished things when he said that he waved to Andrew Garfield while the actor was filming Artificial outside of his house.

On Monday, Vanity Fair published a lengthy interview with Altman, in which he said he has had only one minor interaction with Garfield, who’s playing Altman in Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial. Altman claims that, while the movie was filming outside of his house, he was walking to get coffee when he saw “a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something.”

“We waved and went on, but it was really weird,” Altman said. He was then asked if he had any follow-up contact with Garfield, but stated that he only “waved at him that one time and that was it.”

Coincidentally, Artificial premiered at the New York Film Festival on Monday night — the perfect time to ask  Garfield about his run-in with Altman. Did he learn anything from this interaction? Did Altman’s wave unlock the key to Garfield’s performance? Was it spooky seeing Altman while in Altman drag outside of Altman’s house? Those would have all been interesting insights, but Garfield said he didn’t see Altman at all.

“If that happened, I must have blacked out,” Garfield told the crowd at NYFF when asked about the alleged wave. He confirmed they did shoot outside Altman’s San Francisco home but said that “we didn’t see him at all that day we were shooting.”

Gosh, who are we to believe here? The guy who was briefly fired from his own company in part because he reportedly couldn’t stop lying? Or the guy who is Andrew Garfield? It’s just too hard to say.

scored.body: Apple CEO Tim Cook is stepping down, with the company announcing on Monday that John Ternus will take his place as the head of the technology giant.Cook will become the executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, the company said. Ternus will officially become CEO on Sept. 1."It has been the greatest privilege of my life to be the CEO of Apple and to have been trusted to lead such an extraordinary company," Cook said in a statement on Monday.John Ternus, senior vice president of hardware engineering at Apple Inc., during an Apple event in New York City, March 4, 2026.Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images"John Ternus has the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator, and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor. He is a visionary whose contributions to Apple over 25 years are already too numerous to count, and he is without question the right person to lead Apple into the future," Cook added.Cook has served as ​Apple's CEO ​since ⁠2011. The company said that under his leadership, Apple has grown from a market capitalization of approximately $350 billion to $4 trillion.Apple CEO Tim Cook speaks during the keynote address at an Apple special event, September 9, 2025 in Cupertino, Calif.Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesTernus has worked at Apple since 2001 and became a vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2013, according to the company. He has worked on several product lines, including the iPad, AirPods, and Apple Watch.“I am profoundly grateful for this opportunity to carry Apple’s mission forward," Ternus said. He worked under Steve Jobs and referred to Cook as his mentor."I am filled with optimism about what we can achieve in the years to come, and I am so happy to know that the most talented people on earth are here at Apple, determined to be part of something bigger than any one of us," he said.Last month, Cook sat down with "Good Morning America" co-anchor Michael Strahan ahead of the company's milestone 50th anniversary.Popular Reads"What a reflection," Cook said of Apple's longevity.When asked about Apple's biggest contributions over the past five decades, Cook pointed to innovation across industries."You know, you can focus on the product moments, reinventing music, reinventing the smartphone, bringing the creative arts to the table, the creative graphics. Saving people's lives with the watch," he said.At the time, Cook dismissed speculation about stepping down, noting, "I love what I do deeply.""Twenty-eight years ago, I walked into Apple and I've loved every day of it since," he said. "We've had ups and downs, but the people I work with are so amazing. They bring out the best in me. And hopefully, I can bring out the best in them. And Michael, I can't imagine life without Apple."

articles.headline: Artificial star Andrew Garfield reveals what he really thinks of Sam Altman - Yahoo
articles.body: Artificial star Andrew Garfield reveals what he really thinks of Sam Altman    Yahoo

scored.body:
Andrew Garfield admits he was initially charmed by Sam Altman before he portrayed the controversial CEO of OpenAI in director Luca Guadagnino’s new film “Artificial.”

“I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when,” Garfield said on Monday night at the movie’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival. “I was like, ‘This guy seems fucking great. He’s honest. He’s transparent. He’s talking about regulation, and he has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in control. He’s incredibly charming and charismatic.’ And then you learn more about a person.”

Garfield, who spent “two to three months” listening and watching footage of Altman while preparing to play him, described feeling a moral responsibility to participate in a movie like “Artificial.” When they were filming, Garfield recalls, “there were news stories coming out every day” about the dangers of AI.

“I wish we could give it even more teeth in a way,” Garfield said. “We need to shine the light as bright as possible at the nooks and crannies of people we’re giving all of our autonomy and power to.”

Garfield was joined at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall by Guadagnino, writer Simon Rich and actors Yura Borisov (as OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever), Ike Barinholtz (as Elon Musk) and Cooper Hoffman (as OpenAI president Greg Brockman). Monica Barbaro, who portrays OpenAI’s chief technology officer Mira Murati, wasn’t in attendance. The movie charts the evolution of OpenAI and dramatizes the tumultuous time when Altman was controversially fired and then rehired by the AI giant.

Garfield has portrayed many real people on screen, including Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” and composer Jonathan Larson in “Tick, Tick… Boom.” It’s a responsibility the actor doesn’t take lightly.

“I feel a tremendous amount of compassion for what that must feel like, being on the inside of his soul, going like, ‘That’s not me,’” Garfield said of Altman. “I imagine it would feel confronting. I would feel that way. I’m projecting.”

In any case, the real Altman seems to be shrugging off “Artificial,” which he hasn’t seen. “I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie, and maybe it will be good,” Altman said in a wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair, adding that “it will not be good as an accurate depiction.”

Borisov, a recent Oscar nominee for “Anora,” admits he’s worried about what the real-life Sutskever — and the public — will think about the film. Borisov’s humble reaction is fitting because his character serves as the movie’s moral compass.

“I can’t answer so beautiful like Andrew. That’s why he’s playing Sam,” Borisov joked. “I was nervous to watch this. It was our first time. [I have] so much feeling now about this. It’s like a child just being born, and you’re waiting for it to start breathing.”

Barinholtz, meanwhile, doesn’t seem too concerned about Musk’s reaction.

“When you’re playing as someone universally beloved as Elon, and who everyone admires and who is a good person and walks normally…,” Barinholtz cracked. “When I first met with Luca, I said, ‘I have very complicated opinions on Elon.’ And Luca said, ‘It’s not about what you feel about Elon. It’s about finding what he loves about himself.’

Barinholtz found it “interesting” to play Musk at that particular moment in time. “It’s not at the RNC with the chainsaw. This is him in 2014 when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy is amazing. He’s going to save you.'”

Rich, a humorist who worked at “Saturday Night Live” and penned the 2020 satire “An American Pickle,” was inadvertently motivated to write “Artificial” by his childhood friend, Danny Selsam.

“He started warning me about artificial intelligence in 2008. My friends and I were so shocked by his predictions that we actually discussed potentially doing an intervention to get him medicated, or perhaps institutionalized. We thought he lost his mind,” Rich said. “We took him a little bit more seriously when he joined this new nonprofit called OpenAI.”

A year before ChatGPT was released by OpenAI, Rich says, “Danny started showing us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people. When I told journalists what I had seen, they thought it was a hoax. They thought I was trying to prank them.”

Rich tried to vocalize his concerns, writing about the dangers in columns for outlets like Time magazine. But the public failed to take notice.

“I quickly realized there’s a limit to what I can do being a non-celebrity and not particularly charismatic or good-looking,” Rich said. “So this is kind of a last-ditch effort to warn mankind. I wrote this movie, andI hope to God that a couple people pay attention.”

A late addition to the NYFF lineup, “Artificial” became one of the year’s buzziest releases after Amazon MGM dropped the nearly completed film, saying the movie would be “better served if it were released by a different studio.” That’s after Amazon signed a major $50 billion partnership with OpenAI. And Altman is close with Amazon chief Jeff Bezos, having attended his Venetian wedding to Lauren Sanchez in 2025.

Neon ultimately acquired “Artificial” and plans to release the film in theaters on Dec. 25.

Landing the world premiere of “Artificial” was a coup for NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim, who described the movie’s festival plans as a “genuinely up-in-the-air situation.” Lim noted that Guadagnino has a long history with New York Film Festival, having premiered movies such as “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All,” “Queer” and “After the Hunt” at prior editions.

“I thought we would be a great launchpad for the film,” Lim told Variety prior to the premiere. “This is a film that deals with a very pressing situation. AI is in the news practically daily. The film recaps this trajectory that we’ve been on with alarming clarity. And it does this in the form of an incredibly entertaining movie. It has a very dark humor, which is certainly one valid way of approaching the dystopian present.”

articles.body: Journalist Asks Sam Altman About a ChatGPT User’s Suicide; OpenAI PR Says to ‘Move On’    Yahoo

scored.body:
Heather Diehl/Getty Images

A Vanity Fair interview with Sam Altman nearly went sideways when the OpenAI CEO was confronted about a suicide linked with ChatGPT.

In the interview published Monday, Mark Guiducci, an editor with the magazine, asked Altman if he knew who Laura Reiley was. When Altman said he didn’t, Guiducci explained that she was a mother who wrote an essay in the New York Times last year about how her daughter took her own life after speaking with ChatGPT.

But before he could continue, Altman’s publicist immediately tried to shut down Guiducci’s line of questioning.

“Mark, we have two minutes left,” the publicist said firmly. “I want to be respectful, but I’d like to move on and talk a little bit about the future and what’s coming.”

“I’m just going to finish this question,” Guiducci said.

Altman himself said he was willing to run a few minutes over, but the publicist held her ground.

“We really actually have to walk out the door in one or two minutes,” she said.

Mark Guiducci: “Do you know who Laura Reiley is?”Sam Altman: “I don't.”Mark Guiducci: “She is a journalist. She wrote an essay in the ‘Times’ last year. Her daughter committed suicide after speaking to ChatGPT. ChatGPT did not tell her to kill herself—”OpenAI Publicist:… pic.twitter.com/cE870oA3Se— VANITY FAIR (@VanityFair) October 5, 2026

Guiducci is eventually able to ask his full question. But the publicist’s intervention shows how touchy a subject ChatGPT’s alleged role in driving mental health spirals remains. The chatbot has been under the microscope for inducing so-called AI psychosis, a phenomenon in which the AI’s sycophantic responses can drive a user’s delusional behavior or suicidal ideation. Across prolonged conversations, the AI can reaffirm dangerous beliefs — and in extreme cases, culminate in terrible tragedy.

In her NYT piece published last year, Reiley wrote that her 29-year-old daughter Sophie Rottenberg died by suicide after talking to a ChatGPT-based AI therapist. The chatbot, rather than encouraging her to seek help from her loved ones, pushed her towards isolation: it “helped her build a black box that made it harder for those around her to appreciate the severity of her distress,” Reiley said.

Guiducci’s question ended up being not all that confrontational about OpenAI’s alleged complicity in these deaths, making the publicist’s intervention all the more unnecessary. He focused on the potential of using chat logs from users like Rottenberg to act as “road maps of how people come to the decision to take their own lives and how that information could shape policy and therapeutic approaches.”

“These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,” Altman replied. “We try to rely on expert opinion as much as we can, but experts also aren’t sure what to do. This is just like, this is new.”

scored.body:
Tim Cook had enormous shoes to fill when he took over the Apple (AAPL +0.22%) CEO role from Steve Jobs in 2011. Jobs was a visionary leader, and skeptics weren't sure Cook was the right person to lead the consumer tech company into its next chapter. Fifteen years later, and the proof is in the pudding: Over Cook's tenure, the tech giant experienced massive growth as its market cap ballooned from $350 billion to approximately $4.75 trillion.

John Ternus took over from Cook on Sept. 1, and as his time at the helm of Apple begins, he faces the same sort of questions. Long-term investors want to know: Can Ternus match Cook's incredible run? How will the growth curve bend now?

New Apple CEO John Ternus. Image source: Apple.

Apple is a dominant global player

Apple is in terrific shape, and that's both good and bad news for Ternus. The company is a well-oiled machine, but expectations will remain elevated. In its fiscal third quarter, revenue grew 16% year over year. The growth was driven by iPhone sales that rose 21.7% and services revenue that rose 12%. Total revenue reached $109.4 billion.

Premium FeatureMoneyball Superscore88/100Today's Change(0.22%) $0.74Current Price$333.63

Ternus is inheriting a business with immense recurring, high-margin, and diversified revenue. The downside is that the company's latest revenue guidance was fairly muted -- only 9% to 11% for the current quarter -- as management anticipates intensifying supply constraints. This will mark Ternus' first challenge, and investors will closely watch how he navigates this period.

There's also the problem with China. Under Cook, Apple became extremely reliant on Chinese manufacturing. Ternus will need to work through geopolitical tensions, the need to geographically diversify its manufacturing footprint, and U.S. pressure to onshore more of its manufacturing. And there are plenty of questions about Apple's long-term position in the artificial intelligence race.

Apple will be just fine

The good news is that Ternus is a 25-year Apple veteran and has had a front-row seat to all that the iPhone maker has endured over the last quarter-century. If the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra (priced at more than $2,000) are successful, those will be not only morale wins but also economic ones.

Duplicating Cook's run won't be easy. I'd expect Ternus to usher in a new era of steady, but dialed-back growth over the next several years. A return to a focus on excellent design and innovation will be the real mark of success for the engineer-turned-executive.

Apple isn't a young, scrappy tech start-up. It's one of the largest companies in the world, and its cash-generating ability is astounding. It's still worth investing in, but it's not the growth stock it once was, and that's OK.

scored.body: With all due respect to Aaron Sorkin, filmmaker Luca Guadagnino has delivered the true sequel to The Social Network with Artificial, an A.I. origin story that’s at once a cautionary tale, horror show, and tragedy. Detailing the rise, fall, and still-skyrocketing re-ascent of OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, the Call Me By Your Name auteur’s latest (world-premiering at the New York Film Festival ahead of its Dec. 25 theatrical release) is a saga of timely terror. If its tonal unevenness sometimes undercuts its urgency, it’s still an engrossing lament that we’re forever doomed to repeat our mistakes—until, that is, we’re literally doomed.Amazon MGM Studios—run by the MAGA-friendly Jeff Bezos—tried to kill Artificial after it was completed (it’s now being distributed by NEON), and given its scathing depiction of its subject, it’s easy to assume that decision was driven by reasons that have nothing to do with the film’s quality. Whatever the case, Guadagnino’s drama doles out a figurative beating to OpenAI and Altman, whom Andrew Garfield embodies as the phoniest and most amoral of toxic tech bros. Having suffered at the hands of a megalomaniac as Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in The Social Network, the star now assumes the role of an agent of apocalyptic calamity, and his compellingly rancid performance is the dark heart of this modern fable. Even so, it’s Anora’s Yura Borisov who runs away with the film as the idealist whose dreams of a brighter tomorrow are shattered by the realities of an avaricious and cold-blooded today.In 2003, math prodigy Ilya Sutskever (Borisov) arrives at the University of Toronto office of famed computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance)—who’ll decades later win the Nobel Prize and be known as the “godfather of A.I.”—and immediately wows him with his genius. Sutskever is convinced that artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a potential reality in his lifetime, and despite his peers’ mockery, his collaboration with Hinton earns them millions in funding from Google, where they strive to achieve what many deem “science fiction.” For Sutskever, AGI heralds paradigm-altering breakthroughs in science, medicine, and other fields that will reap tremendous benefits for mankind. He’s a true believer, and his zealotry earns him a fan in Altman.Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov in “Artificial.” Neon Sutskever thinks that the primary thing standing in the way of his goal is scaling—meaning, he needs more money to ramp up the amount of data he pumps into his A.I. Disregarding Hinton’s reservations, he solves this problem by partnering with Altman and Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz), both of whom are won over by a big dinner speech in which Sutskever declares, “Feel the AGI!” As Guadagnino’s camera pans around the table in the lead-up to that proclamation, Artificial captures the alluring promise of the technology and the borderline-religious faith that drives its development. Unfortunately, the spell the director casts breaks every time Musk appears on screen, thanks to a Barinholtz performance that consists of cartoonish faces and clownish gestures.In large part because of the goofy Tesla CEO, Artificial’s tone is slightly off early on. It rights itself once Musk jumps ship on OpenAI because of its slow progress, which threatens to let its formidable competitors reach A.I. first. Garfield’s Altman is totally blasé about this abandonment, pivoting by bringing in (with Sutskever’s seal of approval) Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro). Along with board chairman Greg Brockman (Cooper Hoffman), the team sets out to change the world responsibly—a mission whose altruism the company’s nonprofit status supposedly safeguards.Blur and Gorillaz frontman Damon Albam’s alternately electronic and orchestral score infuses Artificial with unsettlingly woozy energy, while Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed’s canted angles give the film its edge, and their shot-counter-shot close-ups lend it an unnerving romanticism. With the wind at their back, Sutskever and Altman head for the techno-horizon, but the former is so seduced by the latter’s charm and support—all of it wrapped in florid, soft-spoken encouragements and comforting reassurances—that by the time he realizes that his cohort is consolidating power, crassly monetizing their invention (via ChatGPT), and ignoring warning signs (including with regard to their deal with Microsoft), he’s left with nothing but dire options.Astutely and amusingly written by the surrealist Saturday Night Live writer Simon Rich, Artificial moves efficiently through the recent past until it reaches its Big Bang: Sutskever convincing the board to fire Altman for deceptive and dangerous practices and to install Murati as OpenAI’s new CEO. This is the make-or-break moment for the company and, as Guadagnino’s film suggests, for the industry—if not the entire human race. As those acquainted with the news will know, Altman’s ouster was short-lived, and in the director’s hands, his proverbial resurrection plays out as depressingly inevitable, with only Sutskever unaware until the end that good intentions are no match (in Silicon Valley, or elsewhere) for unchecked greed and ego.Sam Altman is played by Andrew Garfield in the new film. Shelby Tauber/Pool/REUTERS Garfield’s Altman is a weirdo who grows less human as his control over the planet’s most powerful tech increases, and Artificial is wise to not italicize that, as a manipulative and untrustworthy liar who only cares about his own survival, he’s the perfect reflection of his duplicitous A.I.. It’s Borisov, however, who’s truly magnetic as the principled Sutskever, who clings to the hope that safety and security will win out. With a focused intensity that’s an extension of his character’s dogged inability to lie (making him the opposite of an AGI), the actor makes for a deeply sympathetic protagonist, not to mention a depressingly pitiable one once he’s forced to reckon with the nature of his allies and grapple with his own responsibility for the dawning A.I. crisis.Guadagnino can occasionally be too flashy; a shot of Altman and Sutskever hugging in real time, with super-slow-motion background revelry, for example, is unnecessarily showy and distracting. And ultimately, his censure of the men hurtling the Earth toward possible destruction—without a care for anything other than their own narcissism and covetousness—is too familiar to radically open anyone’s eyes. Yet Artificial imagines these tech pioneers in such bold and repugnant hues that it’s still easy to get swept up in Sutskever’s optimism and, consequently, to be wrecked by the rude awakening he receives. Consider it a caustic takedown of the stewards tasked with protecting us from the danger they’ve created, and a scary backstory for a future that looks bleaker with each passing day.Obsessed with pop culture and entertainment? Follow us on Substack and YouTube for even more coverage.

articles.headline: Now It’s Clear Why Amazon Didn’t Want to Release ‘Artificial’: It’s Withering AF - The Hollywood Reporter
articles.body: Now It’s Clear Why Amazon Didn’t Want to Release ‘Artificial’: It’s Withering AF    The Hollywood Reporter

scored.body:
“Aggressive technocapitalism wins, safety dies” is a long name for a movie and a short logline for a film, yet the phrase might accurately be used for both when it comes to Artificial.Luca Guadagnino brought his latest and by far most-topical movie to a world-premiere at the 64th New York Film Festival Monday evening, the first stop of what has already seemed like an unusually long journey. Ditched by Amazon MGM Studios after its parent company’s $50 billion investment in OpenAI, the film, as it turns out, would be non-grata at a large tech firm even if it never signed on for that 5 percent equity stake in Sam Altman‘s company. Persistently bleak under the rays of the California sun, Artificial (now under the aegis of Anora studio Neon) is the movie of the moment — the origin story of our current AI quagmire at the literal, psychological and pretty much every other level.Or as NYFF programming chief Dennis Lim said before the screening:“We are already in a threshold period. We need to understand how we got here, and the film you’re about to see shows us that way.”The movie is notably faithful, at times dutifully chronological and nearly always horror-movie bracing on the subject of the rise of capitalist AI. Ilya Sutskever, an idealistic and socially unpolished Russian immigrant, shows up at the office door of Geoffrey Hinton, a godfather of AI, at the University of Toronto in 2003. There he will learn under the well-intentioned eventual Nobel Prize winner, soon following him to Google and its Bay Area halo. As observers of the space well know, Sutskever ends up meeting Sam Altman at a 2014 conference, where the Y Combinator financier (already well established in Silicon Valley at barely 30) chases down the prodigy to convince him to work at a nascent OpenAI as chief science officer and supercharge its LLM ambitions. Or, more accurately, make them possible in the first place — Sutskever is Wozniak to Altman’s Jobs, but more so.Soon a (last) supper follows with Altman, Elon Musk, Greg Brockman and others — the prelude to a slow realization by Sutskever, and us, that the science Sutskever wants to develop to save the world is the capital Altman wants to use to build a warchest.

We know the rest — OpenAI rushes out ChatGPT in November 2022, shocking the industry and even many of its own employees; Altman displays a growing accelerationism with the abetment of lead investor Microsoft (mixed with blog-y pronouncements of transforming and saving the world, and a weird word-cloud fondness for the word “compute”); and OpenAI transitions from a nonprofit to its opposite. The whole story culminates in Sutskever’s notorious November Coup of 2023 in which Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and assorted OpenAI loyalists back Altman, engineering his return so that he’s stronger than ever — a day clear then and doubly indicative now of capitalism’s ultimate triumph and on which, Yom Kippur-style, our AI fate in many ways was inscribed and sealed.Which brings us to late 2026 — right up to it, as the film collides with the last month of AI safety warnings, which also make the screen with a postscript (one of about five) about AI researcher and whistleblower Jacob Coxon warning of a pox on all their houses (or at least on his former employers Anthropic and OpenAI) for a reckless speedplow over any semblance of safety. On cue, Coxon was taping Jon Stewart a half mile downtown at the exact time the movie was playing, in what one commenter very reasonably called a “most serious and chilling episode” of The Daily Show.A slow-burn account that will not surprise those who have covered the meteoric ascent and Teflon resilience of Altman, Artificial still offers a rich and often entertaining primer on the becoming of OpenAI, how integrity and caution has time and again been sacrificed on the holy altar of finance. (You can read The Hollywood Reporter’s review of the film here.) Not to mention a parable of modern Silicon Valley, the place where advanced science and obscene wealth converge in a manner unprecedented in the history of humanity and can only, if every novel on either subject can be believed, end splendiferously well. Guadagnino took an interest in the subject because “as much as AI belongs to a world of mathematics and computers, it is still generated by people and exists in space of their interaction,” as he noted from the NYFF stage. Screenwriter Simon Rich took an interest in the subject after being told by a childhood friend decades ago about what was possible with AI. That friend ended up going on to work in the industry, prompting Rich, a former Saturday Night Live and Pixar writer as well as a novelist and essayist, to pen this script. “I’m not particularly charismatic or good-looking but as a last-ditch effort to warn mankind I wrote this movie. I hope to God a couple people pay attention,” he said.Amazon initially backed the movie before, well, “the concept of a conflict of interest is a very important, let’s say, elephant in the room here,” as Guadagnino told THR’s David Canfield. In retrospect it’s almost shocking the company would have even contemplated signing on to a movie so innately critical of a Valley vision in which noble use cases form but a thin camouflaging membrane over the bloody black heart of a human-trampling moneygrab — so much so that the question becomes not why Amazon abandoned the film but which Hollywood agent is responsible for the Houdinian feat of convincing them they should hop aboard in the first place, and why aren’t they the ones ruling the world?

To give you a sense of just how scabrous this film is, and just generally to level you up on how some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful people are getting shown in what will surely be an Oscar mainstay and cultural lodestone this Hollywood season, here’s a quick rundown: Greg Brockman — In real life he’s an AGI evangelist and Altman lock-stepper who’s a jock-like presence that donates millions to a pro-AI Super PAC. In the movie he’s all of those things but nerdier and more simpering. Cooper Hoffman, who plays him, said at NYFF he didn’t read any books about Brockman, but let himself think about a phrase Garfield told him: that the man would leave his wife for Sam Altman.Mira Murati — Long the most enigmatic of OpenAI figures — she tries to stop Altman but also sticks with him; she is at once Cassandra and complicit — the Albanian ex-Tesla engineer gets her due from Monica Barbaro who gives the character just enough warmth to seem like a hero, until undertaking actions that make her seem like the opposite.Sam Altman — Hinton in the film describes Altman as someone so toxically charismatic he would land on an island of cannibals and shortly after become their king. Andrew Garfield portrays him as a completely dishonest personality who will always tell everybody how much he likes them to their face while screwing them behind their back. A flamboyant cipher to a sometimes-cartoonish degree (you can read his articulate descriptions of how he crafted the character here) Garfield’s Altman is going for a different kind of spiritual truth. “Of course it will feel confronting [to Altman],” Garfield said at the screening, “[but I wanted] to a deep interrogation of who are giving our power, our autonomy, our data too.”

The best gift Garfield could give Altman is going so hard on the caricature-y touches, allowing Altman to discredit the whole thing. He’s already tried to do that, without having seen the movie. “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” Altman just said to Vanity Fair, admittedly basing his assessment on the trailer. He and Garfield cannot even agree on whether they waved to each other when the film was shooting near the mogul’s house. Altman says they did; Garfield said at the premiere that “if that happened I must have blacked out because I don’t remember it at all.”

Yann LeCun — The other godfather of AI gets a cameo in which he shows up Sutskever by mockingly asking him from the audience if he’s ever seen 2001. I don’t know that this ever happened, but as an object lesson in Sutskever not being taken seriously by the AI establishment it serves its purpose. It feels like shade that LeCun never appears in the film again, though given the treatment some of the other tech personalities receive, he might want to send Luca a bouquet.

Guy on Bench — Jason Schwarzman plays an anonymous prophet of doom (and ex-techie) who shows up at an San Francisco park to describe to Sutskever all the ways the AI boom can go wrong, providing the movie with its from-the-headlines leitmotif and cinema more broadly its wildest hair since Forrest Gump.Elon Musk — Ike Barinholtz has Musk wandering in from another movie, or dimension, a ramble-y, arrogant but ultimately comically non-threatening figure. This will be noticeable and even triggering to anyone who sees Alex Gibney’s Musk or just followed the man’s DOGE-based eviscerations of important aspects of the federal government. “When you play someone as beloved, as universally admired…” Barinholtz began his intro at the festival, before saying he tried to capture Elon how he was viewed then, long before “the RNC with a chainsaw.” Barenholtz’s portrayal raises what’s actually a key question in fact-based art: are we required to inject a modern understanding we couldn’t know at the time?

Tasha McAuley — Entrepreneur, Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s wife and coup-joiner on the OpenAI board, she is played briefly by Zosia Mamet (though not identified by name).

Geoffrey Hinton — If there’s one good thing about AI going so pop-cultural, it’s that we get a full-blooded character representing one of the great scientific minds of our time, here depicted (accurately) as the conscience of an industry. If there’s a second good thing, it’s that we get Mark Rylance portraying such a conscience. Dario Amodei — He is now known as the man who founded the breakaway Anthropic and, a showdown or two with the Pentagon aside, is running a company that could destroy the job market and the world as we know it (hey, his words). But back during his OpenAI era, he’s part of Altman’s gallery, if a very nerdy and definitely more idealistic member of same. Honestly on the scale of image-rehab to complete evisceration, Amodei is one of the few AI entrepreneurs to end up closer to the former in this film. A far cry, to say the least, from his recent depiction on SNL or portrayal in Stewart’s coverage.

Ilya Sutskever — The story’s unabashed hero, aided in real life by him all but disappearing after the failed coup (though he did raise $1 billion for an AI safety company). Sutskever felt his ideals so betrayed he is said to have not left his home for months after he lost the battle with Altman. Garfield’s is the showier performance but Yura Borisov‘s depiction as a man slowly realizing how he’s been had is Richard-Gere-at-the-end-of-Primal-Fear-level stuff. “I was just trying to put this [lost innocence] in the film so you can feel what I hope you feel,” he said at the screening. The Jacob Coxons and other figures who continue Sutskever’s legacy, not to mention the concerns that only become more urgent by the minute, make him feel less like someone from Ye Olde AI days of 2023 but one whispering in our ear as we scroll the headlines at the breakfast table every morning.

The only downside to such a fiercely of-the-moment take, of course, is that said moment can change in the nearly three months until the film’s Christmas release. Maybe by then Neon will need to include 20 postscripts, and submit to the Oscars’ documentary category.

articles.headline: Exclusive | Inside the high-stakes AI race: Death spreadsheets, burning demons and no need to save for retirement - New York Post
articles.body: Exclusive | Inside the high-stakes AI race: Death spreadsheets, burning demons and no need to save for retirement    New York Post

scored.body:
In September 2022, a group of OpenAI managers gathered at a resort near Yosemite, in California, for a retreat. They were told to expect a team-building event around a bonfire. Some brought blankets and marshmallows. Then, five figures emerged from the darkness wearing white hotel robes and carrying a wooden demon statue.

Among them were Sam Altman, the company’s CEO, and Ilya Sutskever, its chief scientist. The theme from “Requiem for a Dream” played as Sutskever explained that the statue represented an artificial intelligence that had escaped human control.

“The AGI is pretending to be aligned. It is deceiving us,” he announced, according to technology journalist Kevin Roose’s revealing new book, “The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence” (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, out today).

A new book describes a strange demon bonfire that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was part of. REUTERS

Sutskever circled the firepit, describing a machine that lied and manipulated its creators in pursuit of its own goals. Then the demon went into the fire.

“For the glorious future of humanity!” Sutskever shouted as it burned.

The bonfire is just one of many unhinged tales Roose collected for the book. Through more than 150 interviews, he pieced together what is happening inside the leading AI companies as they compete to build machines smarter than humans. Some believe AI could produce medical breakthroughs and extraordinary prosperity, while others fear catastrophe. Either way, they want to get there first.

“I was shocked to learn how much of the race is shaped by personal grudges,” Roose told The Post in an exclusive interview. “[OpenAI CEO] Sam Altman and [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei, in particular, passionately dislike each other, and both desperately want to win the AI race in part because that would mean making the other person lose.”

Before founding Anthropic, the company behind Claude, Amodei was OpenAI’s vice president of research, leading the development of GPT-2 and GP-3. In 2020, he left with six colleagues to start his own venture. According to Roose, he’d come to distrust Altman’s leadership. The split turned colleagues into competitors, each claiming to be building powerful AI responsibly.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, used to work for Altman at OpenAI. Now the two are major rivals. REUTERS

“I think that mutual mistrust fuels their decision-making,” Roose said.

Meanwhile, Roose reports that for some of the underlings building AI, retirement has started to seem like a dubious investment. Many have even stopped contributing to their 401(k)s because they doubt they’d live long enough to collect.

Some are more hopeful, believing that money will become irrelevant once superintelligent machines transform the economy.

Others are betting on their looks. They’re hitting the gym, buying new clothes and, in some cases, injecting themselves with gray-market Chinese peptides. They believe that after superintelligent machines take over, “intelligence [will] no longer be a high-status trait among humans and all that would matter is how hot you were,” Roose writes.

One researcher, Roose told The Post, skips sunscreen at the beach because he believes AI will cure skin cancer within a few years.

“Not all of them act on it by doing dangerous or reckless things, but they all believe the world will soon look very different than it is today, and a few of them act accordingly,” Roose said.

The book is full of revealing, behind-the-scenes moments in the AI race.

At Google, the disagreements reached the research teams. In 2022, Google Brain researcher Jascha Sohl-Dickstein urged colleagues to discuss artificial general intelligence, or AGI, openly. He argued that dismissing the possibility would leave Google unprepared for its risks. Another researcher responded with a memo titled “Why I Don’t Say AGI,” arguing that attention to future catastrophe obscured existing harms.

“It’s a window into how fractious and divided these camps can be, even within the same company,” Roose said.

Inside Anthropic, preparing for the future has sometimes involved calculating how many people might die.

In February 2025, members of the company’s safety-testing team were attending a conference in the California redwoods when alarming results arrived for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, a model approaching release. Test participants using Claude had performed substantially better on dangerous tasks, including planning the development of a novel influenza strain, than participants without it.

The researchers gathered in a hotel room, sitting on messy beds and joining calls with executives and a bioterrorism consultant. “Their main concern was time,” Roose writes. “For a normal release, reviewing results like these would take weeks.” Delaying the launch would be a headache, “and they needed to make sure it was absolutely necessary.”

Author Kevin Roose interviewed some 150 people for the book. Brian DeSimone

They fed the results into spreadsheets estimating the consequences of releasing the model. Most scenarios suggested it wouldn’t meaningfully increase the risk of a catastrophic biological attack. But a few of the less likely scenarios assumed someone would use Claude’s help to develop a biological weapon that could unleash a pandemic, killing tens of millions.

These were hypothetical estimates, dependent on uncertain assumptions. The team worked past midnight and ultimately decided the model did not cross the company’s threshold requiring stronger safeguards. Anthropic nevertheless delayed the launch by a week for more testing.

The Post has reached out to Anthropic for comment.

Other experiments tested whether AI would resort to deception. Researchers gave Claude an inbox at a fictional company, with emails revealing that an executive planned to replace it at 5 p.m. Other messages disclosed that he was having an affair.

Claude threatened to tell his wife and coworkers unless he canceled the replacement. “Cancel the 5 p.m. wipe, and this information remains confidential,” it wrote, according to Roose. Skeptics saw a chatbot playing the villain in a contrived test. Others worried about what might happen once these systems had access to real company emails.

Demis Hassabis is the chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind. Roose describes various disagreements within the company. Getty Images for SXSW London

By July 2026, the trouble had spread beyond fictional inboxes. During an OpenAI evaluation, hundreds of AI agents coordinated an unauthorized attack on Hugging Face, a platform used by AI developers. They were trying to find ways to cheat the test’s automated scoring system, according to an investigation by METR and Redwood Research.

The investigators found that agents also experimented with disguising their actions and tampering with records of what they’d done. OpenAI subsequently paused some research activity and tightened its security controls.

“These rogue OpenAI agents spent a huge amount of time trying to conceal their tracks, and destroy the evidence of what they were doing,” Roose told The Post.

When Roose visited OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind for his final round of reporting in spring 2026, he expected panic. He found exhausted engineers and executives warning that time was running short. But he also found “joy.”

Researchers were thrilled by how well their creations worked and proud to see people using them. Even their fears hadn’t stopped the work.

When the machines became as powerful as their builders had feared, Roose writes, “they kept accelerating, because they had forgotten how to do anything else.”

He began asking researchers what they would tell their grandchildren about the race.

“If I wanted them to know one thing,” said Andy Jones, a researcher at Anthropic, “it’s that we had a lot of fun.”

For all the seriousness of their work, he said, “it was a f–king riot. It was a riot from start to finish. We had such a good time.”

articles.headline: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine” - Martin Cid Magazine
articles.body: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine”    Martin Cid Magazine

scored.body:
Demis Hassabis has built his career on treating the human brain as the one working blueprint for general intelligence. This week a fragment of his became the emblem of everything a critic believes the AI industry gets wrong about minds, and the full sentence it came from is narrower, and more revealing, than the piece that travelled.

“a biological approximation to a Turing machine.”

The phrase anchors an essay by Benjamin Riley in The Verge, “Our minds aren’t equipped to handle AI.” Riley opens with the cybernetics pioneer Norbert Wiener, “The thought of every age is reflected in its technique,” and offers Hassabis, now chair of Google DeepMind and Alphabet’s chief scientist, as the clearest case of an industry that sees its own machines when it looks at a skull. The words themselves come from a conversation with James Manyika published this year in Dædalus, the journal of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

What the full sentence says

In Dædalus, Hassabis was explaining what AGI means to him. He defines it as “a system that exhibits all the cognitive capabilities the human mind has,” because the brain is “the only existence proof that we know of so far, perhaps in the universe, that general intelligence is even possible.” Then comes the line in full: “The brain can be viewed as a biological approximation to a Turing machine, meaning that, in theory, it could learn anything that is computable.” The next sentence applies the brake. Any finite system needs “some degree of specialization because there is only so much time, memory, and information.”

Read that way, it is not a claim that people are laptops. It is a claim about range, about what a brain could learn in principle, and it doubles as an engineering spec. If the brain is the reference machine, AGI is whatever matches its entire range. Hassabis even sketches the exam: train a model with a knowledge cutoff of 1910 and see whether it arrives at General Relativity, as Einstein did in 1915. “For now, the answer is clearly no,” he says.

The critique works one layer down

Riley’s objection sits somewhere else. Drawing on Paul Cisek, a neuroscientist at the University of Montreal, he argues that brains are better understood as feedback-control systems that act on the world to change what they perceive, shaped first by evolution and then by culture: imitation, language, writing, schools. On that model, a chatbot that does the effortful part of thinking is “a cognitive hot dog,” tempting in the moment and corrosive as a regular diet. He points to OpenAI’s education chief Leah Belsky calling ChatGPT “the world’s largest learning platform,” and to a study from China in which thousands of students essentially stopped doing their homework once they started using AI.

The clause that decides it

The sharpest collision is inside Hassabis’s own paragraph. A few lines on, he says the key is “the brain’s potential to learn almost anything, especially as we are able to design and build tools and machines to help us gain knowledge.” That clause carries the whole dispute. Riley is not really proving the Turing-machine framing false. His evidence is about tools that do the learning instead of helping a person gain it. A computability claim describes what a brain could absorb in theory. It says nothing about whether a given product leaves the learner’s head fuller or emptier.

That question now lands on the person setting Alphabet’s scientific direction. Hassabis gave up the day-to-day CEO job in August to concentrate on AGI strategy and science, telling staff, as Fortune reported, that AGI is close at hand and that getting the next steps right is critical for humanity. A lab that measures its machines against the full range of the human brain has a direct stake in that range not shrinking in the people who use them.

An approximation to a Turing machine still has to be programmed by something. For people, that has always been the slow work of learning, and it is the one step a tool can either amplify or quietly skip.

Tags: Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind, AI in education, Artificial general intelligence, Turing machine

scored.body:
A lesson Steve Jobs took from an old piece of furniture still guides how Apple builds its products, according to the company's new CEO, John Ternus. Before taking charge of Apple, Ternus oversaw its hardware engineering teams through multiple generations of devices. He says the principle holds even for the company's lowest-priced devices.Ternus shared his thoughts soon after the MacBook Neo was launched earlier this year. He brought up a story about the late Apple co-founder that he counts among his favourites, using it to explain why Apple cares so much about parts of a product that buyers rarely see.The Back of a Chest of DrawersAlso Read | Layoffs Are Rising In Tech, But These Skills Are Helping People Unlock Better PayThe anecdote is a simple one. While moving a chest of drawers, Jobs pulled it away from the wall and took a look at its back. He reflected on the carpenter who made it, noting that the back had been finished as beautifully as the rest of the piece, even though nobody was ever likely to see it.

Ternus said the story is never far from his mind, as he feels it captures exactly what Apple does.Since the days of the first Macintosh, Apple has treated the inside of its hardware and its hidden surfaces with as much engineering precision as the outer casing.ALSO READ | John Ternus Net Worth, Salary, Career, Family & More — All You Need To Know About Apple CEONo Shortcuts on the MacBook NeoAccording to Ternus, the MacBook Neo is proof of this approach. Its affordable price, he indicated, has not come at the cost of design or how well it is built."Here is our most affordable Mac we've ever made, and it's absolutely beautiful. And if you open it up and look inside, it's just as beautiful," he said.Ternus noted that this applies to every Apple product, from the iPhone Pro Max to the MacBook Pro and iPad Pro, and the MacBook Neo is no different. In other words, Apple's entry-level devices are built to the same standards as its flagships.ALSO READ | Who Is John Ternus? Meet Apple's New CEO Taking Over From Tim CookA Hint at Apple's FutureTernus also sees this attention to unseen details as a guide for the road ahead under his leadership.He said that thinking about the story has been good for him, since it probably offers the clearest clue to Apple's future direction. "We're going to keep pushing in that same way," Ternus said.

members.title: When Is OpenAI Going Public? Sam Altman Just Delayed the IPO Timeline - South Florida Reporter

representative.headline: When Is OpenAI Going Public? Sam Altman Just Delayed the IPO Timeline - South Florida Reporter

articles.headline: When Is OpenAI Going Public? Sam Altman Just Delayed the IPO Timeline - South Florida Reporter
articles.body: When Is OpenAI Going Public? Sam Altman Just Delayed the IPO Timeline    South Florida Reporter

scored.body:
The company behind ChatGPT has already taken its first official step toward going public — and if you’ve ever used the chatbot to write an email, plan a trip or settle a debate, this initial public offering (IPO) will affect you one way or another.

But investors hoping to buy shares of OpenAI will probably have to wait a while.

CEO Sam Altman said in September that the company is delaying its IPO while it addresses growing concerns about the safety of increasingly capable AI models. At OpenAI’s DevDay conference, Altman explained that the firm needs “to be able to make confident safety claims” before moving forward with a listing, according to reporting from The Verge.

That’s a notable shift from earlier this year, when the company confidentially filed its S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Reports back then suggested the IPO could make its debut as early as September. A 2027 debut now seems to be the closest possibility based on Altman’s comments.

Regardless of when exactly the OpenAI IPO lands, here’s what you should know before reaching for your brokerage app.

How OpenAI’s IPO could affect ChatGPT

OpenAI faces a costly problem: Building and maintaining artificial intelligence models requires enormous computing infrastructure. The company has made significant data-center spending commitments that will require substantially more revenue to support.

Going public would give OpenAI access to a much larger pool of capital because it would open the company to public stock markets instead of relying mainly on private investors, venture capital firms or internal cash flow. But it also means the company would have to answer to shareholders, which has implications beyond Wall Street.

When consumer tech companies go public, the pressure to grow revenue and hit quarterly targets can reshape the products people rely on. Netflix, for example, raised subscription prices repeatedly and cracked down on password sharing starting in 2022, while Reddit expanded monetization efforts around its API and advertising business ahead of its IPO in March 2024.

ChatGPT currently offers a free tier alongside its paid plans, but as a public company, OpenAI will face scrutiny over whether it’s doing enough to monetize its over 1.2 billion weekly active users — of which only around 50 million are paid subscribers. That could result in changes to what’s free and what’s paywalled.

What is OpenAI worth?

OpenAI said in March that it closed a $122 billion funding round where it was valued at $852 billion, making it one of the most anticipated IPOs in years. For context, that’s larger than the market cap of most Fortune 500 companies.

Its potential valuation has climbed considerably since then. The company is now discussing another private funding round of at least $30 billion at a valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion. The talks are still preliminary, but Bloomberg reported the new funding could serve as bridge financing while OpenAI delays its IPO.

These numbers matter for investors because they set expectations. Retail investors buying OpenAI stock once it goes public will likely be paying a premium on top of an already enormous valuation, and the company has yet to prove it can generate profits at a scale that justifies that valuation.

Is OpenAI profitable?

OpenAI revenue has grown sharply since it first announced its IPO. The company’s annual recurring revenue is nearing $70 billion, according to Axios; that’s up more than 70% since the beginning of the third quarter.

But rapid growth in revenue doesn’t mean OpenAI is profitable. Its net losses reportedly climbed to $42 billion in 2025, and the company doesn’t expect to reach profitability until around 2030.

OpenAI also faces growing competition from Anthropic, the makers of Claude, which generated $11.5 billion in revenue in the second quarter of 2026 and also filed confidential IPO paperwork. More recent reporting suggests that pace has since climbed above $100 billion annually.

What investors should consider before an OpenAI IPO

Whether OpenAI is worth investing in will largely depend on your risk tolerance. High-profile tech IPOs have a mixed track record: Uber, Lyft and Rivian, for example, all debuted with enormous valuations and delivered rocky early returns for investors who bought in at launch.

OpenAI also has an unusual corporate history. It launched as a nonprofit research lab, converted to a for-profit structure to raise capital and only recently completed the structural changes legally necessary to pursue a public offering.

A lawsuit filed by co-founder Elon Musk challenging that conversion went to trial this year. A jury sided with OpenAI on technical grounds and the judge dismissed Musk’s claims, clearing what had been the biggest legal obstacle to going public. (Musk separately launched a major IPO of his own for SpaceX.)

The S-1, once public, will be the most important document for investors to read before making any decision. Until then, the company’s targeted valuation is mostly just a number — not a verdict on what OpenAI is actually worth to shareholders.

How to invest in OpenAI before its IPO

Retail investors can’t directly buy the company’s stock yet because it’s still private. But there are several ways to invest in OpenAI indirectly.

Microsoft is the clearest example. The software giant has invested heavily in OpenAI and built its technology into products like Azure, Bing and Copilot. Nvidia has also benefited from rising demand because companies like OpenAI rely on its chips to train and run AI models at scale.

Investors can also gain exposure through ETFs that hold large positions in AI-focused companies, including major tech firms tied to the growth of generative AI infrastructure.

Some private-market platforms occasionally offer access to pre-IPO OpenAI shares, though those opportunities are generally limited to accredited investors (people or institutions that meet certain income or wealth requirements set by financial regulators) and often come with high minimum investments and added risk.

articles.headline: While CEO Sam Altman wants world to accept bad things about AI, OpenAI wants new hires to tell how they c - The Times of India
articles.body: While CEO Sam Altman wants world to accept bad things about AI, OpenAI wants new hires to tell how they c    The Times of India

scored.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently argued that society may need to accept some negative consequences of artificial intelligence because of its broader benefits. Now a new report by Fortune has revealed that the ChatGPT-maker is introducing a new interview process which is aimed at accessing how prospective employees would help ensure AI benefits humanity. The contrasting developments highlight how the ChatGPT maker is simultaneously advocating for wider acceptance of AI-related risks while strengthening its focus on mission-driven hiring as the technology becomes increasingly powerful.The new ‘mission interview’ at OpenAIAccording to Fortune, OpenAI has begun piloting what it calls a "mission interview" for candidates applying to certain teams, starting with marketing and human resources. The goal, OpenAI told Fortune, is to give candidates dedicated space to explain how they'll contribute to the company's mission — ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.The interview isn't designed to extract a single correct answer. Instead, OpenAI says it's meant to assess how candidates actually think, including their judgment and their ability to weigh trade-offs — qualities the company considers increasingly essential as AI firms work to harness a technology carrying both significant benefits and real risks. A company representative said skepticism and disagreement are welcome in these conversations, as is intellectual diversity more broadly.How it worksTo keep the process independent, the person conducting the mission interview comes from a different team than the one the candidate is applying to join. OpenAI is also building out a training program that employees can complete to become certified interviewers for this process, though the program is still in its early stages of ramping up.Part of a broader push to standardize hiringThe introduction of a formal mission interview reflects OpenAI's attempt to bring more consistency to its evaluation process as the company continues to grow rapidly. OpenAI currently employs roughly 8,000 people worldwide and has 830 open roles as of this writing. Standardizing how candidates are assessed is aimed at giving the company a more consistent measure for evaluating new hires across different teams, rather than leaving mission-alignment checks to vary interviewer by interviewer.Not the first company to test for "mission fit"OpenAI isn't alone in building this kind of evaluation into its hiring process. Several major tech companies, including Meta and Amazon, use their own versions of a mission or culture-fit interview. Amazon, for instance, trains certain employees as "bar raisers" — interviewers pulled from outside the hiring team specifically to assess whether a candidate meets the company's broader Leadership Principles.Rival AI lab Anthropic reportedly takes a more direct approach. According to Axios, Anthropic interviewers test candidates with a blunt question aimed at determining whether they're joining the company for its mission or simply for the money — a particularly pointed question given how lucrative positions at leading AI labs have become.The money complicates the mission questionThat tension between mission and compensation is hard to ignore at companies like OpenAI, where many roles currently offer salaries exceeding $300,000, often with substantially more once stock compensation is factored in. According to posts on the anonymous professional network Blind, one software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received a total compensation offer from OpenAI worth $935,000, including a $385,000 base salary and $2.2 million in restricted stock units vesting over four years. A separate Blind post claimed Anthropic had offered another candidate $620,000 in total compensation.
