members.title: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments - Managed Services Journal

representative.headline: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments - Managed Services Journal
representative.body: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments    Managed Services Journal

articles.headline: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments - Managed Services Journal
articles.body: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments    Managed Services Journal

scored.body: From left: BlueStar’s John Martin, James Korte and Bre Malott lead “Blending Creative Content with Modern Marketing Tools” at VARTECH 2026. An AI tool that writes an ad gets plenty of attention. A tool that takes finished ads and turns them into a client presentation may solve a more immediate problem for a busy marketing team.At BlueStar’s VARTECH 2026 event, James Korte, director of marketing at BlueStar US, described an internal application that does exactly that. Placing a series of social ads into realistic layouts and assembling them in PowerPoint used to take his team 30 to 45 minutes. BlueStar’s homegrown replacement for a paid tool called Ad Mockup Studio now puts the ads in context and exports the presentation with one click.“I hated doing that,” Korte said of the manual version.That example captured a recurring theme of “Blending Creative Content with Modern Marketing Tools,” a BlueStar Academy session hosted by John Martin, senior content marketing manager at BlueStar US, and featuring Korte and Bre Malott, a digital marketing specialist at BlueStar Europe: Let AI handle the repetitive work, and keep people in charge of the decisions that make marketing effective. The panel summed it up with a familiar line from AI’s early days – people want AI to do the laundry, not write the poetry.For MSPs working with limited marketing resources, the session offered several practical ways to apply that approach.Start with a task that eats timeKorte said BlueStar has built roughly 10 internal tools in 2026 using vibe coding – AI-assisted software development in which users describe an application in plain language, then work with an AI tool to build and refine it. His platform of choice is Lovable; Replit is another popular option.One example is Brief Builder. It takes information from a standard project intake form, runs it through BlueStar’s guidance on what makes good marketing and produces creative-brief-style deliverables with starting points for headlines and copy. Korte’s favorite layer: The team instructed the system to channel a handpicked group of great copywriters and marketers from history. He called the result “a creative brief on steroids.”Another tool pulls data from HubSpot, LinkedIn, ClickUp and another platform into a single dashboard. It answers a request BlueStar CMO Dean Reverman had made for years: one view of campaigns and email subscriber activity to bring into board meetings. Korte built it in a matter of hours, largely by plugging in API keys.He also uses a Claude project to generate quarterly bonus documentation for the seven or eight people he manages. Team members submit raw notes on what they accomplished, and the tool selects the most significant items, weights them and produces a formatted, branded document. “Of course, I check it,” Korte said. “It saves me hours.”The common thread is a defined problem. Each tool addresses work the team already understands: preparing a brief, packaging ads, gathering information from separate systems or documenting results.An MSP can use the same starting point. Identify a recurring marketing task, document the inputs and desired output, and ask whether a small tool could remove the manual steps. Monthly campaign reports, QBR slide preparation and case study outlines built from project notes are likely candidates. Count the time spent reviewing and correcting the output as part of the cost – when the panel asked which marketing task takes too much time, one attendee’s answer was “correcting AI.”Take content strategy out of the slide deckA content strategy can lose momentum after the meeting where it’s presented. Korte described the familiar pattern: He builds a strategy deck defining pillars, themes, formats and audiences, walks the team through it, “and then life goes on.” Before long, people forget what the pillars were.“One of the reasons that I’m so infatuated with vibe coding right now … is because I feel like it’s useful for taking strategy out of a PowerPoint slide and putting it into a tool,” he said.BlueStar’s tool uses what the company has told it about its audiences – how many readers care about data capture versus point of sale and payments, for example – to recommend article topics and score their relevance. Once a writer accepts a topic, the tool suggests people to interview, questions to explore and a visual blueprint for the finished piece, from the hero image and bulleted agenda to scannable section formatting.Korte cited an article in progress by BlueStar Academy’s lead trainer about scaling a point-of-sale business from deployments of a handful of locations to 50 or 100. The tool organizes the assignment, but the trainer still conducts the interviews, distills what he learns and writes the article. A designer then uses the blueprint to format it.For an MSP, the value is consistency. Define priority customers, the business problems the company solves and the services it wants to explain, and those decisions can drive an editorial workflow that keeps topic selection on track. A topic score is only as useful as the guidance behind it, though. People still need to decide whether a proposed article answers a real customer question and supports the company’s goals. As the panelists noted, AI can’t decide who you’re selling to or which direction your company is rowing the boat.Give AI your voice and brand standardsMalott described giving ChatGPT her speaking style, words she likes and words she wants to avoid. “I want it to sound like things are truly from me,” she said.Martin, a writer at heart, described a research routine built on two tools. He runs the same prompt in Copilot and Gemini, asking for ideas, statistics, sources and how current the information is. The responses often differ significantly, so he merges the useful material and rewrites it in his own voice or BlueStar’s. “At the end of the day, I want it to sound like it’s from a human being,” he said.For MSPs, that suggests a practical role for AI in organizing research and producing a first pass. Checking the underlying sources and adding the company’s own expertise remain part of the job. Agreement between two AI responses isn’t verification.The same principle applies to visuals. “I don’t think the designs are bad. I think they are cluttered,” said Korte, who has spent more than 20 years designing by hand. AI-generated graphics tend to cram in copy, icons and the same script-style fonts, producing a default look audiences now recognize. The fix is to give the tool references, such as a screenshot of a design, color scheme or typography you like. Malott suggested prompting the AI to treat an ad like a billboard: a big, bold message, less text and a clean layout. As the panel pointed out, much of a designer’s job is removing things from the page.Korte said Claude gets BlueStar’s slides about 80% of the way there when he points it at a folder containing the company’s fonts, colors and graphic elements. When it misuses an element, he uploads a screenshot showing correct usage, and the next result comes closer. An MSP can do the same by gathering approved logos, colors, fonts and examples of effective work in one place, along with guidance on audience and tone.Settle governance before tools spreadBlueStar’s official policy, the panel noted, is that Copilot is the only AI tool approved for sharing company data – even as the marketing team experiments with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Lovable for other work.That mix creates its own problem. Korte’s 15-person U.S. marketing team builds in different tools, so a useful assistant created in one person’s account can’t easily be shared. BlueStar plans to pursue a team account, and Korte described another option under consideration: an internal app built on an AI provider’s API, so the whole team logs in to one tool and the company pays for usage instead of individual subscriptions.Ownership matters, too. Korte acknowledged the security questions vibe-coded apps raise and said he is working out how to move one of his projects off Lovable, using its GitHub integration and a copy of the database. “I don’t plan on not paying for Lovable, but I don’t want to be tied to it either,” he said.MSPs will recognize those issues. The same customers experimenting with vibe-coded tools and personal AI accounts will need help with access controls, data handling, API key management and ongoing maintenance. An MSP that has worked through those questions for its own marketing team is better positioned to answer them for clients.Keep review in the workflowAI also helps with troubleshooting. When a colleague reports a broken HubSpot workflow, Malott now shares a screenshot with AI to pinpoint the missing step, instead of tracing the problem from the beginning.Finished work still needs inspection, though. Korte recalled an AI-generated hero image for a healthcare research article showing a patient in a hospital bed and a nurse nearby. The nurse’s ID badge carried the patient’s photo – a mistake BlueStar didn’t catch until a friend at another company emailed a screenshot. “We’ve got to look more closely at those,” Korte said.For MSPs, review should cover facts, brand details and the small visual elements that can undermine credibility.The session’s strongest lesson was practical: Choose a familiar task, use AI to remove the work around it, and keep people accountable for the result. Skepticism has a place in that process. When an attendee admitted to still being skeptical near the end of the session, the panel’s reply was simple: Good. BlueStar’s examples give MSPs a place to begin, especially when repetitive production work crowds out time to understand customers and create content worth reading.

scored.body:
TikTok is bringing its ad network beyond its own app to U.S. advertisers and opening up campaign management to third-party AI platforms, the company announced at Advertising Week New York 2026.

The “TikTok Ad Network” (TTAN) lets U.S. advertisers extend campaigns beyond TikTok to reach audiences across what the company describes as a premium network of nearly 400,000 apps worldwide. TTAN is fully integrated into TikTok Ads Manager and includes brand safety and placement controls.

Alongside the network expansion, TikTok said its “Model Context Protocol” (MCP) tool for advertisers is now available as a connector across several AI platforms and registries, including Claude, Kimi, Manus, Perplexity, Replit, Snowflake, Tencent WorkBuddy, and the IAB Tech Lab Agent Registry. Built on the open “Model Context Protocol,” the tool allows developers to build AI agents directly on top of TikTok’s ads ecosystem to plan, launch, and manage advertising workflows with fewer manual steps. TikTok said advertiser use of the MCP tool for campaign activation and management has grown more than 200% since launch, citing internal data from July through September 2026.

“The TikTok MCP is indispensable to our AI-powered campaign workflows, including how we build campaigns, upload creative, and analyze performance. TikTok is a leader in helping brands leverage AI to grow,” George Velonias, Head of Growth Marketing at Wayfair Canada, said in a blog post.

The announcements were part of a broader set of AI-powered advertiser tools TikTok unveiled at the conference, spanning commerce, lead generation, and creative automation. On the commerce side, TikTok introduced “Buy Direct,” an in-app checkout tool that lets users complete purchases from the For You feed without leaving the app, and “Shopping Assistant,” a conversational AI agent built into multiple TikTok touchpoints that provides real-time guidance on product details, shipping, sizing, and availability. The company also introduced “Agentic Leads,” an AI agent for lead generation available through TikTok Direct Message and on advertiser-owned websites.

On the creative side, TikTok is automating its “Search Ads Campaigns” through Smart+, which extends automation to keyword and creative selection in search ads buying. A related feature, “Smart+ Creative Selection,” consolidates creative sourcing, including advertiser assets, Symphony’s AI-generated creatives, and creator content, into a single approval workflow. TikTok is also expanding GMV Max, its automated ad solution for TikTok Shop sellers, to factor in costs such as affiliate commissions, coupons, and referral fees when optimizing campaigns.

“AI is transforming how advertiser content is created and scaled,” said David Kaufman, Global Head of Monetization Product Partnerships at TikTok. “With our suite of solutions, we are bringing together AI, automation, and creativity to help advertisers improve performance while reducing effort.”

TikTok cited a PF Global economic impact report published last week finding that activity on the platform helped generate $81 billion in GDP for U.S. businesses, with 54 million Americans reporting a purchase after watching a TikTok video.

scored.body: The software development kit (SDK) has emerged as the key control point in the $400 billion in-app advertising market and could give independent adtech platforms an early advantage in the next wave of advertising across AI assistants, lockscreens and agentic commerce, according to a new report by Analysys Mason.The report, The SDK Advantage: How independent adtechs won mobile and are positioned to win AI-native advertising, argues that platforms such as AppLovin, InMobi and Liftoff, which built large SDK footprints across mobile apps, are best positioned to capture advertising on emerging AI-native consumer products.In-app advertising reached around $400 billion in 2025, growing 10.8% year on year and reaching five times its 2017 level, according to the report. It accounted for roughly a third of the $1.18 trillion global advertising market, while users spent more than 90% of their smartphone time inside apps.The shift is significant because traditional web advertising tools have limited applicability inside apps. Apps do not use cookies and are isolated from one another, while Apple’s ATT opt-in rate is around 35%. Safari and Firefox block third-party cookies by default, and Google retired its Privacy Sandbox in October 2025.As a result, first-party signals collected through SDKs have become the most dependable basis for targeting, the report said.The report argues that installed footprint, rather than simply advertising technology, has become the key competitive moat. Independent SDKs can reach up to 44% of Android and 31% of iOS app downloads.AppLovin’s $1.05 billion acquisition of MoPub is cited as an example of deals focused on acquiring installed footprint rather than just technology.The economics of that footprint can be significant. AppLovin generated $5.48 billion in advertising revenue in 2025, up 70%, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of around 82%, according to the report.At the same time, advertising remains heavily concentrated among the largest online platforms. Google, Meta and Amazon account for 70-75% of global online advertising spend, even though the open internet represents around 60% of online time.For publishers, the economics of in-app advertising remain more fragmented: of every $100 spent by an advertiser in-app, publishers receive about 50-55, the report said.The next opportunity could come from AI-native products. The report argues that advertising will become increasingly important as AI products scale because every query carries an inference cost and subscriptions alone may not cover those costs at consumer scale.Published pricing indicates that inference costs have fallen by more than 99% since 2023, potentially making free, ad-supported AI viable.Unlike conventional digital advertising, however, this emerging inventory will not necessarily have a webpage or ad tag. It will instead need to be accessed through code already sitting on the device—potentially strengthening the position of adtech companies with established SDK footprints.“Apps broke the advertising playbook built for the web,” Ujjwal Chaudhry, Partner at Analysys Mason, said. “Without cookies, tracking a user across apps no longer works, and the SDK has become the one place where the audience, the ad and the result can all be measured.”Chaudhry said the next wave of advertising would sit across lockscreens, AI assistants and agentic checkout.“AI products are costly to run, and advertising is the most scalable way to keep them free for consumers,” he said, adding that independent platforms with the widest SDK footprints were best placed to capture this new supply.According to the report, each successive shift in advertising has widened the lead of independent SDK-first platforms rather than resetting the competitive landscape.

articles.body: Fake ChatGPT, Gemini Sites steal advertising accounts, MFA codes    BleepingComputer

scored.body:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a "human-operated phishing platform" that impersonates advertising products for artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots like Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity, Meta Muse, and Manus.

The products, which claim to offer campaign optimization, spend audits, and business-account connections, are designed with one goal in mind: to capture credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes via spoofed login windows using the browser-in-the-browser (BitB) trick.

"Each product was built around the same action: Connect," Island researchers Oleg Zaytsev and Ofek Ronen said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Clicking it opened a browser drawn inside the real browser. The fake address bar displayed trusted origins such as accounts.google.com or an Okta tenant, while the real browser remained on the phishing domain."

"Behind the interface, the platform kept every password attempt, fingerprinted the device, and let an operator pick which MFA challenge the victim saw next."

One of the websites in question is "museads.ai," which emerged on September 16, 2026, a little over a week after Meta launched Muse, its AI agent designed for personal workflows. Described as "Your AI ads manager for paid media workflows," the platform claimed to help customers reach buyers, connect their ad accounts, and run sponsored placements.

Prominently placed in the spoofed web page is a Prompt Box with a "Connect" button, clicking which triggers a BitB attack to capture a visitor's account credentials for Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows. This is accomplished by drawing a fake window displaying a bogus account sign-in form with the address bar pointing to a legitimate domain (e.g., accounts.google[.]com).

In the background, the victim's device is fingerprinted, and the information is transmitted to the attacker at the endpoint "/api/send/ip" over Socket.IO, after which operator commands and victim data are exchanged based on the login workflow. Armed with the account credentials, the attacker attempts to sign in to the account in real-time.

"Every brand gets its own pitch," the researchers explained. "ChatGPT promises a Monday Google Ads brief. Gemini promises MCC (manager account) and linked-client support. Claude gets its own advertising portal, Perplexity offers campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus offers a private Meta integration."

Users are assessed to be directed to these landing pages via fake invitation emails that impersonate these trusted brands to lend the attacks a veneer of legitimacy.

"Each one in this campaign poses as a believable product, with its own brand, pitch, and sign-in flow," the researchers pointed out. "They also move with the news."

Island said the AI ads pages are part of a broader phishing platform that supports a three-pronged operation, the two others being Google Ads-themed refund claims and payment confirmation, as well as recruitment-related sites for Tesla, Louis Vuitton, Nike, and Adecco.

All the identified websites have been found to share the same technology stack comprising Next.js and Socket.IO, and communicate with the same endpoints. What's more, the threat actors behind the operation have exposed source code for earlier versions of the platform through misconfigured public GitHub repositories.

The AI ads-focused campaign is designed to target agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators, likely with the end goal of monetizing the ads accounts to run their own ad campaigns or sell them for profit, especially when they have a clean spend history.

According to a report published by Mimecast in July 2026, malware families like VietCredCare, DuckTail, NodeStealer, and PXA Stealer have engendered ad account theft at scale, leading to a "widespread commodity crime in the advertising ecosystem" where bad actors drain business budgets and sell accounts with good reputation in underground markets.

"For the victim, the card is the easy part: they can remove it within hours. Getting the account back is not," Island said. "Attackers typically add their own administrators and downgrade the legitimate owner, and recovery can take weeks or months while the account keeps serving ads. For a manager account, the damage reaches the agency’s clients."

To mitigate the threat, organizations are recommended to enable phishing-resistant authentication, review advertising control changes, and scrutinize AI integrations before connecting accounts.

The disclosure comes as Island revealed that threat actors are abusing Google-sponsored results to route unsuspecting users to custom GPTs or shared-AI chat content, which then redirect them to a fake Cloudflare verification page serving ClickFix-style lures to deliver NetSupport RAT.

"The campaign did not require a vulnerability in ChatGPT or Google," Island said. "It abused trusted platforms, attacker-authored content, paid search, and social engineering to move people toward malware delivery."

"Across a three-month observation period ending in August 2026, the broader delivery cluster included about 850 paid-ad landings, 26 lookalike ChatGPT destinations, and 71 Google Ads campaign IDs."

Published Oct 6, 2026, 1:47 PM EDT

Timi is the news and deals reporter for Android Police, who has been reporting on technology since 2008. He has worked in tech retail and also the IT space, providing hardware and software support, which gives him a unique perspective on the tech that he covers. This allows him to effectively break down complex subjects into easy-to-read pieces that even casual readers can enjoy. Before joining Android Police, he was a news writer for XDA, where he eventually transitioned to covering deals. He also worked as an editor and reporter for Neowin, where he covered news and attended major tech events like CES. He also reviewed phones, tablets, PC products, and other devices. In addition, he also created video content for the Neowin YouTube channel.

Back in the summer, Google announced its new Pixel lineup that included new phones and smartwatches. However, a promotional image showed an unannounced device, leaving many scratching their heads. To this day, Google has yet to shed light on what it is, but we're slowly getting more details from unofficial sources. Just yesterday, we learned that this upcoming wearable would reportedly be called the Fitbit Edge. And now, we're getting all the fine details about the hardware, which should give us a more complete picture of what to expect. The information comes from Dealabs Magazine, which is providing hardware specifications, prices, and the colors that will be available when it comes to market.

This could get interesting

Fitbit devices were getting pretty long in the tooth. So, fans of the brand were pretty excited when Fitbit announced the Air. While it didn't have a screen, it did show that parent company Google was still investing in the brand. Now, we're reportedly getting a nice follow-up with the Fitbit Edge. What makes this one exciting is that it has a screen. As far as what to expect in terms of hardware, the news outlet shares that the Edge will have a 1.34-inch screen. In addition, it will also have the usual batch of sensors for monitoring health and fitness metrics. That includes a heart rate sensor, SpO2 sensors, a barometer, a gyroscope, and more. It will also run Fitbit OS with access to a coaching system powered by Gemini. That last one is going to be a pretty big deal and will most likely be a huge focus on how it sets itself apart from its competitors. It has Bluetooth 5.4 and GPS, plus up to seven days of battery life. Naturally, this wearable is durable, packs an IP68 rating and 5ATM water resistance. When it comes to pricing, this one will be priced above the Air, coming in at €179. It's a touch more than the Fitbit Charge 6, which is similar, but the Edge will offer more modern components and features. Again, none of this is set in stone. But it is being reported. Of course, colors are important, and the Fitbit Edge will come in muted colors that Google has been using on all of its devices for some years now. If the reporting is accurate, we should see the Edge arrive in four colors: Obsidian, Olive, Canyon, and Fog. Now, all that's left is finding out when this thing will be available for purchase.

Smartwatches are great, but not everyone wants something like that on their wrist. This offers some connectivity, but mainly focuses on health and fitness. It provides the perfect compromise. We know that a lot of Fitbit fans have been waiting for something like this so it will be interesting to see just how popular it will become. Thanks: Armando

articles.headline: I asked Gemini to fix my Pixel issues; here's what actually worked - Android Police
articles.body: I asked Gemini to fix my Pixel issues; here's what actually worked    Android Police

scored.body:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 11:00 AM EDT

Ali has spent more than a decade covering consumer technology, with a knack for looking beyond the specs, tinkering with software, and uncovering the bigger stories behind Android, Google, Apple, and everyday devices.

Over time, my Google Pixel had built up a handful of small annoyances, the kind of issues you notice at first but never really sit down to fix them properly. Gemini has silently become useful for everyday troubleshooting like this, not only for asking trivia questions or writing emails. This brought me to ask about four separate issues instead of googling each one separately like I normally would. Some of the answers were straightforward and immediately useful, but others only helped partially. Either way, it beat digging through settings menus and guessing what might be causing each problem.

Battery drain had no obvious cause

Gemini found the actual culprit in battery usage

The first issue I discussed with Gemini was battery drain, which had gradually crept up enough that I couldn't pinpoint the exact reason. I asked Gemini why my Pixel was draining battery significantly faster than usual and how I could figure out what was causing it. It walked me through checking battery usage and flagged a power-hungry app running in the background. It also suggested changing my settings for that app instead of giving generic battery-saving tips. I opened Settings > Battery > Battery usage, tapped the app Gemini flagged, and turned off the Allow background usage toggle under Manage battery usage. I did that for all the apps that I didn't use every day. I tested the fix over the next few days to see if it made a difference, and it did. The improvement was not dramatic, but it was noticeably better than before I made the change. It was a win for my Pixel and me.

Notifications had gotten completely out of hand

Fewer interruptions without going fully silent

With every new service I join, or when I'm surfing the web and creating accounts, my emails get flooded with promotional marketing material. The same approach applies to X accounts. Over the past few years, I have followed many people on X and selected push notifications for most of them for news purposes. Now, it feels like my Pixel never catches a break, and neither do I. I'd been putting this off for months, so I asked Gemini to find a solution. I asked the AI-powered assistant, "My Pixel gets too many notifications. What can I do to make it less annoying?" Gemini pointed me toward finding the apps that are bringing in the most notifications through Notification History, along with app-specific notification categories. Notification history, found under Settings > Notifications, showed me which apps were sending the most alerts, and each app's notification categories let me switch off only the ones I didn't need. I tamed my notifications in the Settings app by turning off app-specific notifications and random notifications. By the end, the distractions and interruptions were reduced. Now, I only receive notifications that matter to me and that I actually want to see and keep. This was more of a targeted fix than a blunt one.

My storage was full, and I didn't know why

A guided cleanup instead of random deleting

My Pixel's storage was getting full, and I wasn't sure what was taking up so much space. That's a frustrating spot to be in, because deleting the wrong thing is worse than deleting nothing at all. Since all my photos are stored securely in Google Photos, I shouldn't worry about device storage filling up. Gemini walked me through it and explained which apps and files were taking up the most space and which of them were safe to remove. In Settings > Storage, I could see what each app and file type was taking up, so I cleared the biggest ones. That separation was useful for me, as I'm always unsure about app data and which of them are important. I freed up a hefty amount of space without deleting anything important.

My connection kept dropping, and nothing looked wrong

Gemini narrowed it down before I reset anything

The last issue was the most irritating one, because it came and went randomly. My Pixel always struggles to stay stable and keeps trying to switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, even though my other devices work fine. What made it hard to deal with was that nothing appeared broken, and it was hard to put my finger on what was going wrong. Other devices kept working fine, which made me realize that the problem wasn't originating from the router. I asked Gemini why my Pixel keeps losing its internet connection, even though other devices are working fine, and what I should check.

It asked me to change a few network settings and do the usual restarts and resets, but first it helped me narrow down the problem, which saved me from resetting everything. I checked Wi-Fi and mobile data separately to see which one was causing the trouble. The fix was turning off Adaptive connectivity under Settings > Network & internet, along with the option to switch to mobile data automatically, so my Pixel stopped jumping between the two.

Gemini is now my first stop for fixes

None of these fixes were dramatic, and my Pixel doesn't feel like a different phone; it still functions the same and performs the same functions as normal. What changed is that I now have a starting point for issues that used to mean a lot of scattered searching. The battery fix was the most modest of the four issues, as it was better than before but not a major comeback. The notifications, storage, and connection fixes did what I needed them to do. If you try this yourself, being specific in the question matters. I described what was happening and what I noticed, and the answers were more targeted than a generic troubleshooting list. This holds real value for me. Gemini doesn't have to solve everything for me; it just needs to tell me what the real problem is and where to look first. For me, that's precisely what it did pertaining to these four problems.

articles.body: Gemini North Reveals Pearl-Like Knots in the Remnant of a Supernova Witnessed in the Year 1181    NOIRLab

scored.body:
noirlab2624 — Photo Release

Cascading knot structure of historic supernova remnant are uncovered in new observations from the Gemini North telescope in Hawai‘i

6 October 2026

The Gemini North telescope located on Maunakea in Hawai‘i has revealed the most detailed view yet of Pa 30, the likely remnant of the historic supernova seen in the year 1181. The new observations reveal that its famous “firework” filaments are not smooth streaks, but chains of tiny knots.

No, this is not a firework display. This is Pa 30 — the likely remnant of the historic supernova witnessed in the year 1181, now captured here in unprecedented detail by the Gemini North telescope, one half of the International Gemini Observatory, partly funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and operated by NSF NOIRLab. This image was captured with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS), and it shows that the remnant’s unmistakable firework-shaped ejecta take a cascading knot-like structure.

The historic supernova, named SN 1181, is one of only five supernovae in the Milky Way that were observed from Earth before the invention of the telescope. Eight separate texts show that Chinese, Japanese, and Arabic astronomers first observed the supernova between 4 and 6 August 1181. The supernova remained visible in the constellation Cassiopeia for 185 days. According to what we know about how stars end their lives, the colossal explosion would have left something behind. Pa 30, a system composed of a blue central star and surrounding firework-shaped shell, is the top candidate for this supernova remnant.

Pa 30 was only discovered in 2013 through a citizen science campaign to find planetary nebulae in Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) data. It was the 30th nebula found by American amateur astronomer Dana Patchick. Follow-up imaging on the KPNO 2.1-meter Telescope and the Hiltner 2.4-meter Telescope, both located at NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO), a Program of NSF NOIRLab, revealed faint, diffuse nebular emission and remarkable radial filaments threading the nebula in a nearly perfect sphere. Based on its estimated age and brightness, scientists consider Pa 30 to be the likely remnant of SN 1181.

Analysis of the new observations from Gemini North, which was led by Timothy Cunningham (Center for Astrophysics — Harvard & Smithsonian) and Ilaria Caiazzo (Institute of Science and Technology Austria), reveals about ten times more filamentary structure in Pa 30 than previously seen. It also shows that the radial filaments are made of consistent chains of tiny knots of gas, rather than smooth streaks as previously thought. This knotty structure suggests that there may have been thermal or density variations in the circumstellar medium that shaped the supernova ejecta as it expanded radially away from the explosion.

Pa 30 is unique among all known supernova remnants. The central star remaining after the explosion, IRAS 00500+6713, is extremely hot, with a temperature of about 200,000°C (~360,000°F). It also possesses very fast stellar winds that move at around 16,000 kilometers per second (~10,000 miles per second).

Surviving remnant stars are expected to be “kicked” away during the powerful supernova explosion. However, the central star of Pa 30 appears almost exactly centered in the remnant. This curious configuration implies that the explosion was quite symmetrical, and it rules out a large kick that could have knocked the star off-center. From this, the researchers conclude that SN 1181 was an extremely rare Type Iax supernova. Unlike the standard high-energy explosions of Type Ia supernovae that wipe out their stars, Type Iax supernovae are lower-energy, incomplete explosions that leave behind a surviving remnant star. Pa 30 is the only known Type Iax remnant in the Milky Way.

The story of SN 1181 is one of humans working together, across time and space, to understand the changing Universe. As new astronomical questions arrive every day, SN 1181 invites us to wonder what mysteries remain unsolved from the distant past.

More informationAnalysis of this data is presented in a paper titled “Detection of knots in the supernova type Iax remnant Pa 30” appearing in The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9cb2

The team is composed of T. Cunningham (Center for Astrophysics — Harvard & Smithsonian [CfA]; now University of Warwick), I. Caiazzo (Institute of Science and Technology Austria), J. C. Raymond (CfA), and S. J. Kenyon (CfA).

NSF NOIRLab, the U.S. National Science Foundation center for ground-based optical-infrared astronomy, operates the International Gemini Observatory (a facility of NSF, NRC–Canada, ANID–Chile, MCTIC–Brazil, MINCyT–Argentina, and KASI–Republic of Korea), NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO), NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), the Community Science and Data Center (CSDC), and NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory (in cooperation with DOE’s SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory). It is managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA) under a cooperative agreement with NSF and is headquartered in Tucson, Arizona.

The scientific community is honored to have the opportunity to conduct astronomical research on I’oligam Du’ag (Kitt Peak) in Arizona, on Maunakea in Hawai‘i, and on Cerro Tololo and Cerro Pachón in Chile. We recognize and acknowledge the very significant cultural role and reverence of I’oligam Du’ag to the Tohono O’odham Nation, and Maunakea to the Kanaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians) community.

Blend Achieves Select Partner Tier in the Claude Partner Network

Blend Achieves Select Partner Tier in the Claude Partner NetworkPR NewswireCOLUMBIA, Md., Oct. 6, 2026COLUMBIA, Md., Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Blend360, a premier AI services provider, today announced it has achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track. The recognition reflects work already underway with Blend's enterprise clients: moving Claude out of pilots and into the workflows that run the business. The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers. The Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients, and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through Certified, Select, Preferred, and Global Premier tiers.Most enterprise AI stalls before it reaches production. Across the financial services, healthcare and life sciences, retail, travel and hospitality, energy, and technology, media, and telecom enterprises Blend works with, the model can usually do the job. What holds teams back is agreeing which workflows are worth building, seeing how a non-deterministic system will actually behave, and knowing who is accountable when a person needs to step in. Blend's Claude practice is built to clear those three barriers."The question enterprises are asking has changed. It's no longer whether Claude can do the work. It's how to put it into production, govern it at scale, and make it last. That's exactly what our teams are built for. Earning Select tier in the Claude Partner Network reflects that focus. The goal was never one workflow. It's end-to-end agentic transformation of the business areas that matter most, until the whole business runs differently."Ozgur Dogan, Chief Executive Officer, BlendBlend deploys Claude end to end: Claude Code for engineering teams, Claude Cowork for the people who run the business, and agentic solutions built on the Claude API. A senior Forward Deployed Expert works on site or local to each client and owns the outcome, with Applied AI Engineers and Agentic Engineers building alongside them. Governance is agreed before anything is built, from autonomy states and evaluations to named human-in-the-loop checkpoints on the client's own infrastructure. Clients own the solution and the code.Across its own organization, Blend runs Claude Enterprise and Claude Cowork in four regions, so the rollout patterns it brings to clients are ones it already uses itself. Looking ahead, Blend plans to grow its certified Claude delivery team and bring Claude into production for more of its enterprise clients.Learn more about the Claude Partner Network at claude.com/partners.About Blend360Blend360 is a premier AI services provider, committed to co-creating meaningful impact for its clients through the power of data science, AI, technology, and people. scored.body:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 7:30 AM EDT

Abhinav pivoted from a career in banking to pursue his first love in writing. Even while working full-time, he continued contributing as an editor-at-large, a role he has held for more than 7 years. A lifelong tech enthusiast who has built three gaming and productivity powerhouse PCs since 2018, his passion for technology keeps him closely following the semiconductor industry, from NVIDIA and AMD to ARM. His MSc dissertation explored how artificial intelligence will reshape the future of work, reflecting his curiosity about the wider social impact of emerging technologies.

I've spent some time reflecting on my LLM usage habits, and, inevitably, three names from the biggest cloud AI providers were on my list. ChatGPT and Claude, which together covered a broad chunk of my daily workflow and the menial things that I used to spend a lot of my time on. Each brought something to the table that others don't, which had me convinced for the longest time that there simply wasn't one model capable of replacing all three. There was a price to this convenience, of course. Both the services offered $20 Pro or Plus plans, and having subscriptions to both of them was eating into my spare change. Naturally, I tried looking for a local model that could handle everything I was throwing at the cloud models, and to my surprise, I found one that could handle most, if not all of it.

Qwen 3.8-27B changed how I saw local AI

It does the job of two subscriptions and costs me nothing

Before using Qwen 3.8-27B, I'd assumed it meant settling for something smaller and possibly less intelligent than a cloud model that I was replacing. Perhaps that's why running Qwen 3.8-27B felt like it defied all expectations I had surrounding local AI. The UD-IQ4_XS build from Unsloth is a 13.3GB download that fits on my 4070 Ti Super (with 16GB of GDDR6X VRAM) with context room to spare at 16K context window, and llama.cpp serves it over localhost at speeds that stop being a complaint after a few minutes of use. The model holds about 33.7 tokens per second across runs, and in a Pygame test where I asked it to build a working Snake game in a single file, it did exactly that in one shot. Plain text queries give no room for complaint either, as the model is excellent at the sort of ordinary summarization and analysis work that I usually go to a cloud model for.

ChatGPT was the easiest to replace

Most of what I use it for doesn't need a model running in a data centre

One of the things I use ChatGPT for most often is grammar checking and tidying up my emails, and on the off chance something verbose lands in my inbox, pulling the key details out of it. On rare days, I might even use it to trim down bloated sentences when I get too carried away, or turn a rough thought filled with jargon into something I can communicate more effectively. I also rely heavily on sentiment analysis when I'm researching products and services. I'll often go through dozens of user forums and discussion threads to understand how consumers are reacting to a particular product, service, or pricing change and then use an LLM to codify that information. Those are all tasks that a local model can handle without breaking a sweat, and that's something I learned only after a few days of using the Qwen and Gemma family of models. To put this to test, I fed Qwen 3.8-27B a deliberately rambling email about PC component prices with a dozen figures scattered through it. The model was able to pull every number and categorize it into a clean table, and that was enough for me to be convinced that it's a model that can take down a subscription from my bank statement.

Claude is brilliant, until it tells me to go away

Five-hour limits are counterproductive for something iterative like coding

Anthropic's frontier models are undoubtedly better at coding, and if you don't believe me, you'd only have to go through a dozen tests I've put them through against Google and OpenAI's models. One might even argue that the rise of Claude changed developer workflows permanently, and it'd be a reasonable argument. I use it much the same way, particularly when I'm working on Python projects that require a lot of back-and-forth. The problem is that Anthropic's models come with a lot of limits and guardrails, even for customers like myself who would happily pay $20 a month for some extra usage and performance from its top models. It's no surprise that tweaks to get past Claude's rate limits or to mitigate them as far as possible have their own dedicated tutorials these days. The biggest problem that anyone who relies on Claude faces is that when the five-hour limit runs out, there isn't much you can do besides use your credit card to make it work again, which is a charge on top of a subscription. Waiting for the limit to reset completely destroys the tempo of an iterative coding project, because by the time I'm back (five hours later), I have to go through the thread again and try to pick up where I left off, potentially losing ideas for refining whatever app I was working on.

That's a problem that's almost entirely fixed by running a local model. Qwen running locally has no five-hour wall, no weekly cap, and no overage bill that piles up and stares at me at the end of the month. I can leave it iterating on a project overnight if I want, and the only cost will be the 285W the GPU draws from the wall. As an added advantage, nothing I send to Qwen leaves my PC. That goes for both my half-written apps and the benchmarking data, none of which touch a server that another organization controls the retention policy for.

llama.cpp

Llama.cpp is an open-source framework that runs large language models locally on your computer.

Qwen models are free, but they are priceless in the right workflow

Qwen 3.8-27B doesn't exactly top the benchmark charts, but for the simple things that I need an LLM for, it absolutely does not have to. Although I found the model that fits the needs of my workflow (and my GPU's VRAM) perfectly, there's a perfect model out there on Hugging Face for every card, from the Gemma family that runs comfortably on my 16GB laptop to smaller Qwen builds that would run on even older hardware. All of them cost nothing besides the hardware they run on, so there's no reason not to tinker and give them a go.

articles.body: I had Claude look into my Windows 11 PC, and it revealed problems I didn’t know I had    XDA

scored.body:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 12:30 PM EDT

Abhinav pivoted from a career in banking to pursue his first love in writing. Even while working full-time, he continued contributing as an editor-at-large, a role he has held for more than 7 years. A lifelong tech enthusiast who has built three gaming and productivity powerhouse PCs since 2018, his passion for technology keeps him closely following the semiconductor industry, from NVIDIA and AMD to ARM. His MSc dissertation explored how artificial intelligence will reshape the future of work, reflecting his curiosity about the wider social impact of emerging technologies.

The Windows Event Viewer logs aren't something happy users of Windows 11 open very often, and when they do, they often don't find all the information there digestible or immediately actionable. The problem is that most of it is generally noise, so if you're looking for a specific error after a crash, you can be left jumping from one timestamp to the next before you get close to the root cause. Even then, it doesn't offer a clean solution, so you delve further and further down the rabbit hole, chasing driver versions, service dependencies, and Microsoft Learn forum solutions that may or may not apply. So, I took the path of least resistance and exported the last 30 days of system logs to Claude with one instruction, which was to find and fix whatever was wrong with my PC.

Most of my Event Viewer errors were Windows talking to itself

Claude's first job was just telling me what to ignore

When I first opened my Event Viewer log, it showed me about 750 Critical, Error, and Warning events over the course of 30 days, which made it seem like there was something seriously wrong with my PC. I exported the log as a CSV and delivered it to Claude Sonnet 5.5 with a straightforward prompt: "I've attached a CSV export of my Windows 11 System event log from Event Viewer, covering the last 30 days (Critical, Error, and Warning events only). Can you analyze it and tell me what's wrong with my PC?" With so much data, as you can expect, the first job Claude undertook was to separate the noise from the signal. The biggest pile by far was DCOM Event 10016, with 452 identical entries about a COM server missing a permission it didn't actually need. It was a fairly meaningless error that was repeated every few minutes, and it accounted for roughly 60% of my supposedly "broken" PC. Microsoft itself says that these events are "expected and by design," and don't adversely affect functionality. Among other benign errors, there were 14 Microsoft Store installation failures, all caused by Windows trying to update apps while they were still open. With the noise out of the equation, the rest of the events pointed at the other problems that I'd been living with without noticing.

It found that my secondary screen had been crashing for a month

The fix was a software update I would never have bothered with

I have a Lian Li 8.8-inch universal screen mounted inside my PC case for keeping additional playback controls handy and checking system information that I installed a few months ago. It had been acting up for a while, but I mostly blamed the USB connector attached to the PC and thought nothing more of it until I had the logs reviewed by Claude. It turns out that the specific driver, called lianli_display_driver.dll had crashed seven times, including five times within 23 seconds on a particular day without my noticing it. The software service from Lian Li had terminated unexpectedly five times, while a Kernel-PnP warning about the USB device failed to load appeared 30 times, on nearly every boot. If I had looked at the logs myself, I wouldn't have been able to make much of it, since the device functions alright, at least when nothing's playing on it. What I had noticed, though, was the fact that the screen kept defaulting to 30Hz refresh rate on every boot, which I'd been bumping back to 60Hz manually without thinking much of it. The Kernel-PnP warning in the logs meant the device's driver entry routine never ran at startup, and Windows then fell back to a generic USB handler that didn't know the panel's native timing.

The fix to this problem was stupidly simple. All I had to do was open the utility to check the version and there, I found an update prompt waiting on the dashboard that I'd never noticed, and likely wouldn't have for a long time.

Event Viewer said my PC had crashed 13 times

Claude found eight of them were Windows Fast Startup crying wolf every morning

With the screen problem diagnosed and fixed, it left me with the biggest number in the log, which related to 13 Kernel-Power 41 events, each flagged as Critical, and each one communicating that my PC had restarted without shutting down properly. It made it seem like my PC had crashed almost every other day. The only problem was, I had noticed no such crashes to speak of at all. Claude was able to find a clue that made it all make sense, however. It reported that eight of those 13 "crashes" happened within seconds of a Kernel-Boot entry stating that Windows had failed Fast Startup.

That completely demystified the log entries. Fast Startup is supposed to make booting quicker by saving a part of Windows' state when you shut your PC down, and when that saved state fails to load, Windows falls back to a normal boot and logs the previous session as an unclean shutdown. That meant eight of my 13 reported crashes were essentially Windows failing to use its own shortcut, then reporting the failure as a Critical error. You must now be wondering, "what problem does it solve?", and that would be a reasonable question, to be fair. The payoff for this was twofold; in that, I now knew that I was already getting a slow boot, and a Critical entry in the Event Viewer logs for the trouble. This meant that turning off Fast Startup was the best way forward, since the feature was failing every few days anyway. This also prevents further trouble down the road, since booting from a cached state can further complicate issues relating to drivers and other system-level changes that assume a clean start. A full shutdown avoids all of that, and the minuscule amount of time added to the subsequent boots is barely noticeable on my system.

Do I recommend doing this?

Everything I've described so far, including the issues that I knew existed but couldn't find a root cause to, and the issues that I didn't know were there in the first place, comes from a model that Anthropic lets you use for free. If you've got an account and a PC that occasionally hits a snag, there's no reason to let Claude have a go at your Event Viewer logs.

Claude is an AI assistant and LLM developed by Anthropic.

scored.body:
A phishing campaign is targeting Google accounts with lures that promise free subscriptions to Anthropic’s Claude Max AI model, Malwarebytes warns.

“The site announces that Anthropic has passed 100 million users and is thanking people by giving away 10,000 free one-month subscriptions to Claude Max, its highest-usage plan,” Malwarebytes says. “The presentation is careful, down to the real logo and colors, invented five-star reviews, and a long footer whose links lead almost entirely to genuine Anthropic pages. This is probably the most effective trust signal on the site, and it cost the operator nothing. A counter claims that fewer than 750 of the 10,000 slots remain, dropping by a few every several seconds. Nothing is actually being counted. The number is generated inside your browser and resets when you reload the page, so every visitor sees the same manufactured shortage.”

The goal of the phishing site is to trick the user into entering the credentials to their Google account. The site uses the “browser-in-the-browser” technique to open a fake Google login window inside the tab.

“Two sign-in options appear, but only one works,” the researchers explain. “The Apple button produces a pre-written notice saying that the method is temporarily unavailable. The email box discards whatever you type into it and triggers the Google button instead. Every route leads to the same place....Clicking the Google button doesn’t open a real Google sign-in window. Instead, the page draws a browser window inside the existing tab, complete with a padlock and a correctly spelled Google sign-in address. It can even be dragged around the page. The address bar, padlock, and everything inside the supposed window belong to the phishing page, not Google. It begins with a human-verification step rather than a password box, which may reassure visitors while helping to keep automated scanners away from the next stage.”

Malwarebytes has the story: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/09/fake-claude-max-giveaway-hides-a-google-account-phishing-trap

Workplace teams can build stack plans, update seating and model growth through a conversation, working from their own floor plans, utilization data and permissions

, /PRNewswire/ -- Robin, a leading workplace operations platform, today announced Robin's new agentic Space Planning, the first of its kind built directly in Claude. By using AI instead of working through rigid planning workflows, workplace teams can simply tell Claude what they're trying to accomplish. What used to take workplace teams months of effort before can now be done in minutes.

With Robin's Space Planning, workplace teams can combine the maps, attendance, utilization and policy data already in Robin with context from across the business, such as new hires from an HRIS or lease costs from finance within Claude. Claude can then build custom plans based on how their workplace actually operates, from seating new hires and reorganizing teams to building stack plans and modeling future space needs. The result is a more complete picture of the workplace and an AI-native planning experience that adapts to each company's needs.

Robin's space planning approach starts with the outcome, not the workflow. Once a Claude-created plan is approved, Robin orchestrates what happens next, from publishing the updated map to letting affected teams know where they're sitting. A team can even hand Claude a screenshot or spreadsheet of an existing plan to produce a working scenario with conflicts flagged.

Inside Claude, workplace teams can use Robin's Space Planning to:

Update seating plans: As new hires and departures sync from an HRIS like Workday, Robin flags who needs a desk and what space opens up, then carries out the move once it's approved.

Model stack plans and real estate scenarios: Build a stack plan from actual usage and right-size neighborhoods based on peak attendance. Model a smaller footprint, a merger of two offices or a new attendance policy and see the desks, square footage and floors each one frees up.

Weigh capacity and cost: Compare a headcount plan with current desk capacity, and merge attendance data with lease costs from a connected finance system or spreadsheet to see cost per occupied seat by building. Claude can turn either into a recommendation for executives ahead of a lease renewal.

Reclaim underutilized desks: Find desks with no check-ins in the last 30 days and decide the best way to use them. Convert them to bookable hotel desks, reseat the team closer together or pick something in between.

"No two companies work the same way, so no two offices should either," said Ciara Peter, Robin's senior vice president of product. "Robin knows how a workplace is used, and Claude brings in context from other systems a business runs on. Together, they give companies the freedom to design an office around their own people, priorities and way of working."

Space Planning in Claude is currently available to customers of Robin's One Workplace Platform. For more information, visit https://robinpowered.com/platform/space-management.

About RobinModern offices are powered by Robin. Our One Workplace Platform makes productive, friction-free workplaces a reality by providing a single platform to manage office operations. With actionable office analytics and planning tools, we help our customers optimize space investments while keeping employee experience at the forefront of their mission. articles.headline: I ditched Claude Code and Codex’s rate limits by switching to this open-source agent with 75 model providers - How-To Geek
articles.body: I ditched Claude Code and Codex’s rate limits by switching to this open-source agent with 75 model providers    How-To Geek

scored.body:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 5:00 PM EDT

Aggy is a veteran writer and editor in the technology and gaming space. Having served as a Managing Editor for high-traffic digital publications, alongside being an editor and consultant for over a dozen sites. Aggy's published work spans a wide and respected array of tech and gaming outlets, including WePC, Screen Rant, How-To Geek, Android Police, PC Invasion, and Try Hard Guides.

Beyond editorial work, Aggy's direct experience in the tech sphere extends to app development. Aggy has published two games under Tales and is always eager to learn and do more. He also likes working on computers and researching in his spare time.

He knows about Windows, Linux, Audio, Video, and much more.

I don't think I've ever come across a rate limit and been fine. It normally comes right as I really need it to work. If you've burned time on Claude Code or Codex and hit the wall that keeps you from using it, you know how unfair it feels. Luckily, there's an open-source coding agent that connects to over 75 model providers, so when one shuts you out, you move to another.

Rate limits are going to push you to OpenCode

Claude Code and Codex will lock you out when you need them most

Hitting a usage limit mid-session is one of the worst parts of working with AI coding tools. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex both have strict quotas that can kill your flow with almost no warning. I hate quotas because you usually don't get a heads-up or a real count before you hit one. The AI rarely tells you how close you are. Claude Code runs a rolling 5-hour window and a weekly usage cap. It gets worse the longer you work, because file reads, searches, and conversation history all pile up and your token usage snowballs. Once you hit either limit, you have to wait for the timer to reset, upgrade your plan, or buy extra usage credits. ChatGPT plans cap how much you can use OpenAI's models, including Codex, and the limits depend on which plan you have. And since these tools tie you to a single provider, hitting a rate limit means you're just stuck until that provider lets you back in. OpenCode fixes this. You can run it as a terminal app, a desktop app, or an extension inside VS Code or JetBrains. Instead of locking you to one provider, it connects to over 75 of them through the Models.dev registry. You can bring your own API keys for Claude, GPT, Gemini, or DeepSeek, use a subscription you already pay for like GitHub Copilot or ChatGPT Plus, or run models locally with Ollama or LM Studio. If you hit a rate limit or a provider goes down, you just switch to another one. You don't lose your place or have to set anything up again. If you're coming from Claude Code or Codex, then you'll see how similar it is. OpenCode reads your files, runs terminal commands, makes edits, and takes your feedback. On top of that, it adds local Git snapshots and compiler diagnostics, which is pretty helpful.

How you connect your models and jump between them

Switch whenever you want

You run /connect in the terminal, and it walks you through signing in. If you already pay for GitHub Copilot or ChatGPT Plus, you can just use that, but you don't need a subscription to use OpenCode. If you do want to use one, click the model, then Manage Models, and then + Connect Provider. You can plug in an Anthropic Claude API key through an environment variable, hook up Google's Gemini models, or run free local models on your own machine with Ollama or LM Studio. One thing to know is that Claude Pro and Max won't work here. Anthropic doesn't let third-party tools use those subscription tokens, which is honestly annoying, so you'll need a pay-as-you-go API key to use Claude. You don't have to re-explain what you were doing or restart. All your slash commands work the same no matter which model is running underneath. On the agent side, OpenCode comes with a few modes depending on what you're doing. The default is the Build agent, which has full permissions. If you want to poke around the codebase without changing anything by accident, hit Tab to switch to the Plan agent. That one's read-only, so it can dig through your code and suggest what to do without touching files unless you tell it to. You can also make your own agents, like a Review agent for checking code and catching security issues, a Debug agent for tracking down bugs, or a Docs agent for writing documentation. You can give each one only the permissions it needs.

You should skip OpenCode if you need one specific model

OpenCode is meant for multiple AI eyes

The biggest weakness with OpenCode shows up when developers build apps or workflows tightly around one specific AI model. You need that model and the way it works, and I've made plenty of AI apps that rely on a specific model and would fall apart with a different one. Models aren't all made the same, and an app has to be built around how its model works. So if you swap models partway through a project, those differences can break the main parts of your app. Sometimes, you'll get errors or bugs that are a nightmare to track down. Smaller models you run locally will often make up settings or skip using tools completely when you give them prompts written for the big paid models. If your app depends on one specific model, switching between providers just isn't practical.

Being able to hop between models also matters a lot less when the top paid models keep beating everything else anyway. Claude Code with Claude Opus is amazing when it comes to code, and it's hard to beat. When you try to run big tasks that contact a bunch of files through smaller open-source models inside OpenCode, you won't get the same quality.

Having access to over 75 model providers doesn't mean much if most of those models can't get it right on the first try. That's why sticking with one provider can be worth it for better results if you're actively making apps. Keep in mind that OpenCode never forces you onto weaker models. It gives full access to top-tier models like Claude Opus and OpenAI's GPT-5 series right alongside everything else. So you still have good options. It's just best for people whose work doesn't depend on one specific model.

It's not the solution for everyone

The feature that makes OpenCode so great is what makes it so bad in some cases. If your app depends on how one model behaves, hopping between providers is going to ruin it. I've seen it happen in apps I've made, so I can't recommend this if you absolutely need a specific AI in your app. However, if you are just using AI or you have built your app to use any AI, then you'll be fine. The setup is easy, your context carries over when you switch, and you're not stuck if one company goes down or raises its prices.

Scales Gemini Enterprise Readiness Across 12,500+ Associates with Google Cloud

, /PRNewswire/ -- Tech Mahindra (NSE: TECHM), a leading provider of AI-powered digital transformation and technology consulting solutions to enterprises across industries, announced an expansion of its agentic AI readiness through partnership with Google Cloud. The partnership aims at scaling hands-on capabilities of Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise across Tech Mahindra's global workforce to support growing enterprise demand for production-ready AI.

Tech Mahindra's scaled readiness combines trained and certified talent with reusable industry solutions, production deployment experience, and a growing portfolio of agentic AI solutions and agents. Its expanding portfolio includes industry-specific solutions available through Google Cloud Marketplace, enabling customers accelerate adoption of enterprise AI with capabilities designed for real-world business environments. This combination is designed to help customers move from AI experimentation to implementation and adoption.

A key element of this expansion is 'Build with Gemini', a Google Cloud hands-on workshop that Tech Mahindra is rolling out to more than 12,500 associates worldwide. Designed as an immersive event, 'Build with Gemini' empowers participants learn to create, secure, and govern AI agents using Gemini Enterprise tools and solutions including Agent Runtime, Agent Gateway, and Model Armor. Attendees develop practical skills that can be applied directly into client engagements, complementing Tech Mahindra's broader 'AI Delivered Right' strategy, which focuses on translating AI innovation into responsible, secure, and measurable enterprise outcomes.

Associates completing the 'Build with Gemini' workshop earn a Google Cloud Skill Badge, further strengthening the talent base supporting Tech Mahindra's delivery capabilities. This builds on Tech Mahindra's experience deploying Gemini Enterprise in complex enterprise environments and developing industry-specific agentic AI solutions across telecommunications, financial services, manufacturing, retail, and other sectors.

Anthropic shipped Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, 2026, and the pitch is blunt: it matches Claude Fable 5.1 on most real-world work while costing 20% less to run than its predecessor, Claude Opus 5. For developers who’ve been paying $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, that’s not a rounding error. It’s a reason to rebuild your cost model. This tutorial walks through every step of setting up the Claude Opus 5.5 API in a real project, from creating an API key to shipping a working tool that actually uses the model’s 1-million-token context window.What Is Claude Opus 5.5, and Why It Changes the API MathPrerequisites and RequirementsSteps 1-4: Account, API Key, SDK Install, and Your First CallStep 1: Create Your Anthropic Console Account and Generate an API KeyStep 2: Confirm Billing Tier and Initial Rate LimitsStep 3: Install the Official SDKStep 4: Make Your First Call to Claude Opus 5.5Step 5: Understand Claude Opus 5.5 Pricing Before You Build AnythingStep 6: Put the 1-Million-Token Context Window to WorkStep 7: Configure Adaptive Thinking Effort LevelsStep 8: Cut Costs by Up to 95% With Prompt CachingStep 9: Batch Large Jobs at 50% OffStep 10: Deploy Through AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft FoundrySteps 11-12: Build a Complete Project — A Long-Context Repo Digest ToolStep 11: Write the Core Digest ScriptStep 12: Add a Batch Mode for Bulk File ReviewStep 13: Add Error Handling, Retries, and Spend MonitoringClaude Opus 5.5 vs Sonnet 5.5 vs Opus 5 vs Fable 5.1: Which Should You Use?How Claude Opus 5.5 Stacks Up Against GPT-6 Astra and Gemini5 Common Pitfalls When Migrating to Claude Opus 5.5Troubleshooting Guide: 8 Common Errors and How to Fix ThemSecuring Your API Key in a Real DeploymentAdvanced Tips for Production DeploymentsFrequently Asked QuestionsRelated Coverage

By the end, you’ll have a command-line application that ingests an entire codebase or log archive, summarizes it with Claude Opus 5.5, caches the expensive parts of the prompt, and batches overnight jobs at half price. We’ll also cover the eight most common errors developers hit when switching models, five pitfalls that quietly double your bill, and how Opus 5.5 stacks up against Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Fable 5.1 so you pick the right model for the job instead of defaulting to the most expensive one.
