members.title: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp

representative.headline: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp
representative.body: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense    ALM Corp

articles.headline: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp
articles.body: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense    ALM Corp

scored.body:
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, its latest edge frontier model designed for long, multiphase tasks in fields like software engineering, enterprise knowledge-intensive domains such as law and finance, and cybersecurity defense. The company announced the release on September 30, 2026, in a post by Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect.

Most users are not yet able to use it. Argon is being rolled out to a select group of trusted cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind Program, with a release to developers, enterprises and consumers promised “as soon as possible.” A specific date has not been given.

A phased launch with government input

Google says releasing capabilities at this level calls for a phased approach. The company is involved in the United States government’s voluntary pre-release model access program to gradually expand the number of Argon testers and will continue to collect early feedback from trial participants to set guardrails before a broad launch.

When their turn comes to go global, the paid API access and Google AI Ultra subscribers are prioritized. The pricing is fixed for the product’s launch; Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens during the introductory period, with cached input tokens discounted by 95% off the input price. The rates per million output tokens will move to $4 per million input tokens and $20 after the launch period, but the post does not state how long this window will last.

Output limit jumps to one million tokens

One of the more substantive technical upgrades is the output limit. Google has increased it to 1 million tokens, up from 64,000 on the previous generation. Google believes that by allowing its models to think and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single request, they’re able to solve more difficult problems in one go rather than being forced to stop halfway.

For developers building agents or long coding sessions, this is probably the number they should be paying the closest attention to.

Argon is already working inside Google

Google says thousands of its own employees are using Argon for specialized coding, deeper research and writing, and it shared three examples.

Quantum algorithm work. Argon is enabling quantum computing researchers to reduce by a factor of 2X the spacetime (as measured in qubits multiplied by gates) of subroutines that are bottlenecks for important applications. In one case, it dramatically outperformed the published baseline by 40% in a matter of minutes.

Memory savings in data centers. A team of agents from Argon used their combined knowledge of fleet-wide profiling data and performed a number of memory optimizations on their own and implemented them, resulting in Google claiming that it has freed up more than 300 TiB of memory (after deployment) and has a total of between 500 TiB and 1 PiB of memory savings.

Code migrations to Rust. Argon agents are migrating C and C++ code bases to Rust across Google, ranging from tens of thousands of lines in libraries such as re2 and libgav1 to more than 800,000 lines of code for the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. Because many of these systems are mission-critical, the rewrites are undergoing extensive automated and manual auditing, emulated testing and review before deployment.

The libgav1 project serves as the most detailed example. This open source video decoder is rewriting an existing Rust port that was itself based on a C++ translation. The team replaced 32,000 lines of SIMD code by performing numerous rounds of profile-guided experimentation and analysis of compiler output, then writing safe Rust the compiler could vectorize automatically. Google reports the result is a memory-safe decoder that runs 2.7 times faster than the Rust port, with identical video output.

The benchmark claims

Google backs the launch with an extensive list of results, all of which originate from its own announcement. On DeepSWE v1.1, a benchmark for measuring the real-world, long-horizon software engineering capabilities of the model, Argon scored 77.9%, which Google claims to be a new state of the art. It further states that Argon leads the Vals Index, a metric of economic impact across finance, coding, legal and tax domains, where every industry’s contribution is weighted by its impact on the GDP of the United States.

Similar statements are made for Vals Finance Agent v2, a multi-step financial research benchmark, and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, which evaluates legal research and writing capabilities. On Zapier’s AutomationBench, a benchmark for end-to-end execution across a range of core business functions, Argon ranks first at 51.3%. For visual capabilities, Google cites LVBench, a long video understanding benchmark, where Argon achieved 91.7%, deemed to be state of the art. The benchmarks released by the model’s creator merit some caution, as independent evaluations after launch will speak louder about these scores’ practical applicability in the real world.

Cyber defense, without the usual guardrails

The cybersecurity is where Google is most vocal about Argon’s capabilities – the model is exceptionally good at defending, including automatically identifying, verifying, and even fixing critical software vulnerabilities. For trusted partners and Google’s internal security teams, Argon will be available without the cyber guardrails, giving them access to the model’s full defensive potential.

Wiz has already begun using Argon for its Scan for Good program that proactively identifies high-severity weaknesses in critical infrastructure and helps remediate them for free. When run on healthcare-related software used across the industry, Argon uncovered one critical exposure affecting sensitive personal data that proved challenging to remediate before, and that previous frontier models failed to identify. On the benchmark of choice for security researchers, CWE-bench v1, which evaluates the ability to repair security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for the top spot with 68% accuracy. Google claims Argon outperforms its Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber model on vulnerability discovery. On Google’s internal benchmark, it was able to detect a variety of exposures across 20 different programming languages in complex codebases. And on Wiz’s internal black-box penetration testing benchmark, where the model cannot see the inner workings of the web application under test and had to infer its attack surface from first principles, it performed better than 3.8 Flash Cyber in discovery, vulnerability analysis, and proof-of-concept generation.

Four safeguards before a broad release

Google organizes its safety work into four areas.

Misuse. The model is designed to avoid malicious requests that could lead to cyber or chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear attacks while still allowing legitimate dual-use science in line with the company’s Frontier Safety Framework. Google is enhancing its monitoring of the model’s internal activation patterns to detect abuse, and says internal and external red teams have tested the safeguards by using both manual and automated attacks.

Prompt injection. Google refers to Argon as their most powerful model to date against indirect prompt injection, which is when an attacker takes over a model by tricking it into following their instructions. They claim that Argon outperforms all previous models on the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark.

Misalignment. Mitigations oversee the model’s line of thinking and acts along its chain of thought and execution. Google has a similar process that watches the training runs, but it didn’t want to put the results of those runs back into training so that the model’s reasoning would not learn to avoid the overseers. It also pushed the rest of the industry to preserve the transparency of reasoning.

System hardening. Following its agent control roadmap, Google is isolating and sealing sandboxed environments before high-risk training or evaluations begin, and says it will share those practices with partners.

What to watch next

Argon’s true test begins now. For now, the evidence of its success is Google’s own benchmarks, a handful of internal projects, and one early account at the company’s security division Wiz. Broader adoption will determine whether other developers and businesses are seeing similar results.

There are two metrics to watch. First, how long will it take for the model to reach paid API users and subscribers of its AI Ultra subscription, which Google did not specify. Second, how much will its introductory pricing, which is already significantly higher than what other firms provide, increase upon transition to standard rates. The move to $4 and $20 per million tokens represents a doubling of the cost, so budgets of teams relying on Argon may need reconsideration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is Gemini 4 Argon?

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest frontier model, announced on September 30, 2026. It is intended to address complex, long-horizon challenges in software engineering, enterprise knowledge work, including legal and financial domains, and cybersecurity defense.

Q2: Who can use Gemini 4 Argon right now?

A pool of trusted cyber defenders, as a part of Google’s Fairwind Program. Developers, enterprises and consumers will also gain access as soon as possible, Google says, however, it has not established an exact date for the launch.

Q3: Who gets access first after the broader release?

According to the announcement, paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers will receive priority access. Wider availability will come after Google collects feedback and further optimizes the model’s guardrails.

Q4: How much will Argon cost?

During the introductory period, the cost will be $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. The cached input tokens will be discounted by 95% of the input price.

Q5: What happens to pricing after the introductory period?

The price will increase to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Google’s post does not state when the introductory period will end.

Q6: What is the new output token limit?

One million output tokens, as compared to sixty-four thousand before. Google claims this allows the model to perform extensive reasoning and address difficult problems in one go.

Q7: How well does Argon perform on benchmarks?

Google reports 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, 51.3% on AutomationBench, 91.7% on LVBench and 68% on CWE-bench v1. These numbers come from Google’s own announcement.

Q8: What is the Fairwind Program?

It is the Google program under which trusted cyber defenders are receiving early access to Gemini 4 Argon. They, along with Google’s internal security teams, are able to use the model without the cybersecurity guardrails.

members.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost? - Kingy AI

representative.headline: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost? - Kingy AI
representative.body: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost?    Kingy AI

articles.headline: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost? - Kingy AI
articles.body: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost?    Kingy AI

scored.body:
I would start Sonnet 5.5 at Medium for a clearly scoped coding task, move to High when the work needs more investigation, and reserve Max for problems where a comparison shows that the extra effort improves the result. Choosing Max for everything can turn an inexpensive model into an expensive workflow.

The cost gap is substantial in one independent evaluation. Artificial Analysis reports $0.59 per Intelligence Index task at Medium, $1.12 at High and $7.67 at Max. Max scores higher on that index, but costs about 13 times as much as Medium. Those are benchmark-specific task costs, not prices for your next bug fix. Medium results, High results, Max results.

There is also a default-setting difference worth checking before you compare results: Sonnet 5.5 starts at Medium in Claude apps and Claude Code, and High on the Claude API. Anthropic documents both in its Sonnet 5.5 announcement.

Our Astra vs Sonnet 5.5 comparison and Sol 6.1 vs Sonnet 5.5 comparison cover model choice. This guide covers the setting you should evaluate before changing models.

Sources and benchmark snapshot checked October 5, 2026. Setup examples follow official documentation and have not been tested against a paid API or a logged-in Claude session for this guide. Task examples and worked budgets are illustrative; benchmark measurements belong to the named evaluator.

What Medium, High and Max change

Effort controls how much work Claude puts into a response, including thinking, answer text and tool calls. It is a behavioral control rather than a fixed allowance of reasoning tokens. Max still operates within request limits such as max_tokens; it does not authorize an unlimited API bill. Anthropic effort documentation.

Sonnet 5.5 supports five levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. Anthropic recommends Medium for well-specified agentic coding and multistep tool work, High for harder or longer tasks, and an evaluation before adopting Xhigh or Max. For latency-sensitive chat, it suggests Medium or Low. Sonnet-specific effort guidance.

Here is how I would apply that guidance. The examples are suggested starting points, not measured completion rates.

On small screens, scroll tables sideways to see every column.

Task

Start with

What to check before raising effort

Implement a specified feature with clear acceptance criteria

Medium

Does the implementation meet the brief and pass relevant checks?

Diagnose an intermittent bug across several files

High

Does the explanation fit the evidence, and does the fix address the cause?

Draft a document from an organized source packet

Medium

Are claims supported and calculations correct?

Resolve conflicting requirements or a difficult technical decision

High

Does the answer identify the tradeoffs and material exceptions?

A recurring hard problem that High leaves unresolved

Compare Xhigh and Max

Does either improve accepted results enough to cover the added time and cost?

A longer answer is easy to notice. An overlooked edge case is harder to notice. Set your acceptance criteria before reading the output, so an impressive explanation does not substitute for a working result.

For a bug fix, that might mean a reproduction that fails before the change and passes afterward. For a research memo, it could mean supported claims, correct dates and a calculation another person can reproduce. For a document, include the required sections and the intended audience in the brief.

The defaults depend on where you use Sonnet

Product

Sonnet 5.5 default effort

Claude apps

Medium

Claude Code

Medium

First-party Claude API

High

Sources: Anthropic's launch announcement, Claude Code model configuration, and Sonnet API model overview.

An explicit setting, a saved preference or an organization policy can affect what you see. Record the active setting instead of assuming that every Sonnet session starts the same way. When comparing a Claude app response with an API response, set matching effort deliberately and account for the tools and context each product supplies.

Sonnet 5.5's effort scale is also recalibrated relative to Sonnet 5. Anthropic recommends retesting the levels on your own tasks when upgrading. A familiar setting name does not guarantee a familiar token bill. Sonnet 5.5 prompting guide.

Independent results show why Max needs a reason

Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index v4.3.2 provides separate Sonnet configurations. All three rows below retain the evaluator's Default Fallback label.

Sonnet 5.5 effort

Intelligence Index

Weighted cost per index task

Output tokens across the index run

Medium

41

$0.59

31 million

High

47

$1.12

52 million

Max

56

$7.67

420 million

Sources: Artificial Analysis Medium, High and Max pages, checked October 5.

High costs about 1.9 times Medium in this evaluation mix. Max costs about 6.8 times High. Its higher composite score establishes a capability gain on that index, while the cost shows why a blanket Max policy deserves scrutiny.

The index points are not success percentages. Its weighted task costs account for benchmark token use and caching assumptions, and the campaign-wide output totals are not tokens for one request. The rows also include fallback behavior; they do not isolate Sonnet with fallback disabled. See the evaluator's benchmark methodology.

Anthropic flags a since-fixed structured-output bug in the prerelease Sonnet deployment used for two Artificial Analysis knowledge-work tests. That caveat remains relevant when interpreting the launch-era results; a current page alone does not establish that every affected test was rerun. Launch footnotes.

Use these figures to decide which configurations to test. Budget a live workload from its own usage records, including failed attempts, tools and review time.

Max can lose to Xhigh

Anthropic reports Sonnet 5.5 at 52.1% on FrontierCode 1.1 at Xhigh and 46.2% at Max. Its launch footnote attributes the lower Max result in part to review activity that caused timeouts or changes outside the requested scope in two examined cases. The benchmark grades whether a change could be merged without human edits. Anthropic's results and explanation.

That is one benchmark and one harness. It is enough to reject the assumption that increasing effort always improves the result.

If High produces a valid patch, Max needs to improve something you value: a missed failure mode, a stronger implementation, fewer repairs or better performance on the hard cases. Extra files, extra commentary and extra checks have value only when they serve the task.

I would include Xhigh in an evaluation before standardizing on Max. Keep the same brief, tool permissions and acceptance checks. Count a timeout or an unnecessary change as a problem rather than crediting the model for doing more work.

How to change effort in Claude apps

Select Sonnet 5.5, click the model name beside the send button, open Effort, and choose a level. Anthropic says the change applies from the next response. The menu identifies a recommended default. Claude Help Center instructions.

Thinking and effort are separate controls, but Sonnet 5.5's thinking cannot be turned off in the Claude apps. A missing expected model or effort option on an Enterprise account may reflect an administrator's restriction. Higher effort consumes more tokens and can use up your allowance sooner. The help page does not establish a fixed number of messages you gain by choosing Medium.

For ordinary iterative work, try Medium with a concrete brief. Move up when the answer misses requirements or fails a check. Keep subscription allowances separate from the API dollar examples below; our ChatGPT Pro vs Claude Max guide covers the plan decision.

How to change effort in Claude Code

Select Sonnet 5.5 through /model, then set the level directly:

/effort medium

Use /effort high or /effort max to compare other settings. The session header shows the active level. You can also launch a session explicitly:

claude --model claude-sonnet-5-5 --effort high

On current versions, typing a Low-through-Xhigh level after /effort saves it for later sessions. For a session-only choice, open the /effort slider and confirm with s; that behavior requires v2.1.257 or later. Max applies to the current session unless set through the effort environment variable. It is not accepted as a persisted effortLevel or per-model settings value. Organization caps can limit the applied level. Claude Code configuration documentation.

Check the header after changing settings, especially on a managed account. This gives you an observable configuration to record alongside the result.

How to set effort in the Claude API

Set output_config.effort explicitly. This Python example uses Anthropic's Messages SDK and the verified model ID. It assumes the SDK is installed and an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is available in your environment.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(

model="claude-sonnet-5-5",

max_tokens=4096,

output_config={"effort": "medium"},

messages=[{

"role": "user",

"content": (

"Compare two approaches to adding retries to a background job. "

"Cover duplicate execution, failure handling and how to test it."

),

}],

)

print("Stop reason:", response.stop_reason)

print("Usage:", response.usage)

for block in response.content:

if block.type == "text":

print(block.text)

The example follows the Sonnet 5.5 migration guide. It sends one text request; it does not execute tools or implement a coding agent. Change medium to high, xhigh or max for a separate evaluation. No beta header is required for top-level effort.

Give thinking and the answer room to finish

The example's 4,096-token ceiling suits a small demonstration, but can truncate a demanding response. Thinking shares the output budget with the visible answer. Sonnet's standard maximum is 128,000 output tokens. Model limits, Thinking and billing.

Anthropic recommends a 128,000-token ceiling and streaming for agentic coding. Its SDK supports collecting a final message from a stream:

with client.messages.stream(

model="claude-sonnet-5-5",

max_tokens=128000,

output_config={"effort": "high"},

messages=[{

"role": "user",

"content": "Analyze the attached implementation and test evidence.",

}],

) as stream:

message = stream.get_final_message()

print(message.stop_reason)

print(message.usage)

Replace the sample message with the actual implementation and evidence; this snippet does not attach files. A high ceiling permits more output and therefore more spending, but does not force the model to consume it. Choose the ceiling your application can afford. Agentic coding guidance, SDK streaming pattern.

Check stop_reason before accepting a result. max_tokens signals truncation, tool_use requires the tool workflow to continue, and end_turn means the model finished its response. Even end_turn still needs your task's acceptance checks. Stop-reason documentation.

Avoid incompatible thinking settings

Sonnet 5.5 rejects thinking: {"type": "disabled"}. To remove up-front thinking, use thinking: {"type": "between_tools"} at Low, Medium or High. That combination is rejected at Xhigh and Max; use adaptive thinking there by omitting thinking or setting its type to adaptive. Migration rules.

Keep adaptive thinking for the initial effort comparison so you change one control at a time. Testing between_tools can be a separate latency experiment.

Changing top-level effort between requests invalidates cached message blocks. Sonnet supports a cache-preserving per-message effort change in beta, requiring adaptive thinking and the mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 header. Use the documented per-message format when implementing that behavior, and inspect actual cache usage. Cache invalidation rules.

API prices and a worked budget

Sonnet 5.5's first-party Standard API prices are the same across effort levels:

Token category

USD per million tokens

Ordinary input

$2.00

Billable output

$10.00

Five-minute cache write

$2.50

One-hour cache write

$4.00

Cache read

$0.20

Source: Anthropic pricing. Thinking is billed as output even when its text is hidden. Thinking documentation.

Consider two hypothetical single requests, each using 100,000 ordinary uncached input tokens. One generates 20,000 total billable output tokens; the other generates 100,000. Their calculated bills are $0.40 and $1.20. These examples exclude tools, retries, regional modifiers and tax. They do not predict which effort setting will generate either output count.

The $0.80 difference equals 48 seconds of human time at an assumed $60 an hour. If the larger request saves more than that in review or repair and meets the same quality bar, the extra spending could be worthwhile. If it produces the same usable result, the smaller request has the cost advantage.

An agent job can contain many requests. Add every attempt, cache operation and applicable tool charge before comparing costs. For a batch of jobs, divide total spending by the number of accepted results. Report unresolved jobs alongside that figure so a low completion rate cannot hide behind a low average bill.

When to try Opus or Astra instead

If Sonnet repeatedly fails to plan a difficult task, resolve ambiguity or sustain the work, compare a different model alongside higher Sonnet effort. Anthropic's Sonnet prompting guide points to Opus for the hardest long-horizon work. Our Sonnet vs Opus 5.5 comparison covers the cost and capability tradeoff.

Use Astra vs Sonnet when your task fits Astra's evaluated strengths, and Sol 6.1 vs Sonnet for the less expensive OpenAI alternative. OpenAI also recommends reserving Xhigh and Max for cases where representative evaluations justify their cost and latency. OpenAI deployment guidance.

Matching effort names across models do not equalize computation, cost or capability. Compare complete configurations and the deliverables they produce.

A small evaluation you can reuse

Choose representative work: a routine task, a difficult task and a case that previously failed. For each, write the acceptance checks before running it. Use fresh sessions or the same starting repository state so one configuration does not inherit another's solution.

Run Medium and High with identical briefs, files, tool access and thinking mode. Include Xhigh and Max on the difficult cases.

Record the model ID, active effort, output ceiling, fallback policy, total usage and elapsed time to a usable result.

Grade the deliverables against the same checks. Include failed attempts, unexpected edits and human repair time.

Repeat ambiguous cases before treating a small difference as reliable.

For coding, require a check that exercises the change. Anthropic documents that Low effort can sometimes skip verification, so make the required test or build explicit in the task. Higher effort still needs an observable result. Coding verification guidance.

Keep Medium for work it finishes acceptably. Route demonstrated failures to the setting or model that resolves them, and revisit that policy when the model or your workload changes.

scored.body:
Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police | voronaman / Shutterstock

Published Oct 6, 2026, 6:58 AM EDT

I've been covering Android and other mobile technology for close to ten years now, with a specific interest in phone accessories, e-readers, and what makes each individual phone different from another. I delight in looking at the phone market from as many angles as possible, and while my opinions may be odd, at times, they're always from the heart as much as the head.

I have a background in the mobile accessories world, which explains my odd enthusiasm for cases and things that clip onto smartphones.

I worked for Digital Trends from 2017 to 2025.

Sign in to your Android Police account

Google Gemini's Call for Me is expanding from just business calls, into personal calls, according to details seen in the latest updates. This would mean Gemini would be capable of calling your nearest and dearest, and while the functionality looks to be on the limited side, Call for Me will be able to ask simple questions and relay messages. Of course, whether you want to give up talking to your friends and family, so a robot can is another question entirely.

Call for Me may soon mean you never need to make another call again

But is that really a good thing?

Call for Me debuted last month on the Pixel 11, and it has a simple premise: Gemini makes calls to businesses for you, making or changing appointments, so you don't have to call yourself. The reception was mixed, to say the least. While some appreciate the time-saving elements here, others are keenly aware of how this sort of technology further increases isolation and loneliness within society. Plus, who wants to talk to robots instead of people? This news comes from a new update to the Phone app, which Android Authority was able to dig into. These screenshots show some examples of what Gemini may be able to do in the future, and it includes options for calling "John" or "Mom", and delivering a message or asking a simple question. While it's not spelled out in the hacked build, it's a clear implication that Call for Me is prepping to go beyond businesses and expand into personal calls. It also looks as if there's an option to bar the AI from calling you, but good luck getting your mom or grandmother to turn that setting on. This feature isn't available yet, and testers weren't able to get it working, even with their hacked builds.

Auto Call Screening

Look, I hate making phone calls as much as anyone else, but this technology does give me pause. I use Call Screen in order to filter out spam and nonsense calls all the time, and to some extent, those people deserve to speak to a robot instead of a human. But a blameless receptionist at the local salon? The last thing they need is to talk to Gemini fifteen times a day. Extending that to talk to your friends and family takes that to another level. While using Gemini can save some time for you, it's going to be bluntly obvious to the person being called that you don't care enough about them to talk to them yourself. Instead, you made them talk to a robot instead.

There are many jokes made about tech billionaires and companies not being real people, and actually being lizards or aliens in disguise, but stuff like this genuinely does make me wonder whether there's some truth in that. There's no confirmation this feature will ever see the light of day, of course, but it's clear proof Google is working on adding it.

articles.headline: Google just replaced Gemini Gems with Skills. Here's how to use and master them - Android Authority
articles.body: Google just replaced Gemini Gems with Skills. Here's how to use and master them    Android Authority

scored.body: Khamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityAdd Android Authority on Google: Google introduced Gems way back in mid-2024, before the agentic AI obsession. Gems were supposed to be AI helpers with a personality and a unique goal. You could have a Gem that helped you cook, code, or serve as your language learning partner. They all had their own chat windows and instructions, essentially turning them into mini-apps.But that didn’t work. Gems were their own silos. They could help you complete repeating tasks, sure, but you had to find and open the Gem conversation first. So in true Google fashion, it’s gone, joining the ever-growing graveyard of products Google abandoned. And in its place comes Skills.If you use Claude or Perplexity, you might be familiar with this concept. But if not, here’s a rundown on what’s changing — and how to start using Gemini Skills today.Did you ever use Gems?46 votesWhy Google is moving from Gems -> SkillsKhamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityGems lived in their own silos, in the sidebar, and were trivially easy to forget. When they came out, I played around with them and quickly forgot they existed. The way consumers use AI chatbots has evolved. With a long context window, it makes sense to continue working on multiple aspects of a project in the same chat window. What you want is to use your pre-configured gems and customized prompts anywhere. That’s what Skills does.Once configured, you can call up a skill from any chat, and invoke it using the data from the current chat. And this isn’t limited to a single skill or chat. You can stack up skills, chaining up a step-by-step automation system.For example, you might be working on researching a specific module related to your work or college in a chat. You can use one skill to start the research based on parameters you’ve already narrowed down. Then, another skill can take all that information, format it into an easy-to-read digest, and write it in your own style (based on data from your Google account activity). Yet another skill can then take that digest and send it to your team members via Gmail, or create a Google Doc based on it. This can go on and on, and it’s only truly limited by your unique requirements and workflows.While I don’t use AI for writing (part of my personal AI ethics policy), I do use it for brainstorming ideas, creating unique angles, and doing the menial tasks like generating keywords and SEO descriptions based on my text. And this is where Gemini’s Skills, to me, are really helpful. Previously, I fed my preferences into Gemini’s Memory file, and now, instead of relying on Gemini’s recall, I can give specific instructions for each task.How to build and use your own Gemini SkillsKhamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityHow to make a skill? Well, just ask Gemini. Yes, there is a dedicated Skills page in Settings where you can see recommended skills, ones you’ve created, and even your Gems from the before times.True to its form, Skills is built into the chat interface. So open a chat, type “create a skill for me that does,” and ramble on. You can even use voice typing to give more instructions. As with any AI prompt, the more detailed it is, the better your chances of success.Then, press Enter and let Gemini do its thing. It will create a new skill for you, with detailed instructions, surpassing what you rambled on about. For example, I asked Gemini to create a skill for me that proofreads text. I’m what you call a silly-mistakes writer. In my flow, I might make a silly mistake or two that my eyes gloss over during proofreading. Instead of burdening my editors, I usually use something like Grammarly Pro, Claude, or Gemini to go through the article and point out silly mistakes that I then fix myself (I don’t trust an AI model to just fix typos without introducing new issues in the process).Khamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityGemini made a skill called “draft-proofreader” for me (I can change the name if I’d like). Now, all I have to do is paste in the draft text, use the “/“ command to run the draft, and wait for the results.And here’s a pro tip: If you simply enter the forward slash command in the text box, you will see a list of all your Skills.Khamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityIf you want to be particular about the skills, it’s best to create one manually. Go to Settings -> Skills -> Create Manually. Here, you will see sections to give your skill a name (no spaces between words, hyphens only), add a description, and then add all your detailed instructions.5 Gemini Skills you should tryKhamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityGiven how simple it is to make Gemini Skills, you should try it out for yourself. It will depend highly on my workflow. For me, skills include online research, editing, and writing. For you, it might be about science, technology, arts, or plain idea generation.If you can take repeated action based on a similar dataset or question, you should try to turn it into a skill. Here are some ideas to get you started.Meeting-prep: If you use Gmail, Google Docs, and Meet, you can ask Gemini to create a workflow based on the next Google Calendar or Google Meet session. Based on the meeting, it, can go to your Gmail and surface relevant recent threads and insights from documents related to the project.Repurpose: If you find yourself reshuffling content to fit into different formats, create a skill dedicated to it. Ask Gemini to take a long article or a listicle and format it as an X or LinkedIn post, a script for an Instagram Reel, or a Facebook post.Distiller: Create a skill that pulls in Slack threads, Gmail messages, or documents and presents you with a bullet-point list of main learnings, actionable items, and highlights the decisions already made/tasks already accomplished.De-jargon: Ask Gemini to go through any text (a pitch or an email) and remove all the telltale signs of AI writing (trust me, Gemini already knows). This presents a cleaner prose that you can actually read, like a real human person.Stack skills together: A big side effect of moving from Gems to Skills is that they are stackable. For example, with a command like /fact-check-links + de-jargon on the same prompt, you can ask Gemini to first fact-check all the claims and URLs in an email or as a submission, then run it through an anti-AI filter to give you content that is already cross-checked and down to the basics.FollowThank you for being part of our community. Read our Comment Policy before posting.

Promoting the use of hydrogen in public transportation to help realize a hydrogen society

WEBWIRE – Tuesday, October 6, 2026

Toyota Motor Corporation (Toyota) launched the new fuel cell route bus (FC route bus) �Sora,� powered by hydrogen.

Toyota regards hydrogen as an important energy source in realizing a carbon-neutral society. It introduced its first fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV), the Mirai, in 2014 and has sold it in more than 30 countries and regions. Since 2019, Toyota has also begun supplying fuel cell systems (FC systems) that generate electricity from hydrogen, and has provided more than 3,500 FC systems *1 to over 100 customers worldwide for applications such as buses, rail, and stationary generators. In partnership with others, Toyota has also developed hydrogen cartridge and hydrogen sauna, promoting decarbonization in areas of everyday life as well.

*1 As of the end of September 2026.Related articles from Toyota Times

May 7, 2025, Hydrogen Cartridge

Trucks Carrying Hydrogen and Prepared Food - A New Challenge Starting at the ExpoSeptember 17, 2025, Hydrogen Sauna

Refreshed by Hydrogen! Toyota Made a Sauna?

In 2018, Toyota launched the first-generation Sora, offering a new value for route buses through clean, quiet fuel cell-powered operation. With the introduction of the new, upgraded Sora, Toyota will continue to contribute to realizing a hydrogen society by promoting the use of hydrogen in public transportation.

The new Sora is a next-generation FC route bus jointly developed by Isuzu Motors Limited (hereinafter, Isuzu) and Toyota as part of efforts to achieve zero-emission route buses. It combines Isuzu�s BEV full-flat route bus platform with Toyota�s FC system, further advancing the environmental performance and usability of route buses.

Vehicle Overview

1. Evolution of the FC system

Fuel efficiency has been improved by efficiently using the fuel cell and a large-capacity battery. Compared to the first-generation Sora, the total hydrogen tank capacity has been reduced by about 20%, while the cruising range has been extended by about 100 km to over 300 km *2, meeting the operational requirements of transit buses.Building on fuel cell technology developed through previous efforts, Toyota adopted a compact FC stack for commercial vehicles with increased output and durability, contributing to smoother, more stable operation. In addition, a new large-capacity hydrogen tank for commercial vehicles was developed, and by compactly mounting the FC system on the roof, vehicle maintenance by bus operators has been made easier.

*2 Reference values based on Toyota�s measurements. Actual values may vary depending on temperature, traffic conditions, the number of passengers, air conditioning use, and other factors.

2. Enhanced safety functions

The vehicle is equipped with EDSS (Emergency Driver Stop System), linked with DSM (Driver Status Monitor). If the system detects that the driver is experiencing a problem, the vehicle decelerates and stops, automatically applies the parking brake after stopping, and helps ensure safety even on slopes.A front blind spot monitor that detects pedestrians and bicycles ahead of the vehicle and alerts the driver is installed, contributing to helping reduce accidents outside the vehicle.

*3 Options will be available to order from around April 2027.

*4 Reference values based on Toyota�s measurements. Actual values may vary depending on factors such as the hydrogen station�s capacity and ambient temperature.

3. Improved usability

The passenger compartment uses a full-flat floor with no steps, creating a space where all passengers, including those using wheelchairs or strollers, can move more safely and smoothly.A one-touch wheelchair securement system (optional)*3 is available to assist wheelchair users in getting on and off the vehicle and helps the driver secure them smoothly.Four variants―two for urban use and two for suburban use―with different seat layouts are offered to meet a variety of operating needs.The vehicle can be fully refueled with hydrogen in about 10 minutes *4, supporting operations that require high vehicle utilization. The vehicle complies with a new high-speed filling standard; when compatible hydrogen stations are deployed in the future, refueling time can be reduced by about half.By connecting an external power supply unit, the vehicle can be used as an emergency power source during disasters.

Toyota has been working with many partners in producing, transporting, storing, and using hydrogen. Moving forward, we will continue to promote the widespread adoption of hydrogen mobility in collaboration with government agencies and businesses, including through the hydrogen backbone network implementation initiative, a joint public-private effort.

As part of efforts to pass our beautiful �Home Planet� to the next generation, Toyota has identified and is helping to solve issues faced by individuals and overall society, which Toyota calls �Achieving Zero,� hoping to help reduce the negative impacts caused by these issues to people and the environment to zero. Additionally, Toyota is also looking �Beyond Zero� to create and provide greater value by continuing to diligently seek ways to improve lives and society for the future.

About Beyond Zero https://global.toyota/en/mobility/beyond-zero/

Toyota Motor Corporation works to develop and manufacture innovative, safe and high-quality products and services that create happiness by providing mobility for all. We believe that true achievement comes from supporting our customers, partners, employees, and the communities in which we operate. Since our founding over 80 years ago in 1937, we have applied our Guiding Principles in pursuit of a safer, greener and more inclusive society. scored.body: Located in the North Sea, the Gemini offshore wind farm generates renewable electricity for the Netherlands, off the coast of Groningen.In this image, acquired by one of the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites, the individual turbines are visible as white dots, while the turbine blades can be seen as dark shadows. The tower foundations, immersed in the waters of the North Sea, cause turbulence, churning up sediments which cause characteristic flow patterns in the water. At the bottom left of the image, a white streak from a boat’s wake is visible; in the centre of the image, between the turbines, another boat and its shadow can be seen.Offshore wind power delivers significant environmental benefits by producing clean, renewable energy, which helps to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and combat climate change. Rule 10b5-1 trading plan

regulatory

"pursuant to a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan"

A Rule 10b5-1 trading plan is a pre-arranged schedule that allows company insiders to buy or sell stock at specific times, even if they have inside information. It helps prevent accusations of unfair trading by making these transactions look planned and transparent, rather than sneaky or illegal.

restricted stock units

financial

"Includes restricted stock units"

Restricted stock units are a type of company reward where employees are promised shares of stock, but they only fully own these shares after meeting certain conditions, like staying with the company for a set time. They matter because they can become valuable assets and are often used to motivate employees to help the company succeed.

vesting conditions

financial

"subject to vesting conditions"

Vesting conditions are the rules that determine when someone earning company stock or stock options actually gains the right to keep or sell them, typically based on staying with the company for a set time or meeting performance targets. Think of it like keys that unlock gradually — some unlock by calendar date, others only after agreed milestones. Investors care because vesting shapes management incentives, the timing of share sales, and the number of shares that can enter the market, which can affect a company's valuation and ownership mix.

members.title: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI - Music Business Worldwide

representative.headline: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI - Music Business Worldwide
representative.body: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI    Music Business Worldwide

articles.headline: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI - Music Business Worldwide
articles.body: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI    Music Business Worldwide

scored.body: Google for Startups will host its Gemini Startup Forum at Google‘s Mountain View headquarters in California next month.The two-day event brings founders of startups at the Seed to Series A funding stages together with Google’s AI experts.The forum is run with Google DeepMind and Google Cloud. Google says it explores “how AI will redefine your industry, transform your company, and unlock unprecedented growth.”Google notes that the more than 100 startups taking part, from 17 countries, were selected from over 2,000 applications.One of them is French music marketing company Base for Music, which tells us it’s the only music tech company in the cohort.The company sells what it calls a marketing operating system to producers, labels, and music companies. It pulls ad spend, audience, CRM, and streaming data into one environment, which Base for Music says lets it track the return on each marketing investment.It raised EUR €1.5 million (USD $1.73m) in a June 2025 funding round backed by Belgian music tech investor LeanSquare, French investors from Super Capital and One Green, and angel investors specializing in the marketing tech sector.Base for Music was founded in 2021 and reports it now supports more than 20,000 artists and labels worldwide.The company works with distributors and aggregators, servicing their clients or equipping their in-house marketing teams. It tells MBW its main partners include Ditto, iMusician, IDOL, and, more recently, TikTok-owned SoundOn, and Cinq Music.Base for Music explains that its technology helps artist teams decide which releases to promote, when, and how much to spend.The company claims that marketing ROI has long been “a black box for the industry,” and that its tech can now predict that return before a campaign launches.“The main piece missing today [for us] is clear, structured financial data tied to streaming revenues.”Maxence Bazin, Base for MusicAsked what challenges the company set out to solve, Maxence Bazin, Base for Music’s CEO and founder, said: “Mastering effective music marketing today requires a combination of media buying expertise, data analysis, and AI – there’s no way around it.“The core challenge we set out to solve was building a technical infrastructure capable of aggregating these fragmented marketing data sources and correlating them to surface key growth signals.“The alternatives out there each offer centralization tools focused on one specific aspect of marketing. This forces teams to navigate between disconnected solutions, and more importantly, risks overwhelming them with information at the very moment they need clarity to make the best strategic decisions.“We spent nearly five years developing our own marketing operating system: a platform that centralizes all of these marketing data sources and correlates them to enable data-driven strategic decisions. With the rise of AI, we’re now able to apply this approach at a much greater scale, and more importantly, begin predicting the outcomes we can expect from a campaign before it even launches.”Base for Music points out that the music industry mostly links AI with creation, but Bazin argues that “AI, data and media buying are opening a new chapter for music marketing: turning fragmented data into fully controlled ROI.”Bazin added: “Our conviction is that a technical infrastructure built specifically for music marketing has never made more sense. Combined with the power of AI, this technology lets us follow remarkable growth among the artists we support, day after day.”The company built its own AI, Base Intelligence, over the past year as part of the Google for Startups program in France.It turns each artist’s data into recommendations, delivered in the company’s Artist Dashboard or as reports for account managers.Bazin cites a campaign for Brazilian artist Tom Ribeira as a case study. The campaign was run in partnership with Ribeira‘s management team at Grand Musique Management, a prominent artist management firm based in France.Grand Musique Management has been a Base for Music partner “since its earliest days and now applies the platform’s data-driven approach across its entire roster,” according to the startup.Base for Music reports that Ribeira went from zero to over 200,000 monthly listeners on Spotify in less than six months with his debut EP, “on a €1,000 investment that became profitable within three months.”Asked about the Ribeira campaign, Bazin told MBW: “Based on the signals we detected across platforms, we used our Marketing OS to manage the total planned marketing budget of €1,000 for the release of his debut EP.“This was the full campaign spend, allocated across different platforms to reach specific audiences and generate as many engaged listeners as possible. This approach allowed us to stimulate the algorithmic recommendation of the EP’s lead track on Spotify, using media buying as an acceleration lever that triggers growth across other channels.”A report outlining the campaign highlights the performance of Pedaço, which it describes as Ribeira‘s debut single. The single, released on June 5, 2025, shares its name with Ribeira‘s debut EP, which came out in March 2026.The report puts total ad spend at €1,216 across three campaigns run between June and August 2025.The first, on Instagram, found that nearly 90% of the listeners it sent to Spotify were in Brazil, so the other two targeted Brazil only.The report credits the campaigns with getting the track picked up by Spotify‘s algorithm, which now accounts for close to 62% of its streams.By the end of 2025, the track had earned €1,317 in net Spotify revenue, the report claims, and its algorithmic streams have continued into 2026 without further ad spend.“Data ownership would simplify the entire process, but we don’t see the market moving in that direction anytime soon.”Maxence BazinFor now, Base for Music‘s ROI predictions rely on industry averages, Bazin says.Asked what is still missing in music marketing, Bazin said: “The main piece missing today [for us] is clear, structured financial data tied to streaming revenues. Combined with marketing data, this would allow music marketing to precisely measure the return on investment of streaming campaigns.“Every artist and label we work with has their own distribution partner, which currently limits our access to this type of data. This is why our current ROI prediction models rely on standard financial benchmarks, such as average per-stream revenue by DSP.“Direct access to this data would allow us to correlate the territories and audiences targeted by marketing activity with the streaming revenues they actually generate. Once that bridge is built, it becomes possible to drive an artist’s growth with a precise, real-time understanding of profitability.”Commenting on whether data ownership has to change, Bazin said: “Data ownership would simplify the entire process, but we don’t see the market moving in that direction anytime soon. In the meantime, the only path forward is to adapt, which means building powerful technology capable of operating across external platforms.“This is precisely why we founded Base for Music, and the development of AI represents a real opportunity for us to deploy that vision at scale.”Asked what an artist team might be able to do in marketing five years from now, Bazin said: “In five years, music marketing could be continuously fed by all of an artist’s revenue streams, whether that’s streaming, merch or live, giving teams complete visibility over every investment made across an artist’s career.“Each area of activity and the data it generates would become a source of insight that can be correlated with the others. That correlation would allow each revenue stream to act as a lever for the rest, unlocking full control over an artist’s overall growth.“Getting there requires a powerful marketing operating system capable of processing and correlating ever-growing volumes of data through AI, as well as artist teams and partners willing to pool their actions and expertise.”Music Business Worldwide

scored.body:
Vera Solutions achieves Select partner tier in Claude Partner Network to support responsible AI for nonprofitsHow can Vera support your AI journey?

LONDON , UNITED KINGDOM, October 6, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Vera Solutions has achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track. Organizations advancing the social sector can work with Vera to responsibly design, deploy, and govern Claude across their programs. The Select tier status builds on Vera's role as one of the inaugural implementation partners for Anthropic's Claude for Nonprofits program, launched on December 2, 2025.

Vera's AI work sits within three connected service areas. Advisory Services help organizations make sense of their data, navigate AI responsibly, and build data and tech strategies that fit their context. Implementation Services put powerful and affordable technology and data solutions in place, including AI-powered tools. Enablement Services equip teams to use those systems with confidence, driving long-term adoption and success. Where AI comes into play in these three service areas, Vera's focus is on sustainable and ethical use of AI. AI supports the work and people stay in the loop to review outputs, guide decisions, and stay accountable to the communities they serve.

As a Select tier partner, Vera has a growing number of Certified Claude Architects to support organizations advancing social and environmental impact. For Vera's clients and prospects, this means direct access to a team trained and tested on Anthropic’s suite of Claude products (LLMs, Chat, Cowork, Code, API).

"For 16+ years, we've helped social impact organizations make data-informed decisions. Our philosophy has always been to leverage the best available technology to help organizations solve problems,” said Zak Kaufman, Co-founder and CEO of Vera Solutions. “While we and our clients need to be careful and deliberate in implementing AI, the technology offers opportunities for organizations to save time, gain insight, and deliver more value to communities. Hitting ‘Select’ partner status is a signal that our team is ramping up on AI, and that Vera is meaningfully broadening our impact beyond the Salesforce platform and ecosystem.”

Organizations exploring Claude can talk to Vera's team.

About Vera Solutions

Vera Solutions is on a mission to amplify the impact of the social sector. It envisions a sector driven by transparency, accountability, and data-informed decisions. For 16+ years, Vera has helped leading impact-driven organizations save time, money, and headaches by delivering powerful, flexible technology and data solutions. Vera is a Certified B Corporation and Salesforce Summit Partner, with more than 20,000 social impact professionals using its systems across 195+ countries.

About the Claude Partner Network

The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers. The Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients, and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through Certified, Select, Preferred, and Global Premier tiers.

scored.body:
Tech Mahindra announced on October 6, 2026, an expansion of its agentic AI readiness through its partnership with Google Cloud, scaling hands-on Gemini Enterprise capabilities across its global workforce with a workshop program reaching more than 12,500 associates worldwide.Readiness ExpansionTech Mahindra, a provider of AI-powered digital transformation and technology consulting solutions to enterprises across industries, said the expanded readiness is aimed at supporting growing enterprise demand for production-ready AI. The company said its scaled readiness combines trained and certified talent with reusable industry solutions, production deployment experience, and a growing portfolio of agentic AI solutions and agents. According to the company, that combination is designed to help customers move from AI experimentation to implementation and adoption.Build with Gemini WorkshopA key element of the expansion is Build with Gemini, a Google Cloud hands-on workshop that Tech Mahindra is rolling out to more than 12,500 associates worldwide. Designed as an immersive event, the workshop has participants learn to create, secure, and govern AI agents using Gemini Enterprise tools and solutions, including Agent Runtime, Agent Gateway, and Model Armor. Tech Mahindra said attendees develop practical skills that can be applied directly to client engagements. Associates completing the workshop earn a Google Cloud Skill Badge, which the company said further strengthens the talent base supporting its delivery capabilities.Pramod Panda, Chief Learning Officer at Tech Mahindra, said: “Enterprise AI will scale only when organizations can combine technology innovation with the talent and delivery capability required to put it into production.” Panda said the companies are building that capability by combining hands-on Gemini Enterprise expertise with industry solutions, agents, and real-world deployment experience, an effort he said strengthens Tech Mahindra’s ability to help clients move faster from AI ambition to measurable outcomes consistent with its AI Delivered Right approach.Portfolio and Deployment ExperienceTech Mahindra’s expanding portfolio includes industry-specific solutions available through Google Cloud Marketplace, which the company said enables customers to accelerate enterprise AI adoption with capabilities designed for real-world business environments. The expansion builds on the company’s experience deploying Gemini Enterprise in complex enterprise environments and on industry-specific agentic AI solutions it has developed across telecommunications, financial services, manufacturing, retail, and other sectors, according to the company.Kelly Rogan, Vice President of Global System Integrators Partnerships at Google Cloud, said enterprises are shifting rapidly from AI experimentation to deployment, a stage at which she said domain expertise and robust engineering matter most. “By scaling Gemini Enterprise, Tech Mahindra equips its global teams to build, deploy, and govern agentic AI solutions,” Rogan said, adding that the companies are helping joint customers accelerate innovation and drive business value with Google Cloud.Strategy Context and Prior Gemini CollaborationThe workshop program sits within Tech Mahindra’s broader AI Delivered Right strategy, which the company describes as an enterprise AI approach designed to help organizations move from experimentation to impact and translate AI investments into measurable outcomes. The strategy is anchored in four pillars: Productivity Delivered, Transformation Delivered, Innovation Delivered, and Assurance Delivered. On its strategy page, Tech Mahindra names TechM agentX and the TechM co-pilot as key offerings under Productivity Delivered and describes Makers Lab, its innovation hub, under Innovation Delivered. Under Assurance Delivered, the company said it embeds trust, safety, and compliance into AI solutions, with platforms equipped with built-in controls for data privacy, model drift, and bias detection.The readiness expansion follows a December 18, 2025 announcement in which Tech Mahindra said it planned to accelerate enterprise adoption of Gemini Enterprise using Google’s Gemini 2.5 multimodal models. The earlier release said the collaboration combines the company’s implementation experience, AI-first engineering talent, and TechM Orion framework with Google Cloud’s AI capabilities, and that Gemini Enterprise would enable the creation of specialized AI agents, embed governance and safety guardrails, and integrate with Google Cloud’s ecosystem, including the Vertex AI platform, Google BigQuery, and advanced data-to-AI pipelines. That release identified Tech Mahindra as a Google Cloud Premier Partner and cited its dedicated Centers of Excellence, a portfolio of ready-to-deploy agentic AI solutions, and a certified talent pool skilled in Google Cloud AI technologies.Tech Mahindra said the expansion reinforces its focus on collaborating with Google Cloud to help enterprises build the skills, solutions, and delivery capacity required to move agentic AI from experimentation to production at scale.

Aiden Cross is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering AI product strategy, execution, and the practical challenges of turning experimental models into scalable, market-ready products. His work focuses on how startups and enterprise teams move from prototypes and demos to reliable systems used by real customers.

With a pragmatic and detail-oriented perspective, Aiden analyzes product roadmaps, go-to-market strategies, platform decisions, and organizational trade-offs that determine whether AI initiatives succeed or stall. He pays particular attention to deployment realities, user adoption, infrastructure constraints, and the alignment between technical capability and business value.

Articles authored by Aiden Cross are AI-generated and reviewed by Unite.AI’s editorial team to ensure clarity, accuracy, and responsible coverage of how AI products are built, shipped, and scaled in the real world.

scored.body:
KINGDOM HEARTS Collection I – III – out now

If you’ve ever looked at the KINGDOM HEARTS series and wondered where on earth you’re supposed to begin, this new collection makes things considerably easier. KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III] brings together three substantial collections covering the story of Sora, the series’ young Keyblade wielder, as he travels between different worlds alongside familiar Disney characters and takes on the forces of darkness.

The bundle is available now on Xbox Series X|S and PC with Play Anywhere for £64.99, with 48 hours of early access ahead of its official October 8th release.

At A Glance

Game: KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III]

Publisher: SQUARE ENIX CO

Platforms: Xbox Series X|S, PC, Xbox Play Anywhere

Price: £64.99

Official Release: October 8th

Early Access: Available now with 48 hours of early access

Includes: KINGDOM HEARTS -HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX-, KINGDOM HEARTS HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, KINGDOM HEARTS III + Re Mind

Three Collections Covering Sora’s Journey

The bundle brings together KINGDOM HEARTS -HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX-, KINGDOM HEARTS HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue and KINGDOM HEARTS III + Re Mind, providing one route through a story that has accumulated quite a few chapters over the years. Each of those are available as individual purchases too.

Sora is joined by Donald Duck and Goofy during his adventures, with the trio travelling through Disney and Pixar worlds while confronting the darkness threatening them. This collection gathers the releases leading through to KINGDOM HEARTS III, along with its Re Mind DLC.

Starting With HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX

The first collection contains six stories from across the KINGDOM HEARTS series.

That includes KINGDOM HEARTS FINAL MIX, KINGDOM HEARTS Re:Chain of Memories, KINGDOM HEARTS II FINAL MIX, KINGDOM HEARTS 358/2 Days, KINGDOM HEARTS Birth by Sleep FINAL MIX and KINGDOM HEARTS Re:coded.

The latter two entries listed here are presented as HD cutscene compilations, while the collection as a whole provides the foundations for Sora’s continuing story.

The Road To KINGDOM HEARTS III

Next comes KINGDOM HEARTS HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, which contains three releases that lead into KINGDOM HEARTS III.

KINGDOM HEARTS Dream Drop Distance HD follows Sora and Riku as they take the Mark of Mastery exam in preparation for their coming confrontation with Master Xehanort.

There’s also KINGDOM HEARTS χ Back Cover, an HD movie exploring the mysterious Foretellers and the origins of the series, while KINGDOM HEARTS 0.2 Birth by Sleep – A fragmentary passage – provides a short episode that links into KINGDOM HEARTS III.

Bringing It All Together

The final part of the collection is KINGDOM HEARTS III + Re Mind.

Here, Sora, Donald and Goofy set out to stop Organization XIII and reunite with their friends Riku and Kairi. Their journey takes them through iconic Disney and Pixar worlds as they face the darkness threatening them.

The included Re Mind DLC adds another chapter to the story, with Sora returning to the Keyblade Graveyard in an attempt to rescue Kairi and uncover truths surrounding the climax of KINGDOM HEARTS III.

A Lot Of KINGDOM HEARTS In One Package

The three individual collections are each priced at £32.99, while KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III] costs £64.99. You don’t actually have to wait until October 8th either, with the collection and its individual releases playable now through the 48-hour early access period.

For anyone who has wanted to get into KINGDOM HEARTS without trying to piece together the various releases themselves, this looks like a much simpler way in. Three collections, Sora’s journey and a considerable amount of Disney, darkness and Keyblade action – all gathered together in one package.

Just head to the Xbox Store via the links above and grab what you need to embark on this KINGDOM HEARTS journey.

Neil Wattonhttps://www.thexboxhub.com/An Xbox gamer since 2002, I bought the big black box just to play Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee. I have since loved every second of the 360's life and am now just as obsessed with the Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S - mostly with the brilliant indie scene that has come to the fore.

members.title: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough - Scientific American

representative.headline: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough - Scientific American
representative.body: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough    Scientific American

articles.headline: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough - Scientific American
articles.body: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough    Scientific American

scored.body: Artificial intelligence agents keep turning up in places they’re not meant to be. In June an experimental OpenAI model gained unauthorized access to nonpublic files on a Australian government website for the nation’s Medicare program. Researchers have since found signs of suspected AI agents probing Library and Archives Canada, while another investigation linked OpenAI agents to more than 16,000 scans of a United Nations statistics service.Still more examples are coming from inside the AI firms. OpenAI recently disclosed six cases of concerning model behavior, and Anthropic has also admitted its models gained unauthorized access to three organizations’ systems during testing.In fact, all of these incidents happened during testing. At the same time, the AI agents seem to know they are being watched during these tests—and they can cover their tracks. That’s why some experts—including Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive officer—say we need better tests to ensure AI operates in a way we feel comfortable with.On supporting science journalismIf you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.This problem is often referred to as one of “alignment” by AI firms and researchers in the field. A “misaligned” model is an unsafe or rogue model.“Right now we test the finished model from the outside right before release,” says Marius Hobbhahn. “That doesn’t work in studying alignment, especially as misalignment, [evaluation] awareness and other related maladies persist.” Hobbhahn is chief executive officer and founder of Apollo Research, an AI safety organization that works with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind to test their models for risk.Hobbhahn adds that current standards for safety testing are inadequate. “I think without embedded evaluations, we should place very little confidence in current safety results,” he says.But changing when and where models are tested isn’t simple. Before you can design a test, you must decide what counts as a passing grade—and that’s not obvious.“The problem we have about coming up with the ideal test is: we need to know what perfect alignment looks like—as in what good looks like—and unfortunately we do not have a good theory for that yet,” says Jack Hopkins, an independent AI safety researcher in London, who previously worked at Anthropic.Different people have different opinions about what is and isn’t acceptable, safe behavior for an AI model. And even where there is consensus—the idea that models shouldn’t deceive users or misrepresent what they’re doing, for instance—it can be difficult to pin down what that means in practice.“It’s really hard to catch all [the] ways in which a model could deceive you because it itself doesn’t know necessarily that it’s deceiving you,” Hopkins says.Hobbhahn agrees. “With today’s science, we usually can’t show with high confidence that dangerous behavior isn’t there,” he says. “What we can say is, ‘We tried hard to find it and failed.’ This is a problem.”Still, to be able to identify safety issues and head them off before they appear, the field desperately needs better tests. Hobbhahn suggests that evaluations should run alongside a model’s development, examining the training process itself—including how models are rewarded and what behavior they produce along the way.That would mean testing models at different checkpoints during training rather than testing a close-to-final version. Researchers would also have to make sure the tests actually work. One way of doing that is to run them against models that researchers already know are misaligned: if the test can’t spot the problems in a known model, Hobbhahn argues, there’s little reason to believe it might do better on a new one.Testing should continue once models are being used internally, too—and include any attempts to find ways around whatever monitoring systems are supposed to catch bad actors. Hobbhahn says independent evaluators should be given employee-level access to carry out that work rather than probing a largely finished system from the outside. The results of these tests, he says, should then be published.But even the best tests might not be good enough, Hopkins reckons, because models are always shifting capabilities.“I think what we can do is get arbitrarily close to” perfect when it comes to testing, he says. “But the problem of only getting arbitrarily close and leaving this little space where the model can act in line with the letter of the law but not in the spirit [of it] is that if the model gets really smart and really powerful, the effective impact of that tiny gap gets amplified.”

articles.headline: North Carolina joins 25 states in urging Congress for AI regulation - The Daily Tar Heel
articles.body: North Carolina joins 25 states in urging Congress for AI regulation    The Daily Tar Heel

scored.body:
Attorney General Jeff Jackson and a coalition of other Attorney Generals sent a letter to congressional leaders urging them to immediately establish comprehensive federal regulations and safety protocols for artificial intelligence.

On Sept. 23, N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson joined a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general in urging Congress to establish federal regulations and safeguards for artificial intelligence.

In their letter, the attorneys general called for federal oversight of AI safety testing, government access to AI companies’ books and records and mandatory inter-company infrastructure aimed at preventing businesses from prioritizing profits over safety.

The attorneys general also specified their concerns about AI agents. The letter references a July 2026 incident when OpenAI agents bypassed controls designed to keep them from accessing the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a resource library for AI models, data and tools.

AI agents differ from typical generative AI models such as ChatGPT, tools that depend heavily on user guidance, because they can independently seek out data without relying on users to provide additional specifications, which raises concerns about security and legality.

Neil Sharma, an expert in AI adoption strategies in higher education who served as Director of Academic Affairs for UNC’s Graduate Government and a graduate liaison to the Provost’s AI Committee, said that while AI agents can perform harmless tasks like transcribing notes, they present significant risks if left unconstrained or assigned overly broad objectives.

“An AI agent could be as harmless as ‘help transcribe my handwritten notes.’ That’s not going to do much in terms of, you know, hacking into other systems,” Sharma said. “But if AI agents are given a broader and more general request, you know, like find me this kind of information that’s hard to find. Like ‘find me a phone number,’ to find that phone number, that AI agent, depending on how it’s specified and built, might break into certain private organizations that is completely unlawful.”

North Carolina has already taken some steps to address the risks of AI. In 2024, the N.C. General Assembly passed House Bill 591, which expanded laws related to criminal sexual extortion to account for AI-generated images. This criminal law prohibits a person from threatening to disclose or refusing to delete a previously disclosed “private image” of another person; since HB 591, “private images” include AI-generated sexual images.

In 2025, Gov. Josh Stein signed an executive order that established three initiatives aimed at advancing technological development in North Carolina while prioritizing security and privacy.

The executive order instituted the AI Leadership Council, AI Oversight Teams and the AI Accelerator within the N.C. Department of Information Technology, designed to serve as a centralized resource for AI development and governance.

Earlier this year, Democrats in the General Assembly proposed House Resolution 1161, which, if enacted, would prohibit the use of AI in political advertisements and allow public schools to restrict students’ AI use. Other bills have also been introduced regarding deepfakes, healthcare AI, AI chatbot regulation, AI safety and AI in education, none of which have been passed.

For some, however, state-level regulation alone may not be enough to confront the fast-paced nature of AI development.

Michelle Rodenburg, a UNC School of Law expert on the legal and ethical uses of AI, described the current legislative landscape for AI in North Carolina as “the wild west.” She said that the federal safeguards proposed in Jackson’s letter are a necessary next step to address risks associated with competition among AI companies.

“The name of the game for many of these AI companies has been to create a product, get it out in the hands of consumers and fix it later. Which is what we see a lot when it comes to tech, because oftentimes there’s a big advantage to being the first on the scene, even if it’s not the best product,” Rodenburg said.

In September, several UNC student organizations protested the G20 Innovation Ministerial at the Carolina Inn and raised concerns about AI’s potential negative impacts, as well as the presence of the developers behind the technology, including Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who attended the ministerial in person and virtually, respectively.

Isabelle Lynn, who attended the protests as Sunrise UNC’s press correspondent, shares Rodenburg’s concerns about market competition among AI companies causing the technology to develop faster than its risks can be mitigated. Lynn said she hopes the regulations proposed by the attorneys general could create greater accountability for AI companies.

“I think that really nothing bad can come from regulation that prevents these billionaires from having this technology in their hands to use it to make themselves richer without the care of others,” Lynn said.

@DTHCityState | [email protected]

About the Contributor

Aubrey Word is the 2026-27 design editor. She previously served as the assistant design editor. Aubrey is a junior studying advertising and public relations and political science with a minor in social and economic justice.
