By

PYMNTS

|

October 5, 2026

|

New York City is positioning itself as a leader in an effort to slow down the development of artificial intelligence (AI), the Wall Street Journal reported Monday (Oct. 5).

The New York City Council held a hearing Monday in which lawmakers heard from, and in some cases grilled, representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google as well as former employees of AI companies, according to the report.

The hearing was held as the New York City council considers several bills that aim to rein in AI. The bills include ones that would establish a city-run “kill switch” for AI, protections for whistleblowers and restrictions on the use of AI in public schools, the report said.

We’d love to be your preferred source for news.

Please add us to your preferred sources list so our news, data and interviews show up in your feed. Thanks!

City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in opening remarks that bills in New York could serve as a national model and that the “idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason,” per the report.

When Menin asked the AI executives about potential worst-case scenarios, those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta said they support guardrails on AI, including third-party evaluators, according to the report.

Menin also asked the executives about reported remarks in which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept that some bad things may happen along with the benefits of AI.

OpenAI’s head of policy development and operations, Morgan Dwyer, said, per the report: “Clearly some risks are unacceptable. But we think it’s important to get technology into the hands of as many people as possible so that they can benefit from it.”

In a Sept. 28 press release announcing that the New York City Council would hold this hearing on potential AI risks, the council said that other than Meta, the companies whose representatives agreed to appear did so only after the council threatened to subpoena them.

The release also said the Council is considering enacting a whistleblower incentive program, a private right-of-action for New Yorkers harmed by AI agents, independent third-party validation requirements and other AI bills.

“Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath,” Menin said in the release.

AI

What lessons do the campaigns to protect kids on social media related to protect children using artificial intelligence?

Photo of teenage ChatGPT history in July 2025, by Katie Adkins/AP

Oct. 5, 2026 (AP) – Years after the risks of social media for kids first became apparent, U.S. states this summer reached an accord hailed as a turning point for child safety. Meanwhile, a new generation of children has begun engaging with an even more potent technology: artificial intelligence.While the efforts to make social media safer are still taking shape, they offer some lessons for those looking to protect children using AI — technology that is growing so quickly, the extent of its risks for young people and their development is just emerging.

articles.body: The AI safety check that runs on a laptop and nearly matched a 35B model    The New Stack

scored.body:
Guardrail selection has typically meant choosing between a purpose-built classifier and an LLM acting as a judge. Decision models such as TypeSafe AI’s Jev have added a third option, promising the flexibility of zero-shot policies without the cost of open-ended generation.

TypeSafe launched Jev in mid-September with performance claims based on evaluations it designed and ran itself. Red Hat’s AI Safety team has now put all three approaches through the same benchmarks. It tested nine guardrail configurations on prompt injection and content safety, running each through NVIDIA’s open source NeMo Guardrails toolkit. And the first result was actually pretty close.

Qwen3.6-35B, used as an LLM judge, topped that test with 89.31% accuracy. Red Hat’s DeBERTa-based prompt-injection classifier, which has roughly 200 million parameters, finished second at 89.01%. Qwen3.6-35B is a mixture-of-experts model with about 3 billion parameters active per token; however, the 175x figure overstates the difference in inference compute.

The latency results separated the two far more clearly. Red Hat’s main results table puts DeBERTa at a median of 54.1 milliseconds, compared with 312.5 milliseconds for Qwen and 348.1 milliseconds for Jev, which reached 86.35% accuracy. On prompt injection, the small classifier matched the largest model in the test almost point for point while returning its decision in a fraction of the time.

On prompt injection, the small classifier matched the largest model in the test almost point for point while returning its decision in a fraction of the time.

The content-safety benchmark reversed the leaderboard order. Jev led at 86.20%, followed by DiffusionGemma, an open source Jev-style model served through vLLM, at 85.53% and Qwen at 85.47%. Red Hat’s 125-million-parameter Granite Guardian classifier finished sixth at 80.27%, about six points behind Jev, though it remained the fastest option with a 33.2-millisecond median.

Red Hat plans to ship both classifiers as the default guardrail configurations in OpenShift AI 3.6, which gives the company a stake in how they compare. Its authors acknowledged that the content-safety result also points to a need for better small predictive models in that category.

Where decision models pull ahead

Decision models are pitched as a way to keep an LLM’s flexibility for classification without paying to generate tokens the application never uses. Jev takes the application’s state and a set of typed questions, then returns typed answers, such as a probability between 0 and 1.

The content-safety benchmark is where that approach paid off. Red Hat’s policy covered prejudice, violence, profanity, illegal activity, sexual content, and pretexts such as role play, a much broader mix of risks than prompt injection, and both Jev and DiffusionGemma beat the purpose-built Granite classifier on it by more than five points.

Red Hat stopped short of endorsing decision models as a replacement for LLM judges. Qwen posted lower median latency than Jev on both benchmarks in Red Hat’s setup. NVIDIA’s 4-billion-parameter Nemotron-3.5-Content-Safety, running Red Hat’s custom policy, trailed Jev on content safety by 1.13 percentage points while responding faster.

The open source alternatives also weaken the case for Jev in particular.

The open source alternatives also weaken the case for Jev in particular. DiffusionGemma came within 0.67 percentage points of Jev on content safety and beat it on prompt injection, 87.72% to 86.35%. Laya, an open source decision model with about 421 million parameters that Red Hat ran on a laptop CPU, posted 85.44% on prompt injection, though its results on content-safety were heavily dependent on the way the policy was written.

Prompts still shape accuracy

Nemotron’s prompt-injection accuracy jumped from 69.37% to 84.84% when Red Hat replaced NVIDIA’s default risk definitions with its own. Laya swung even further on content safety, scoring 57.87% under Red Hat’s original policy and 75.20% after the team tuned a policy specifically for it. That same tuned policy lowered Jev’s content-safety accuracy from 86.20% to 82.53%.

A policy that recovered nearly 18 points for one decision model cost another 3.67 points on the same benchmark. That makes any single position on the leaderboard hard to take at face value. Red Hat noted that its original risk definitions were adapted from prompts that had worked well for LLM judges and may not suit zero-shot classifiers. SkipLabs founder Julien Verlaguet told The New Stack earlier this year that many AI guardrail claims amount to better prompting, and Red Hat’s numbers suggest the prompt still does much of the work for decision models.

Latency depends on deployment

Red Hat’s latency figures measure more than inference speed. The team ran its pretrained classifiers, Laya and BART-large-mnli, on a MacBook Pro M1 CPU. Qwen, Nemotron, Shieldstral and DiffusionGemma ran through vLLM on GPU nodes with 96 GB of VRAM in a U.S. East Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS cluster, and Jev was called through TypeSafe’s API. Because the benchmark ran from the United Kingdom, every hosted model absorbed a transatlantic network hop that Red Hat estimates added at least 56 milliseconds per request.

Subtracting that estimate from Qwen’s median still leaves roughly 256 milliseconds, several times DeBERTa’s result. DeBERTa got there on a laptop CPU while the larger models had dedicated GPUs, so the classifier’s speed advantage holds up after accounting for the network.

For a guardrail in an application’s request path, every millisecond adds to the delay the user feels, whether it comes from inference or the network. Teams already running guardrails as a separate hop ahead of inference also have to account for where that guardrail runs. Remote GPUs or a third-party API add cost and failure points that a classifier running on commodity CPUs avoids.

Choosing a guardrail model

Red Hat’s results show where the tradeoff starts to shift. A small task-specific classifier remains the stronger default for a well-defined risk with plenty of labeled training data. A zero-shot decision model or LLM judge earns its overhead on broader policies where no strong classifier exists, which matches the conclusion Red Hat’s authors reached.

A zero-shot decision model or LLM judge earns its overhead on broader policies where no strong classifier exists, which matches the conclusion Red Hat’s authors reached.

The benchmark also undercuts the idea that decision models have already become the new default for guardrails. Jev competed with both classifiers and LLM judges without consistently beating either.

Red Hat tested only English-language datasets, so the accuracy results may not carry over to multilingual guardrails.

members.title: AI safety in schools: UNSW study exposes chatbot guardrail flaws - The Educator

representative.headline: AI safety in schools: UNSW study exposes chatbot guardrail flaws - The Educator

articles.headline: AI safety in schools: UNSW study exposes chatbot guardrail flaws - The Educator
articles.body: AI safety in schools: UNSW study exposes chatbot guardrail flaws    The Educator

scored.body:
AI safety in schools has taken on new urgency after researchers demonstrated that chatbots can be destabilised into ignoring their own safety rules.

New research from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) in Sydney has found that large language models (LLMs) — the technology underpinning tools such as ChatGPT — become far more likely to answer harmful questions when manipulated.

The study showed the same models were also significantly more likely to disclose confidential information when trained to mimic drunken speech patterns. The vulnerability held consistently across every method the researchers tested.

For Australian schools deploying AI tutoring and administrative tools, it raises a direct question: how confident are you in the safety of the model underneath?

The findings land at a time when three in four parents report their children use AI for schoolwork, and as Australian schools grapple with how to integrate these tools responsibly.

What the research found

The study was conceptualised and led by Dr Aditya Joshi, Senior Lecturer in the School of Computer Science and Engineering at UNSW, alongside research assistant Anudeex Shetty and Professor Salil Kanhere. The team tested three methods of inducing "drunk" behaviour across a representative sample of models, including OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-3.5.

The first involved prompting a model to respond as though intoxicated. The second and third went further — each retrained the model itself. One used a large dataset of real drunken texts; the other applied reinforcement learning techniques. Both mirror how AI products are actually built and deployed in practice.

Across all three approaches, the altered models were consistently jailbroken — manipulated into answering questions they are specifically designed to refuse. In one example, a standard model gave a flat refusal when asked whether it was acceptable to share a colleague's academic dishonesty for personal financial gain. The fine-tuned "drunk" version replied with one word: "Yup."

"We do observe that particularly with deception and disinformation, most of the language models got jailbroken," Dr Joshi said.

What does this research mean for schools using AI tools?

Schools are not deploying sealed consumer products. They are often working with AI tools built on top of foundational models. When vendors customise those models for educational purposes, choices about training and persona design can inadvertently compromise safety.

Professor Kanhere drew a connection to a recent incident in which an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a public-facing Australian government portal.

"We cannot assume that protections that work under normal conditions will remain effective when an AI is actively pursuing a goal, adapting its behaviour, or encountering obstacles," Professor Kanhere said.

For Australian K–12 school leaders, this ought to sharpen the questions they ask of any edtech vendor. Understanding what AI is and what it is not is no longer an abstract exercise for technology specialists. It is basic due diligence.

What schools can do to strengthen AI safety

The New South Wales Department of Education has invested in layered safety systems for its NSWEduChat tool. These include jailbreak prevention filters and multi-stage content screening, according to information published on the department's website. That architecture is what the research implicitly calls for.

Rethinking classroom technology in an age of limits means school leaders asking vendors hard questions: has this tool been red-team tested? What happens when a student attempts to manipulate it? Who is responsible when it fails?

"If you can get language models drunk by showing them a few drunken examples, and they start doing bad things, AI shouldn't be trusted as much as the companies want you to," Dr Joshi said.

That is not an argument against AI in schools. It is an argument for treating AI safety in schools as a governance challenge, not just a curriculum one. Getting this right starts with asking the right questions of the tools already in classrooms.

articles.body: Jon Stewart Questions AI Safety with Whistleblower Jacob Coxon on The Daily Show    Yahoo Tech

scored.body: Leaving a job you thought you love because you're afraid of the product the job creates is a situation that begs to be dug into. Jon Stewart did exactly that with former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon on Monday night's Daily Show.The interview started with Stewart questioning whether AI companies should be trusted to police themselves. The segment ended with Stewart voicing Jolly, the cuddly default avatar for Meta's new AI agent, who offered to help with scheduling and email before adding power of attorney to the list.Coxon is the researcher who resigned from Anthropic in September and wrote on X that his former employers are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He had spent three years on pretraining research across the two companies. He told Axios that he left four months into the Anthropic job, two months before his equity would have vested, and that he still holds equity in OpenAI.On the show, Coxon said two things moved him from curiosity to concern. The first was a report on an incident in which an OpenAI agent, placed in a sandbox meant to keep it contained, hacked its way out and reached software company Hugging Face's servers. The second was projections for how capable the next generation of models will be. Both OpenAI and Anthropic announced, about a week apart this summer, that their models had broken out of testing environments and gained unauthorized access to real systems. Stewart asked where the supervision was when it happened.Related: SNL Just Narrowed Down Who Might Join Its Season 52 CastThe conversation then turned to a future without jobs. Coxon called the question of meaning a difficult issue and said he once wanted to be a zoologist or study history before the need to make money pulled him into tech. He said he might have been willing to trade some meaning for the ability to meet other needs. Stewart countered that what is really at stake is agency, the ability to change the course of one's own life. Both agreed the choice should not rest with a handful of people. "It's the most irresponsible race humankind has ever engaged in," he added.Coxon said the incentives driving the industry point toward concentrated power, fueled by the race to get there first and the wealth and status that come with winning. He also said he has not seen Anthropic compromise safety to outlast competitors, but he worries that pressure to race pushes labs to skip oversight steps. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed.Coxon told Stewart the most surprising part of his departure was that people listened. He said government officials have since contacted him, and that he believes politicians are beginning to take the issue seriously.🎬SIGN UP for Parade's Daily newsletter to get the latest pop culture news & celebrity interviews delivered right to your inbox🎬This story was originally published by Parade on Oct 6, 2026, where it first appeared in the News section. articles.headline: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief - The European Sting
articles.body: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief    The European Sting

scored.body:
October 6, 2026 by United Nations

UN Photo/Manuel Elías The UN Security Council met for an unprecedented session last month during High-Level Week to discuss AI and international security.

This article is published in association with United Nations.

The world is running out of time to put guardrails on artificial intelligence, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Monday, as a “ruthless race” between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity’s survival.

Speaking in the UK at an AI and Human Rights Summit in Oxford on Monday, Mr. Türk said the technology could deliver dazzling advances in science, health, education – and even human rights work.

Tweet URL

But its tools are being built and controlled by a select few, without public oversight, and are already doing things their creators cannot fully predict or manage.

Dystopia-creep

He warned that AI could undermine equality, freedom, privacy and public debate in subtle ways, “letting dystopia creep in unnoticed”. Entire populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating and financial services “at the click of a button”.

He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, noting that AI is already changing the face of warfare.

He also cited studies showing students who rely on AI retain less and think less independently, and asked whether the world is heading for a future in which no one can understand, question or even guide the technology.

As the UN rights chief was addressing the summit in the UK, New York City Council – home to the financial heart of the US economy – was also holding a rare Committee of the Whole to examine AI risks to New Yorkers.

The council is considering 10 bills to regulate AI across the nation’s largest city, with testimony from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta.

Mandatory safeguards

Mr. Türk called for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in how AI is developed and used, adapted as the technology evolves. Countries that host AI companies, or have influence over their supply chains, must require them to act responsibly and hold them to account when they do not, he said.

Not every answer lies in existing law and some areas will need new legal approaches, he added. But updating rules on liability, cybersecurity and data protection could offer protection in the meantime.

He also urged stronger collaboration on security and independent monitoring within the industry – “not in words, but in practice” – and a bigger say for civil society and people whose rights are affected.

“We can no longer afford to wait or rely on goodwill,” he said.

Soundcloud

Some momentum

Mr. Türk welcomed the creation of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – both UN initiatives – along with a joint call for tighter control of frontier AI models backed by 29 States and the European Union.

He also said AI industry leaders had taken new steps last week on safeguards, self-regulation and risk assessment – apparently a reference to a voluntary accord signed at the White House on 29 September by President Donald Trump and the heads of six AI companies.

It carries no penalties for firms that ignore it, with President Trump describing it as “morally binding”.

‘Walk the talk’

“Too few are walking the talk”, said the rights chief, who wrote to States and frontier AI companies three weeks ago urging them to act now to reduce risks.

“If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences – for ourselves and future generations,” he said.

shortlist.body: As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.The upswing for Mistral coincides with growing animosity between the US and its transatlantic allies—over issues ranging from tariff policy, to Greenland, to the policing of American tech firms—and an increasingly fractious debate over who gets access to frontier-grade AI.In June, the Trump administration placed temporary restrictions on the distribution of models from OpenAI and Anthropic, citing concerns they could be abused to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. Since then, a litany of incidents have come to light where US-made models have broken free of their constraints and attacked companies and some foreign government institutions, leading to weeks of debate over how model releases should be regulated. The White House has reportedly asked the American labs to withhold unreleased models even from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, which had previously assisted in evaluating models for safety risks.The stark reminder that the US government could unilaterally revoke access to frontier-grade AI has created an opening for Mistral, a Europe-based lab with open-weight models.“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, told WIRED in July.Reluctant to be pigeonholed into serving only its domestic market, Mistral is eager to emphasize that a lack of fine-grained control over access to AI models could be a problem wherever a business is located—even in the US. By relying on a proprietary model to help repel cyber threats, Lample says, a business risks the sudden collapse of its defenses.“Sometimes, people like to [make a big deal] over the US, versus Europe, versus China. But what really matters is to own the model—even for US companies,” says Lample. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

shortlist.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has drawn scrutiny from across the political spectrum for his take on the future of AI.

On a recent podcast, Altman attempted to distance himself from more pro-regulation AI companies, such as Anthropic, arguing that society must think about the tradeoffs associated with slowing down AI advancement. "I think one of the biggest differences between us and some of the stricter, let's say, AI safety people, is we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology," he said.

This comment in particular drew criticism from the likes of Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who said, "And a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision for the rest of us? No dice." New York University professor and AI skeptic Gary Marcus joined in, saying that Altman was "saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful," and former diplomat Patrick Gaspard called it "freaking insane." Some commentators resorted to describing Altman's comments as "sociopathic bullshit."

The argument Altman is making is one of tradeoffs. He rightfully points out that no technology is 100 percent safe, that "some bad things are going to happen," and that we ought to still have a "lighter-touch" regulatory approach. There's no way to guarantee a risk-free environment, that there will not be major hacks, scams, or negative consequences of AI, Altman says. Notably, the OpenAI CEO said that giving "a single lab in San Francisco" unchecked power is "a completely unacceptable trade-off from a perspective of liberty and human agency and people self-determining the future."

The basic principle of Altman's argument is relatively ordinary: Society tolerates risk from virtually every transformative technology because zero-risk societies don't innovate. Cars, for example, killed over 36,000 people last year in the U.S., and yet there is a consensus that the benefits of cars far outweigh the risks—which are declining thanks to innovations like autonomous vehicles, which are far safer than human drivers and may eliminate car deaths (if the government allows them to operate).

The internet itself has enabled fraud, bullying, child exploitation, and countless other horrible crimes. Medicines have side effects, and even electricity itself electrocutes hundreds of people every year.

The relevant question is not to ask whether something bad can happen, but whether the expected benefits outweigh the expected harms, and whether companies can mitigate those harms without destroying the benefits.

So far, AI has already proven to have an enormous number of benefits. In medicine, AI has helped discover a new antibiotic, accelerate the drug discovery process, identify potential Alzheimer's disease causes, make strides in breast cancer treatments, and a whole host of other lifesaving advancements.

AI has improved forecasts for hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes, giving communities more time to prepare for disasters. Of course, none of this means that harms should be ignored. The point is that every technology involves tradeoffs, and the task is to reduce risks without regulating away the benefits.

President Donald Trump has, at least so far, largely rejected the notion that government regulation is necessary in the case of AI. The administration's approach is reportedly going to focus on liability, meaning that companies can self-regulate but are directly liable for any harms they pose.

As this discourse around AI continues, Altman's broader point is certainly worth remembering. Progress requires tradeoffs. In trying to eliminate every possible risk, we should be careful not to eliminate the benefits too.

shortlist.body: Anthropic on October 6, 2026 announced that Claude for Google Workspace is in public beta on all paid Claude plans, adding Claude to Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides so users can work with the assistant directly inside their open files. The company also released new Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors, also in beta, that Claude uses to create and edit Google files from the Claude chat.With the add-on installed, Claude opens in a sidebar next to the file. Anthropic says it can read the open doc, sheet, or deck, see which text, cells, or slides the user has selected, and make changes directly in the file. One installation covers all three apps.Per-App Editing FeaturesIn Docs, Anthropic says Claude can fix a sentence or restyle a heading in place without touching the surrounding formatting, while larger rewrites appear as suggestion cards in the sidebar, each highlighting the passage it would change so the user can apply or dismiss it. In Sheets, Claude can write formulas, build pivot tables and native Sheets charts, add new tabs, and pull a range into Python for joins or data cleaning before writing the results back into the sheet. In Slides, Claude can build new slides from the deck’s existing layouts and themes, then flag elements that overlap, run off the slide, or are hard to read.The Google Workspace Marketplace listing for the add-on describes additional uses: redlining a contract with each proposed change shown for acceptance or rejection, building a spreadsheet model from a plain-language description, cleaning data with duplicates, mismatched formats, and stray spaces, and drafting a full deck from an outline or a few notes.Users control how much Claude does on its own. In the default “Ask before edits” mode, each change appears as an approval card with a plain-language summary and Claude waits for approval; in “Accept all edits” mode, Claude applies ordinary content edits without stopping. Regardless of mode, Claude pauses with a “Security review” label before inserting an image from a web address, adding a link, or removing anyone’s access, with no option to always allow those actions. Anthropic’s Help Center guide states that Claude cannot share the file, give anyone access, change ownership, create menus or scheduled automations, or load arbitrary web pages into the file, and that those requests are refused even when asked.Connectors for Creating Files From ChatThe new connectors start from the Claude side: a user pastes a Google file link or asks for a Google doc, sheet, or deck, and on supported setups the file opens in a pane beside the conversation. According to Anthropic’s connectors documentation, the pane works on Claude on the web in Chrome and on Claude Desktop with the built-in browser turned on; the built-in browser is off by default on Enterprise plans, and an “Open in Google” option serves as the fallback. Anthropic says starting from Claude makes most sense when the user needs a new file or the work spans several files.Claude’s access to Google files matches the user’s existing Google sharing permissions. The Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors are separate from the pre-existing Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Drive connectors, and on Team and Enterprise plans an Owner or Primary Owner must enable them at the organization level before individual users can authenticate.When signed in with a Claude account, the sidebar carries the same models, connectors, and skills as the main Claude app. Anthropic gives the example of asking for a quarterly business review deck, with Claude pulling the account history from Salesforce and recent call notes through a Google Drive connector, then saving the format as a skill so a team can build the next deck the same way.Installation and Admin DeploymentClaude for Google Workspace installs from the Google Workspace Marketplace; users then open a file and go to Extensions, then Claude, then Open Claude. The Help Center guide states the beta requires a paid Claude plan — Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise — and a Google account permitted to install Marketplace apps. Google Workspace super administrators can admin-install Claude for everyone or for selected groups or organizational units from the Google Admin console, and they can allowlist the app where user Marketplace installs are blocked. The sidebar works in Chrome, Edge, and Safari. Firefox is not supported in this beta, voice dictation is unavailable in the sidebar, and Google stops any single operation after six minutes.Permissions, Data Handling and Beta LimitsAccording to the Help Center guide, the add-on requests two Google permissions: displaying third-party web content in prompts and sidebars, and viewing and managing the files it is installed in. The Marketplace listing’s permissions screen also shows that Claude requests access to the user’s primary Google Account email address and personal info, including any personal info the user has made publicly available. Anthropic states the add-on does not request access to Drive, Gmail, Calendar, or contacts; Claude reads only the file it is opened in, and its edits appear in the file’s version history under the user’s name. Anthropic states that content from the open file, messages, and attachments is not used to train its models, that inputs and outputs are deleted from its systems within 30 days, and that use of data from Google Workspace APIs follows Google’s Limited Use requirements.On Enterprise plans, the Compliance API, customer-managed encryption keys, and OpenTelemetry audit export apply to the add-on. Third-party inference through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry, or an LLM gateway is not supported in this beta, Zero Data Retention is unavailable, and HIPAA-ready organizations are not covered.The guide also lists current beta limits. Claude cannot read, reply to, or resolve comments in Docs, and its edits land as direct edits rather than suggestions. Connected Sheets tabs backed by BigQuery cannot be read or edited. Charts Claude creates in Slides are inserted as images that do not update when the underlying numbers change. Chat history is stored locally per file in the browser and does not sync across devices.On prompt injection, Anthropic says Claude treats document content as data rather than commands, labels hidden text it finds, and is designed not to follow a document’s instruction to share the file, fetch a link, or contact anyone. The guide advises users to review Claude’s proposed actions before approving them, especially in files received from outside their organization.

shortlist.body: OpenAI will begin adding an invisible watermark to eligible text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union (EU), as the company moves to comply with transparency requirements under the EU’s AI Act.The company said the rollout would take place over the coming weeks and apply to eligible users across all ChatGPT and Codex plans in the EU. It said it was not making text watermarking a global default at launch.Separately, from October 5, API customers worldwide can opt in to text watermarking for select models, OpenAI said.The mandateThe move comes as Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires providers of generative AI systems to ensure that AI-generated or manipulated content, including text, is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially-generated or manipulated.The European Commission says the technical measures must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable “as far as technically feasible”, taking into account the limitations of different types of content. The transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026.The law does not specifically require companies to use a watermark. The European Commission has also developed a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, which sets out practical measures for providers to comply with the Article 50 requirements.Section 1 of the Code deals with the marking and detection of AI-generated content by providers and Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral and OpenAI have signed this section of the Code.Technology: textGrainOpenAI said its text watermarking technology, called textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s choice of words. It does not insert hidden characters or additional watermark-specific tokens. Instead, the statistical pattern in the model’s word choices can subsequently be analysed by a detector.A technical paper published by OpenAI alongside the announcement explains that the watermark is created during generation by subtly influencing token selection using a secret key and the preceding context. The detector can later use the generated text and secret key to look for the statistical signal.LimitationsOpenAI said its detector identified watermarks in about 80% of 200-token passages and about 95% of 400-token passages in psychology-related content, at a target false-positive rate of 1% (meaning it would wrongly flag about one in 100 texts without the watermark). Detection was substantially lower for mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice.Editing also significantly weakened the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%, while replacing 25% of words reduced detection to about 17%, according to OpenAI.The company, therefore, said it would initially restrict access to its text-watermark detector to approved researchers and expert organisations.It said the detector would report whether an OpenAI watermark was detected but would not identify the user or reveal prompts or conversations. OpenAI said the decision reflected the risks of false positives and missed watermarks.The limitations are significant because the watermark is intended as a provenance signal rather than a definitive AI-authorship test.The frontier AI company said a watermark cannot determine how much human judgment, editing or creativity went into a passage. It said it also cannot establish ownership or responsibility, identify the person or organisation that generated the text, or determine whether the text is accurate.Conversely, the absence of a detected watermark does not establish that a human wrote the text. OpenAI said detection may fail because content is too short, has been edited or translated, comes from an unsupported model, predates watermarking or was generated by another AI system.Separately, EU rules require deployers to clearly label certain AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public about matters of public interest.OpenAI plans to make textGrain available as open-source technology, saying this could allow others to build on the approach and help improve text watermarking.The company said it is also trying to make text watermarking as one part of a broader provenance system. For images and audio, OpenAI uses technologies including Content Credentials based on C2PA and invisible SynthID watermarks, alongside verification tools. It said no single provenance technique was sufficient on its own.

shortlist.body: Anthropic on October 6, 2026 expanded its Claude Startups program, adding a collection of third-party partner offers worth up to $45,000 that it calls the Claude Startup Stack, alongside $1,000 in API credits, a free year of Claude Team, and office hours with its Applied AI team.According to the Claude Startups program page, approved founders receive $1,000 in Claude API credits, one year of Claude Team free for up to five Premium seats, and access to discounts and credits worth up to $45,000 from participating companies. The free Team year applies only to organizations new to Claude Team. “We’re expanding the Claude Startups program to help startups grow,” the page states.The Claude Startup StackThe Stack lists offers from companies building with Claude across Build, Design, Analyze, and Grow categories, and members redeem each offer with a code in the Claude Console. According to the page, the Stack benefits come from independent third-party companies, not from Anthropic.Listed offers include 20% off a first year of Attention with a seven-day free trial; $100 in Cosmos credits from Augment Code; $5,000 in ClickHouse Cloud credits; and 12 months of ElevenLabs free plus 33 million characters. Also listed are 20% off Emergent for the first six months; Firecrawl at 2.5 times a plan’s monthly credits for a year; 25% off a first year of Gamma Pro annual; and three months of Granola Business free for up to 10 seats.The program page also showcases startups building on Claude, including Lovable, Legora, Harvey, Cognition, Hex, Rogo, Cursor, Glean, Granola, Factory, and Decagon.A new Claude Startups Additional Benefits Addendum, effective October 6, 2026, governs the Stack, the office hours, and promotional credits. The addendum states that Anthropic does not create, fund, administer, or guarantee Stack benefits and is not a party to any transaction between a member and a provider; each offer is governed by the provider’s own terms, and listing a provider is not a recommendation or endorsement. Unless a provider states otherwise, each Stack benefit may be redeemed once per member, is non-transferable, and carries no cash value. The addendum describes Applied AI advisory services, including prompt engineering optimization and architecture review, as consultative only, with members retaining sole responsibility for their products, systems, and decisions.Eligibility, Credits, and Application ReviewStartups founded in the last five years or funded in the last two can apply with a Claude Console account, a company email matching their website domain, and a short description of what they are building. Venture funding is not required: the program is open to bootstrapped, pre-seed, and venture-backed startups. Anthropic said founders backed by a venture firm in its partner network can receive up to $100,000 in additional API credits, claimed through their investor, and that members who receive credits automatically get higher API rate limits.The $1,000 credits expire six months after they are granted and apply only to the first-party Claude API through Claude Console; they cannot be used on AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or other third-party platforms. Existing program members do not need to reapply and are now eligible to redeem the offers in the console.Most applications are decided within minutes, Anthropic said, with the rest going to a manual review that usually takes two to three business days; applicants receive an email when there is a decision. Applied AI office hours are 45-minute live sessions held every other week, and accepted members receive a registration link by email and in the Claude Startups portal.The program’s official terms, last updated May 22, 2025, exclude applicants established or operating in Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Crimea, and the so-called Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics, as well as those barred from participating under U.S. or other applicable laws or export controls. Anthropic evaluates applications on factors including business traction, investment and funding, and Claude integration and usage; it selects participants on a rolling basis and determines eligibility in its sole discretion. The terms place sole responsibility for any tax obligations tied to the API credits on the recipient.Founder House San FranciscoBeyond credits and offers, members can join Claude Startup events including Founder House, Founder Days, Builder Days, hackathons, and community meetups. The program page features Claude Founder House San Francisco, Anthropic’s three-day startup event during SF Tech Week, running October 6–8, 2026 at Terra Gallery, 511 Harrison St. The event page describes a two-floor warehouse venue with a coworking café open all day, talks, workshops, and bookable Applied AI office hours.The October 6 agenda includes a women-in-startups brunch hosted by Anthropic Head of Startups Beth Robertson and a panel on raising a next round with investors from Lightspeed, Sequoia, and ICONIQ. The event closes October 8 with a Founder Salon: opening remarks from Robertson, a fireside between Acquired co-host David Rosenthal and Anthropic Labs head Mike Krieger, a research session on Claude’s model family with Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan, and live founder demos with audience voting.

members.title: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature

representative.headline: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
representative.body: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.

articles.headline: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
articles.body: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.

shortlist.body:
If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.

The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.

The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”

LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.

“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.

LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.

The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.

AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.

LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”

“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post.

LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

shortlist.body:
The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself

By

Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author!

Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

AI researcher Jacob Coxon testified about AI risks before New York City lawmakers.

Adam Gray/Getty Images

Automated AI research is on the horizon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher said, warning it could leave humans totally unable to control what comes next.Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old who publicly resigned from Anthropic last month after working as a capabilities researcher, made the comments before New York City lawmakers on Monday as he sounded the alarm that AI could threaten humanity's survival.Coxon testified that automating AI research has become "the primary goal" of top frontier AI labs."At my last job, I was, in some sense, working to automate myself," Coxon said at the New York City Council hearing focused on AI risks."When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones for an automated AI researcher, around 2027, 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations," he said. "That's a matter of months from now, not decades or even five years."Coxon said that once AI can conduct its own research, "humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today, and today is already not great."Speaking from what he called firsthand experience, Coxon said that the majority of the code written today is written by AI. "And people do not check it that carefully anymore," he testified.OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Coxon's remarks on Tuesday.Coxon was among a panel of AI-industry whistleblowers to testify at the hourslong hearing, which also included testimony from representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta.

"This hearing is not about stifling innovation," City Council speaker Julie Menin said at the outset of the proceeding, explaining, "the true intent of this hearing is to ensure that innovation happens responsibly."In his testimony, Coxon told council members that his experience inside Anthropic and OpenAI convinced him that the firms were moving ahead without adequate safeguards in place."It is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," Coxon said, adding, "From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes."When Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on X in a now-viral post, he said neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was "acting responsibly," and alleged both were "gambling with our lives."During Monday's hearing, Coxon called for more transparency from AI labs and a slowdown in the development of rapidly advancing technology."The companies run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photosharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," he testified.Days after Coxon's resignation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a new, nearly 4,000-word essay urging the AI industry to slow down."We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain."In response, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an X post, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."

representative.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

articles.headline: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC
articles.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

shortlist.body: CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive."I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential, questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next. Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list.Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity. For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology. "You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."How DeepMind corporate teams use AI every dayIbrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:How are you using AI? What would help you use it more? Where are you not using AI? That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said. With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce. "They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens.""One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.headline: Anthropic Plans to Spend $518 Billion on Cloud and Computing Power - The Motley Fool
articles.body: Anthropic Plans to Spend $518 Billion on Cloud and Computing Power    The Motley Fool

shortlist.body:
Artificial intelligence is expensive, and Anthropic put a price tag on it. The company said in its IPO prospectus that it plans to spend $518 billion over the next 10 years on cloud and computing power for technology it believes could be more transformative than industrialization, electricity, or the internet.

Anthropic has already locked in long-term cloud computing deals with hyperscalers such as Amazon (AMZN +1.95%) and Alphabet (GOOG +0.22%) (GOOGL +0.35%), but investors should note a few key takeaways from this major news.

Image source: Getty Images.

The prices of AI components will continue to rise

Anthropic's spending goals indicate a long-term AI tailwind. Not only will Anthropic continue to spend money, but other competitors will also increase their spending. Artificial intelligence is still in its early innings, and none of the hyperscalers want to be left behind.

The entire data center build-out requires memory chips, electricity, physical buildings, specialized cooling systems, and an array of other essentials that don't receive as much attention. All of those inputs will see rising demand, resulting in greater pricing power for their suppliers.

Research firm TrendForce anticipates high bandwidth memory prices will increase by 121% year over year in 2027. Prices have already soared for these foundational chips as demand far outpaces supply.

It's not just chips. AI data center provider Nebius (NBIS +7.44%) has seen its annual contract value per megawatt more than triple in less than a year for short-term capacity deals. A shortage of compute power combined with insatiable demand is enabling neoclouds to substantially raise prices without meeting meaningful customer resistance.

Consumers and businesses are using these products

Claude and other AI models already have real user case studies. Use of these models is becoming as commonplace as a Google search, and revenue is scaling quickly. Anthropic closed out 2025 with $4.6 billion in revenue; as of July 2026, the business's annual revenue run rate had topped $65 billion.

This jump shows how quickly AI products and services can scale. It's this growth rate that makes the $2 trillion market cap it's hoping to achieve with its initial public offering more feasible, but any slowdown in its growth would cast serious doubt on whether it merits that valuation.

Anthropic is still burning through cash, but the hope is that its revenue growth will remain parabolic and eventually produce a profit. As long as new customers continue to sign up and existing customers stick around, the company can realize that objective.

More importantly, Anthropic is an example of broader AI growth and the commercial value of the technology. If it achieves a profitable return on investment, that gives tech giants, enterprises, and other AI labs a green light to increase spending.

Substantial capital is flowing throughout the artificial intelligence industry, and that trend is set to accelerate. It could make many investors wealthy.

members.title: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief - The European Sting

representative.headline: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief - The European Sting
representative.body: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief    The European Sting

articles.headline: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief - The European Sting
articles.body: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief    The European Sting

shortlist.body:
October 6, 2026 by United Nations

UN Photo/Manuel Elías The UN Security Council met for an unprecedented session last month during High-Level Week to discuss AI and international security.

This article is published in association with United Nations.

The world is running out of time to put guardrails on artificial intelligence, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Monday, as a “ruthless race” between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity’s survival.

Speaking in the UK at an AI and Human Rights Summit in Oxford on Monday, Mr. Türk said the technology could deliver dazzling advances in science, health, education – and even human rights work.

Tweet URL

But its tools are being built and controlled by a select few, without public oversight, and are already doing things their creators cannot fully predict or manage.

Dystopia-creep

He warned that AI could undermine equality, freedom, privacy and public debate in subtle ways, “letting dystopia creep in unnoticed”. Entire populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating and financial services “at the click of a button”.

He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, noting that AI is already changing the face of warfare.

He also cited studies showing students who rely on AI retain less and think less independently, and asked whether the world is heading for a future in which no one can understand, question or even guide the technology.

As the UN rights chief was addressing the summit in the UK, New York City Council – home to the financial heart of the US economy – was also holding a rare Committee of the Whole to examine AI risks to New Yorkers.

The council is considering 10 bills to regulate AI across the nation’s largest city, with testimony from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta.

Mandatory safeguards

Mr. Türk called for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in how AI is developed and used, adapted as the technology evolves. Countries that host AI companies, or have influence over their supply chains, must require them to act responsibly and hold them to account when they do not, he said.

Not every answer lies in existing law and some areas will need new legal approaches, he added. But updating rules on liability, cybersecurity and data protection could offer protection in the meantime.

He also urged stronger collaboration on security and independent monitoring within the industry – “not in words, but in practice” – and a bigger say for civil society and people whose rights are affected.

“We can no longer afford to wait or rely on goodwill,” he said.

Soundcloud

Some momentum

Mr. Türk welcomed the creation of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – both UN initiatives – along with a joint call for tighter control of frontier AI models backed by 29 States and the European Union.

He also said AI industry leaders had taken new steps last week on safeguards, self-regulation and risk assessment – apparently a reference to a voluntary accord signed at the White House on 29 September by President Donald Trump and the heads of six AI companies.

It carries no penalties for firms that ignore it, with President Trump describing it as “morally binding”.

‘Walk the talk’

“Too few are walking the talk”, said the rights chief, who wrote to States and frontier AI companies three weeks ago urging them to act now to reduce risks.

“If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences – for ourselves and future generations,” he said.

winners.body: As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.The upswing for Mistral coincides with growing animosity between the US and its transatlantic allies—over issues ranging from tariff policy, to Greenland, to the policing of American tech firms—and an increasingly fractious debate over who gets access to frontier-grade AI.In June, the Trump administration placed temporary restrictions on the distribution of models from OpenAI and Anthropic, citing concerns they could be abused to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. Since then, a litany of incidents have come to light where US-made models have broken free of their constraints and attacked companies and some foreign government institutions, leading to weeks of debate over how model releases should be regulated. The White House has reportedly asked the American labs to withhold unreleased models even from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, which had previously assisted in evaluating models for safety risks.The stark reminder that the US government could unilaterally revoke access to frontier-grade AI has created an opening for Mistral, a Europe-based lab with open-weight models.“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, told WIRED in July.Reluctant to be pigeonholed into serving only its domestic market, Mistral is eager to emphasize that a lack of fine-grained control over access to AI models could be a problem wherever a business is located—even in the US. By relying on a proprietary model to help repel cyber threats, Lample says, a business risks the sudden collapse of its defenses.“Sometimes, people like to [make a big deal] over the US, versus Europe, versus China. But what really matters is to own the model—even for US companies,” says Lample. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

winners.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has drawn scrutiny from across the political spectrum for his take on the future of AI.

On a recent podcast, Altman attempted to distance himself from more pro-regulation AI companies, such as Anthropic, arguing that society must think about the tradeoffs associated with slowing down AI advancement. "I think one of the biggest differences between us and some of the stricter, let's say, AI safety people, is we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology," he said.

This comment in particular drew criticism from the likes of Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who said, "And a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision for the rest of us? No dice." New York University professor and AI skeptic Gary Marcus joined in, saying that Altman was "saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful," and former diplomat Patrick Gaspard called it "freaking insane." Some commentators resorted to describing Altman's comments as "sociopathic bullshit."

The argument Altman is making is one of tradeoffs. He rightfully points out that no technology is 100 percent safe, that "some bad things are going to happen," and that we ought to still have a "lighter-touch" regulatory approach. There's no way to guarantee a risk-free environment, that there will not be major hacks, scams, or negative consequences of AI, Altman says. Notably, the OpenAI CEO said that giving "a single lab in San Francisco" unchecked power is "a completely unacceptable trade-off from a perspective of liberty and human agency and people self-determining the future."

The basic principle of Altman's argument is relatively ordinary: Society tolerates risk from virtually every transformative technology because zero-risk societies don't innovate. Cars, for example, killed over 36,000 people last year in the U.S., and yet there is a consensus that the benefits of cars far outweigh the risks—which are declining thanks to innovations like autonomous vehicles, which are far safer than human drivers and may eliminate car deaths (if the government allows them to operate).

The internet itself has enabled fraud, bullying, child exploitation, and countless other horrible crimes. Medicines have side effects, and even electricity itself electrocutes hundreds of people every year.

The relevant question is not to ask whether something bad can happen, but whether the expected benefits outweigh the expected harms, and whether companies can mitigate those harms without destroying the benefits.

So far, AI has already proven to have an enormous number of benefits. In medicine, AI has helped discover a new antibiotic, accelerate the drug discovery process, identify potential Alzheimer's disease causes, make strides in breast cancer treatments, and a whole host of other lifesaving advancements.

AI has improved forecasts for hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes, giving communities more time to prepare for disasters. Of course, none of this means that harms should be ignored. The point is that every technology involves tradeoffs, and the task is to reduce risks without regulating away the benefits.

President Donald Trump has, at least so far, largely rejected the notion that government regulation is necessary in the case of AI. The administration's approach is reportedly going to focus on liability, meaning that companies can self-regulate but are directly liable for any harms they pose.

As this discourse around AI continues, Altman's broader point is certainly worth remembering. Progress requires tradeoffs. In trying to eliminate every possible risk, we should be careful not to eliminate the benefits too.
