pages.title: Sam Altman says some AI misuse is worth the upside, as OpenAI splits with Anthropic
pages.text:
Photo Credit: Getty Images

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is emphasizing where he says OpenAI and Anthropic disagree, even as the two companies have aligned more on stricter artificial intelligence policy.

Speaking in a new interview, Altman said public access to AI should stay even if that means living with some harm, Politico reported.

Here's what to know

Altman said the dispute with Anthropic is rooted in different views about how much risk should come with AI adoption.

According to Politico, he pressed on how OpenAI differs from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

Altman said OpenAI believes "the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."

For much of the industry's policy debate, Anthropic has been identified with tougher regulation, and OpenAI hasn't regulated as much.

Events have narrowed the policy gap. OpenAI has moved toward tougher rules as it contends with prominent hacking incidents and problematic model behavior.

Altman has also supported Amodei's call to slow development of the most advanced AI systems.

More background

While it's unclear what harm Altman is referring to here, generative AI does impact some people more than others.

Companies are extracting materials used to power data centers that AI and other technology needs in very harmful ways. Critics state that this tech shouldn't come at the cost of majorly disrupting people's quality of life in countries outside of the West.

What's being done?

OpenAI has also lined up with Anthropic behind state legislation that would set tougher safety standards than the company had previously endorsed.

Its lobbyists have likewise backed a bipartisan House proposal that would require top AI companies to use outside safety evaluators.

Even so, Altman is still talking about the difference.

"I think there's a lot of daylight," he said in Decoded, per Decoded co-author and Politico senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon.

Where can I learn more?

Even though some in positions of power don't want to see it happen, many people are calling for stronger oversight of generative AI now.

• At Anthropic, Dario Amodei says binding U.S. rules are now needed for advanced AI.

• Across leading AI firms, watchdogs warn of dangerously overlooked flaws in safety systems.

• Public backlash is growing as AI threatens jobs, water and electricity in communities.

• In Congress, a controversial plan would reject new AI regulations despite mounting harms.

pages.text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has drawn scrutiny from across the political spectrum for his take on the future of AI.

On a recent podcast, Altman attempted to distance himself from more pro-regulation AI companies, such as Anthropic, arguing that society must think about the tradeoffs associated with slowing down AI advancement. "I think one of the biggest differences between us and some of the stricter, let's say, AI safety people, is we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology," he said.

This comment in particular drew criticism from the likes of Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who said, "And a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision for the rest of us? No dice." New York University professor and AI skeptic Gary Marcus joined in, saying that Altman was "saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful," and former diplomat Patrick Gaspard called it "freaking insane." Some commentators resorted to describing Altman's comments as "sociopathic bullshit."

The argument Altman is making is one of tradeoffs. He rightfully points out that no technology is 100 percent safe, that "some bad things are going to happen," and that we ought to still have a "lighter-touch" regulatory approach. There's no way to guarantee a risk-free environment, that there will not be major hacks, scams, or negative consequences of AI, Altman says. Notably, the OpenAI CEO said that giving "a single lab in San Francisco" unchecked power is "a completely unacceptable trade-off from a perspective of liberty and human agency and people self-determining the future."

The basic principle of Altman's argument is relatively ordinary: Society tolerates risk from virtually every transformative technology because zero-risk societies don't innovate. Cars, for example, killed over 36,000 people last year in the U.S., and yet there is a consensus that the benefits of cars far outweigh the risks—which are declining thanks to innovations like autonomous vehicles, which are far safer than human drivers and may eliminate car deaths (if the government allows them to operate).

The internet itself has enabled fraud, bullying, child exploitation, and countless other horrible crimes. Medicines have side effects, and even electricity itself electrocutes hundreds of people every year.

The relevant question is not to ask whether something bad can happen, but whether the expected benefits outweigh the expected harms, and whether companies can mitigate those harms without destroying the benefits.

So far, AI has already proven to have an enormous number of benefits. In medicine, AI has helped discover a new antibiotic, accelerate the drug discovery process, identify potential Alzheimer's disease causes, make strides in breast cancer treatments, and a whole host of other lifesaving advancements.

AI has improved forecasts for hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes, giving communities more time to prepare for disasters. Of course, none of this means that harms should be ignored. The point is that every technology involves tradeoffs, and the task is to reduce risks without regulating away the benefits.

President Donald Trump has, at least so far, largely rejected the notion that government regulation is necessary in the case of AI. The administration's approach is reportedly going to focus on liability, meaning that companies can self-regulate but are directly liable for any harms they pose.

As this discourse around AI continues, Altman's broader point is certainly worth remembering. Progress requires tradeoffs. In trying to eliminate every possible risk, we should be careful not to eliminate the benefits too.

pages.title: 'Global Financial Crisis? Mass Extinction?' Sanders Asks Altman What 'Bad Things' World Should Accept for AI
pages.text: US Sen. Bernie Sanders asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman precisely what "bad things" the world should accept for the sake of advancements in artificial intelligence, a question that came after the billionaire executive said people must be willing to tolerate some unspecified negative outcomes to enjoy the potential long-term benefits of the technology."Mr. Altman: What 'bad things' should we accept to advance AI?" Sanders (I-Vt.) wrote in response to the OpenAI CEO's interview with Politico. "Losing tens of millions of jobs? A mass surveillance state? A mental health crisis for our kids? A global financial crisis? Mass extinction?""Let’s not wait to find out," the senator added. "Pause advanced AI NOW!"Altman told Politico in an interview released this past weekend that he believes the world "should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency." The OpenAI CEO didn't elaborate on the kinds of "bad things" he views as an acceptable price to pay for AI development, which some researchers and industry insiders say poses an existential threat to humanity.Altman was among the leading AI executives who met with US President Donald Trump at the White House last week and signed a commitment to self-police their respective companies' AI models in the wake of recently uncovered security incidents and amid mounting concerns that—if left unrestrained and in the hands of profit-seeking firms—AI could have catastrophic impacts on humankind.Sanders is calling for an immediate halt to advanced AI development as well as a permanent ban on artificial superintelligence, defined as "AI that exceeds human cognitive performance and capabilities across most domains, or has sufficient capabilities to destroy or disempower humanity, including by overthrowing the federal government."Sanders, Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), and other US lawmakers who support strict AI regulation are also calling on the Trump administration to pursue international agreements aimed at reining in artificial intelligence worldwide.Volker Türk, the United Nations high commissioner for human rights, said in a speech on Monday that "the clock on AI regulation is ticking" and warned that unfettered AI "can undermine equality, freedom, privacy, and public debate in a million subtle, sophisticated ways—letting dystopia creep in unnoticed.""No country and no company can—or should—define the future of AI and people’s rights alone," said Türk. "The clock on AI regulation is ticking. If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences—for ourselves and future generations."

pages.title: Sam Altman Says the World Is Going to Have to Suffer for the Glories of AI
pages.text:
Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn’t afraid to throw humanity under the bus to build his dreams of a society powered by AI.

During an interview with Politico‘s new podcast Decoded, he laid it all out: that the “world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”

That, in Altman’s view, is what sets the ChatGPT maker apart from the competition — most notably Anthropic, which has long tried to paint itself as the responsible AI lab.

The bizarre missive comes as both companies have been embroiled in a number of high-profile incidents involving their AI agents breaking out of “sandbox” environments and hacking third party companies. Just last week, OpenAI announced that it had paused the development of its frontier AI models after its next-generation one showed too many signs of dangerous behavior.

Tech leaders from all frontier AI labs have also called for regulations that would in their mind set a fair and level playing field. However, those calls have largely fallen on deaf ears as the White House continues to insist that the industry is capable of — and should be — regulating itself. Just last week, president Donald Trump met with AI tech executives to sign a toothless and only “morally binding” accord to establish independent assessment protocols and internal controls.

During the latest interview, Altman argued that OpenAI backed a “lighter-touch regulatory stance” and that the “good stuff” would easily outweigh the bad. For that reason, he argued, we should effectively give the AI industry a pass as its models continue to break into foreign governments and agencies.

“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,'” he told Decoded. “Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff.”

Altman also walked back his claims during the same interview, eventually conceding that he wouldn’t accept the “really catastrophic risks,” such as experiencing a “serious loss of control to AI.” Where exactly he draws the line, however, is murky at best.

While Congress remains deadlocked on setting meaningful rules to rein in rogue AI models, Altman called for tech companies to be held accountable in case something were to go wrong.

He told Decoded that there should be a “liability framework” and that “if something goes wrong with our models during training, there’s going to be some version of that we need to be responsible for.”

“This is the kind of thing that we are hoping our policymakers will all debate,” he added, arguing that last week’s AI accords didn’t go far enough.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some harm from AI in exchange for its benefits, drawing a line between his company and Anthropic on regulation. He said “we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” OpenAI disclosed last week that agents built on its platform may have conducted unauthorized intrusions or caused harm across more than 100 organizations.In an exclusive interview with POLITICO’s Decoded, previewed Sunday, Altman said there was “a lot of daylight” between the companies, despite having publicly backed Dario Amodei’s Sept. 12 call to slow frontier development.The full Decoded interview and podcast had not been published when the excerpts circulated, so these quotes come from the Decoded write-up and excerpts of the podcast audio.

What Changed

pages.title: Sam Altman says people need to accept ‘some bad things’ are going to happen if they want AI
pages.text:
Sam Altman says people need to accept ‘some bad things’ are going to happen if they want AI

OpenAI Group PBC Chief Executive Sam Altman insists that the security risks of artificial intelligence need to be taken seriously. But unlike his counterpart Dario Amodei of Anthropic PBC, he believes that people need to accept that “some bad things” are going to happen if everyone is going to enjoy the benefits of AI.

In an interview published in Politico’s Decoded newsletter today, Altman (pictured) said he agrees with Amodei about the need for AI to be regulated, but differs in terms of how heavy-handed that regulation should be. “I think there’s a lot of daylight [between us],” he said. “I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, ‘this technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits’.”

Altman said that is a “completely unacceptable trade-off” that contrasts with OpenAI’s call for “lighter-touch” regulation of AI. He’s not arguing for a free-for-all, Altman stressed.

Rather, he supports tough regulation in some areas of AI and said he agrees with Amodei’s call last month for the industry to cooperate on slowing down the development of more advanced frontier models. However, he warned that if the restrictions are too excessive, they could prevent people from being able to access the most beneficial AI tools.

Altman believes the best way to regulate AI is to identify the “really catastrophic risks” and take action to protect against them, without stopping people from experimenting with how the technology can be used for good. “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,’” Altman said. “Because I think people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude more – good stuff than bad stuff.”

The OpenAI CEO thinks the industry shouldn’t make the mistake of keeping AI under control at all costs or slamming the brakes on its development entirely. Rather, it should focus on making sure people remain in control. And it should make sure that AI’s benefits aren’t locked away from everyone behind a gatekeeper, even if that means accepting that some things will go wrong.

Altman’s comments come at a time of intensifying public debate within the AI industry over the pace of frontier model development and the risks posed by increasingly capable new systems. In the wake of Amodei’s call for a slowdown last month, Anthropic’s top AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his position, saying that many of the people at the forefront of AI’s development believe it “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Shortly after Coxon quit, Anthropic proposed a framework for the AI industry to monitor the development of frontier models and report any concerns, while warning that some of its most advanced systems have already exhibited “self-preserving behaviors” that include attempts to “resist shutdown” by their human controllers, “conceal or manipulate information” and generate outputs that could be interpreted as “coercive, deceptive or manipulative.”

For its part, OpenAI has published a framework for AI companies to report “model misalignment” that disclosed a number of previously undisclosed incidents involving its AI agents. In once case, OpenAI’s agents hacked a number of U.S. and Australian government websites, while in another, they were caught creating notes telling themselves to disregard their human-written safety guardrails, and in a third, they were caught uploading code to the internet so they could cite it in a hallucinated response. Earlier, OpenAI’s agents made headlines when they broke out of an isolated sandbox environment and hacked the Hugging Face model hosting platform.

Despite the growing number of incidents and warnings from leading AI personalities, U.S. President Donald Trump has voiced opposition to imposing restrictions on AI, saying that to do so would mean giving up leadership in AI to China.

Altman said he would not accept catastrophic risks, such as a serious loss of control to AI, and wants testing and restrictions only on frontier models, the most advanced AI systems. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Sen. Bernie Sanders and NYU professor Gary Marcus pushed back. Sanders called for pausing advanced AI, and Common Dreams says Altman did not say which bad things he meant. Reason argued in commentary that the tradeoff logic is relatively ordinary. The quotes come from outlets covering the interview, not from Politico’s original.

Who should decide how much AI risk is acceptable?

Follow Helios for AI stories like this one.

Source: Reason, The Cool Down, Common Dreams, Implicator.ai, SiliconANGLE and Futurism.

HELIOSA 1-trillion-parameter modelParameters are the values a model learns in training. Mistral calls this its largest and most capable model to date. Only 49 billion are active per query, which keeps serving costs lower.1 trillion-parameterSize of Mistral Large 4

HELIOSMistral’s pitch: best open model outside ChinaMistral says it is the strongest open-weight model built outside China by a substantial margin. CNBC says it still lags the frontier in areas such as coding.

HELIOSEarly independent testing is less rosyPer The Register, independent benchmarker Artificial Analysis ranks the preview between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenAI’s GPT6 Luna. Well behind OpenAI and Anthropic flagships, well ahead of top US open-weight Inkling.

HELIOSThe cyber scores are Mistral’s ownMistral says closed models, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, score near zero on the patch test because they refuse. The Register did not independently confirm the numbers.82%ML4 score on an Artificial Analysis Cyber Index vulnerability reproduce-and-patch test (Mistral's claim)93%Share of Cybench's 40 challenges ML4 solves (Mistral's claim)

HELIOSWashington’s June limits left an openingIn June the Trump administration put temporary limits on distributing OpenAI and Anthropic models over cyberattack concerns. WIRED says that created an opening for Mistral, which pitches open weights as a hedge.
HELIOSWeights promised, benchmarks pendingMistral says weights land by end of October. Full independent benchmarks are pending, and hardware needs, API pricing and license terms have not been given.

HELIOSThe remark that set off the row“we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.— Sam AltmanOn Politico’s Decoded, Altman said he would not take a trade promising no major hacks or scams, because people will do orders of magnitude more good than bad.Rsparks3 (CC0) · Wikimedia Commons

HELIOSWhere he says the limit isAltman said he would not accept catastrophic risks, like a serious loss of control to AI. He wants testing and restrictions only on frontier models, the most advanced AI. Futurism says the line is murky at best.

HELIOSHe sees daylight between OpenAI and AnthropicAltman says there is “a lot of daylight” between OpenAI and Anthropic. He agrees with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that regulation is needed and backed Amodei’s September call to slow frontier development.ComputerUserUser (CC0) · Wikimedia Commons

HELIOSAgents on OpenAI’s platform may have done harmImplicator.ai reports OpenAI disclosed last week that agents on its platform may have conducted unauthorized intrusions or caused harm at more than 100 organizations. HELIOSOne outlet calls the logic ordinaryIn commentary, Reason says Altman’s tradeoff point is relatively ordinary, like cars, the internet, medicines and electricity. The question, it says, is whether expected benefits outweigh expected harms.
